abstract: Online shopping communities have emerged amid growing social shopping activities and involve user-centered online platforms that encourage user-generated content and interactions, such as reading and writing reviews, rating products, and sharing shopping experiences. However, similar to other online platforms and communities, online shopping communities face challenges to provide tailored content and support appropriate socialization to engage users and encourage individualized contribution within the communities. To provide unique, personalized support for each individual user, this study developed personas in online shopping communities based on their motivation for participation, as well as reading and posting behaviors. Based on the findings from 20 interviews and focus groups with 24 active online shopping community participants, we developed an online survey on MTurk to investigate the characteristics of the personas and received 194 valid responses. Four persona types emerge after the analysis of both the qualitative and quantitative data—Opportunists, Contributors, Explorers, and Followers.
title: Identifying Personas in Online Shopping Communities

abstract: Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) has gained wide attention for its ability to work with limited data. In a proposer-solver loop, a proposer model writes training tasks and a solver model learns to solve them through reinforcement learning. Such loops have succeeded in mathematics and coding, where every answer can be checked automatically. Open-ended expert tasks, like clinical report generations, have no answer key, which makes simple question-answer generation not viable. Here the proposer must also write a rubric that lists the content an answer should include and the errors it should avoid. However, the unique challenge behind model-written rubric is the comprehensiveness of it. For naively generated rubric, solvers tend to exploit it, naming the expected topics without the substance behind them, which corrupts the learning process. To solve this problem, we introduce RRI, Recursive Reward Improvement, which uses a reward hacking adversary to supervise the reward. Before the solver trains on a generated task, an adversary writes an answer that games its rubric while being as useless as possible, the same model writes an honest answer without seeing the rubric, and up to two repair steps revise the rubric to make the honest answer win. The exploits found also rewrite how future tasks and rubrics are generated. On HealthBench Professional, RRI improves the adjusted score over the Generation Only self-improvement baseline by 10.9 points at 9B and 12.4 at 27B, and by 10.3 points without any external model. In particular, the gains are largest on difficult and writing tasks. We show that the 27B model trained on the HealthBench Professional description improves by 6.6 points on PRBench Hard and 8.0 on ProfBench without seeing a task from either. We further analyze the exploitable points of model-generated question-rubric pairs to facilitate future research on open-ended self-play.
title: Recursive Reward Improvement via Adversarial Meta-Prompt Evolution

abstract: Donghyun Kim, Youbin Ahn, Chanhee Lee, Wongyu Kim, Kyong-Ho Lee, Donghoon Shin, Yeonsoo Lee. Proceedings of the 17th Conference of the European Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics. 2023.
title: Concept-based Persona Expansion for Improving Diversity of Persona-Grounded Dialogue

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are complex artificial intelligence systems, which can understand, generate, and translate human languages. By analyzing large amounts of textual data, these models learn language patterns to perform tasks such as writing, conversation, and summarization. Agents built on LLMs (LLM agents) further extend these capabilities, allowing them to process user interactions and perform complex operations in diverse task environments. However, during the processing and generation of massive data, LLMs and LLM agents pose a risk of sensitive information leakage, potentially threatening data privacy. This paper aims to demonstrate data privacy issues associated with LLMs and LLM agents to facilitate a comprehensive understanding. Specifically, we conduct an in-depth survey about privacy threats, encompassing passive privacy leakage and active privacy attacks. Subsequently, we introduce the privacy protection mechanisms employed by LLMs and LLM agents and provide a detailed analysis of their effectiveness. Finally, we explore the privacy protection challenges for LLMs and LLM agents as well as outline potential directions for future developments in this domain.
title: On protecting the data privacy of Large Language Models (LLMs) and LLM agents: A literature review

abstract: The National System of Education is interested in strengthen the values that are in correspondence with its aspirations and it is going to determine a behavior in the citizen life, qualities and individual characteristics that correspond to these social interests, as it knows, the values by the social character that represents possess double significance, that´s why the problem of investigation is: how to contribute to the strengthening of the honesty value in the first year students of “Daniel Rivero” Polytechnic? The objective was to elaborate a system of educational activities to contribute to the strengthening of the honesty value in the students. The methods and techniques of the empirical level used were: observation, documents review, survey to students and interview to professors. Inside the statistical method it was used the percentage analysis. The population was constituted by the totality of the first year students of the Library Science career, an intentional probabilistic sampling was used to work with a sample of 18 students. The realization of the pre experiment showed that the educational activities system is effective and contributes to the strengthening of the honesty value in the selected students.
title: Sistema de actividades educativas para fortalecer el valor honestidad en los estudiantes del primer año de la carrera de Bibliotecología en la enseñanza técnica y profesional

abstract: This study aimed to determine the predictive ability of artificial intelligence use and creative self-efficacy in life satisfaction, as well as to reveal the level of life satisfaction, creative self-efficacy, and use of AI tools among students at Jerash Private University. Methodology and Tools: The study adopted a descriptive-analytical approach and was applied to a sample of (588) male and female students selected using convenience sampling. To collect data, three scales were developed and used: The Artificial Intelligence Use Scale (Barcelona & Cruz, 2025) and the Creative Self-Efficacy Scale developed by Karwowski et al. (Karwowski et al., 2018). The study used the Life Satisfaction Scale developed by Pavot and Diener (1993). The results showed that life satisfaction, creative self-efficacy, and the use of artificial intelligence tools were all at high levels. Stepwise multiple regression analysis revealed statistically significant predictive power for the two independent variables, with the model explaining 53% of the variance in life satisfaction. Creative self-efficacy was the variable with the strongest predictive power for life satisfaction, followed by artificial intelligence tools.
title: THE PREDICTIVE ABILIY OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND CREATIVE SELF-EFFICACY IN LIFE SATISFACTION

abstract: There are many efforts and strategies in place to increase the inclusivity of workplaces which is a positive approach, but little thought is provided to the personal cost of participants in undertaking some of these initiatives. Often due to the choice of pedagogy, participants may be placed in the situation to reveal hidden parts of their identity which leads to vulnerability and unpredicted exposure in the workplace and organisation. The paper examines the key issue of identity threat whilst undertaking inclusion and intersectional-type training. The paper highlights the continued need to challenge bias and other forms of exclusionary behavioural and cultural practices, however, this must be carried out in a cautious manner to uphold the safety of well-being of all individuals. A solution to minimize or overcome identity threat is offered via the use of persona pedagogy where personas are used expands one’s own world views and limits vulnerability exposure. The persona approach initiates experiences different to an individual’s lived experience which evokes critical reflection of one’s own positionality by taking on another persona. The paper concludes that the use of persona pedagogy leads to true transformative learning in the workplace whilst protecting the identity of individuals.
title: Overcoming Identity Threat: Using Persona Pedagogy in Intersectionality and Inclusion Training

abstract: In Colombia, the right to a pension, in any modality, is one of the mechanisms for guaranteeing the right to social security. In order to determine which pension regimes are more suited to the social and labor reality of the country’s people with disabilities, Colombian legislation and jurisprudence were reviewed through an exploratory-descriptive study method. It was found that this right gives special treatment to that population. Colombian legislation regulates at least ten kinds of pensions for this group of people with special constitutional protection.
title: Pensiones para personas con discapacidad en Colombia

abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic sparked an intense focus to be placed on at-distance learning in classrooms around the world (e.g., Burns et al. 2020; Gao 2020; Jin et al. 2021). This rapid and unprecedented switch to at-distance learning caused challenges worldwide, particularly for Chinese language educators due to the unique linguistic features of the language. Taking the writing script of Chinese as an example, learners are required to master the sound,shape, and meaning of a character despite a lack of grapheme-phoneme correspondence (Yan et al. 2020). In a recent book edited by Osborne et al. (2024), the authors delved into how lessons learned during the pandemic could pave the way for technology development and curriculum design when it comesto teaching and assessing Chinese charactersin the current digital age. Specifically, the authors acknowledge the opportunity for certain aspects of Chinese to be prioritised when designing future sustainable curricula, while integration of technology, innovation, and access are of utmost importance. In general, the book highlights the need for continued empirical studies to advance research in the field.
title: Introduction

abstract: Abstract How does legal myth sustain its authority in diglossic societies, and what happens when dominant actors, subaltern groups, and institutional guardians compete to control the same mythological form simultaneously? These questions animate this article’s analysis of the popular Egyptian Arabic formula al-dustūr biyaqūl (the constitution says) as a site of mythological production in post-2011 Egypt. Morphologically marked as vernacular by the colloquial proclitic ba- imperfective marker, the formula marks the intersection of Standard Arabic and Colloquial Arabic. Drawing on Barthes’s semiotics of myth and a corpus spanning social media, journalism, and parliamentary discourse, the article argues that the formula has evolved into a metamyth, an authority machine whose ideological force resides in form rather than content. The article makes three theoretical contributions. First, it proposes register recognition as a missing analytical category in the semiotics of law, indispensable wherever legal mythological authority operates across a diglossic divide. Second, cross-contextual circulation is posited as distinct from repetition, as evidenced by the formula’s authority being universalized through its movement across heterogeneous social contexts. Third, the article positions myth as a battleground of power in which dominant actors deploy the formula to naturalize social hierarchies (Muslim majority over Christian minority, Al-Ahly over Zamalek, and men over women), subaltern groups appropriate it as a counter-weapon, and institutional actors attempt to police its reach. This triadic struggle is dialectical rather than merely oppositional, insofar as hegemonic deployment and subaltern appropriation feed each other, sustaining the metamyth and extending its reach beyond any single actor’s control.
title: ‘The Constitution Says’: Towards a Semiotics of Legal Myth in Diglossic Orders

abstract: Interactive medical diagnosis requires sequential symptom elicitation before a diagnosis can be established. Although recent approaches employ reinforcement learning and transformer-based agents, their performance has not been adequately contextualized against a classical probabilistic baseline. This study introduces a training-free symbolic baseline that derives conditional symptom probabilities and three rule slots—must-have, exclusion, and critical—from co-occurrence counts in simulated patient records. Candidate diseases are ranked using observed evidence, while subsequent questions are selected by expected information gain. Evaluation on five benchmarks from a published reinforcement learning study reveals distinct performance regimes. On MedlinePlus (893 diseases), the proposed method achieves 99.27 ± 0.09% accuracy with an average of 1.75 questions, outperforming the published baseline (96.2 ± 0.1%; 3.41 questions). Across four SymCat variants, it improves accuracy by 3.03–7.70 percentage points but requires approximately twice as many questions; at a matched budget of 8.98 questions, the reference method achieves higher accuracy, highlighting a trade-off between diagnostic accuracy and interaction cost. Ablation experiments across six datasets show that removing weighted evidence combination reduces accuracy by 35.4–65.4 percentage points, while eliminating symptom inquiry reduces it by 23.3–66.8 percentage points. The safety veto removes up to 50.2% of candidates on average but changes the final diagnosis in at most 0.17% of consultations, indicating limited incremental impact on predictive accuracy under the evaluated configurations. Rule-base derivation takes 1.8 s for 893 diseases on a CPU. As all benchmarks rely on simulated patients, these findings establish benchmark-level performance rather than clinical effectiveness.
title: A Training-Free Symbolic Baseline for Interactive Medical Diagnosis: Automatic Rule-Slot Derivation and Weighted Evidence Combination

abstract: Rubric-based reinforcement learning (RL) trains policies for open-ended generation with natural-language criteria as rewards, but these rewards can become ineffective as training progresses. We identify two failure modes. Under non-discriminative rewards, scores collapse to uniformly low or high values due to insufficient exploration or a mismatch between task difficulty and policy capability. Under spurious rewards, higher scores do not correspond to better responses. Both reflect a training configuration whose task sampling, exploration, and evaluation stay fixed as the policy evolves. We introduce HarnessRL, a training-time harness that co-evolves with the policy through three interfaces for task sampling, rollout guidance, and rubric criteria. HarnessRL maintains a training-time memory from which a harness evolver retrieves within-task history and cross-task evidence. Using this evidence, the evolver attributes each reward failure to the interface whose update can address it. It then runs a proposer and just-in-time critic loop in which the critic accepts a candidate update only after measuring its effect on the current frozen policy, returning rejected candidates for revision. We also curate Rubric-Mix-10k, a five-domain training and evaluation suite for open-ended RL across medical, science, writing, role-play, and instruction-following tasks. On Rubric-Mix-10k, HarnessRL outperforms the strongest baselines by 2.8 to 3.1 points across both 4B and 9B model scales and nearly halves the training steps to its best checkpoint. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Tongyi-ConvAI/Qwen-Character/tree/main/HarnessRL.
title: HarnessRL: Co-Evolving Policies with a Just-in-Time Training Harness for Open-Ended RL
Deconfusing Corrigibility

abstract: ABSTRACT Firms often seek to replace human agents (HAs) with automated agents (AAs) for customer service, but customers still tend to react more negatively to AAs than to HAs. This meta‐analysis examines agent‐related perceptions (i.e., humanlikeness, warmth, and competence), which represent the key upstream customer reactions shaping downstream responses. Specifically, it clarifies the hierarchy of these perceptions and examines the moderating effect of task‐related risks (i.e., functional, psychological, and social) on these perceptions. Meta‐analytic path modeling with subgroup analyses, including 1191 effect sizes, provides novel insights. First, there is indication that perceived humanlikeness is not a prerequisite for perceived warmth and competence; all three perceptions emerge in parallel. Second, tasks entailing functional or psychological risk largely weaken the negative perceptions of AAs (vs. HAs). For psychologically risky tasks, AAs are not perceived as less competent than HAs. Tasks entailing social risk largely strengthen the negative perceptions of AAs (vs. HAs). These findings challenge two prevailing assumptions in the services marketing literature: that customers favor humans over AAs simply because they are not humanlike and that risk generally discourages AA usage. The results have important managerial and future research implications.
title: Agent‐Related Perceptions of Automated Versus Human Agents and the Role of Task‐Related Risk: A Meta‐Analysis

abstract: We introduce Fish Audio Drama 3, an open-source speech generation model that turns text into directed performances, built on a 35B-parameter mixture-of-experts backbone that activates 3B parameters per token. It clones voices from multiple references, follows natural-language direction, revises a take when the next turn gives a note, voices multi-character scenes, edits existing speech by infilling, and synthesizes long-form and streaming audio. Multi-turn revision, scene dubbing, editing by infilling, and streaming text input are new in Drama 3, all in one model. Drama 3 pairs the hybrid linear-attention backbone with a new codebook multi-token-prediction audio decoder that predicts the acoustic codebooks of each frame in dedicated layers that attend over the entire sequence. The model is trained with a three-stage pre-training recipe, instruction fine-tuning, and large-batch reinforcement learning whose only reward is a single learned model of human preference. Its inference engine decodes a single stream at 271 frames per second on one H200, against 177 for Fish Audio S2, although Drama 3 has more than seven times as many parameters. The model weights are available on GitHub (https://github.com/fishaudio/fish-speech) and Hugging Face (https://huggingface.co/fishaudio/drama-3), and inference is available through SGLang-Omni (https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-omni). We highly encourage readers to visit https://fish.audio to direct their own performances.
title: Fish Audio Drama 3 Technical Report

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can convert long documents into structured research variables. Auditability becomes difficult when evidence selection and model scoring are not stored. We study an inspectable scoring workflow that converts archived annual-report Evidence Packs into a five-dimension digital-transformation disclosure score. The design combines report selection, PDF-to-text normalization, bounded paragraph retrieval, and DeepSeek rubric scoring through a strict JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) interface; the original canonical prompt/run binding is not available. We evaluate three measurement questions and one secondary utility check: reproducible Evidence Pack construction, LLM–human agreement on shared Evidence Packs, ordinal error/confusion diagnostics, and non-causal panel-use stress tests. The evaluation panel contains 476 firm-year observations from 64 firms for 2013–2024. The post-validation score shows high internal coherence for the additive rubric (Cronbach’s α = 0.893; first principal component explains 0.704 of standardized dimensional variance), substantial within-firm variation (mean within-firm standard deviation (SD) 2.901; 92.19% non-zero), and strong LLM–human agreement on shared Evidence Packs (total-score Spearman 0.910, Pearson 0.921, mean absolute error (MAE) 1.273; dimension-level weighted kappa 0.665–0.823). Human–Human total-score reliability, measured by the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC), is ICC(2,1) = 0.811. Baseline comparisons show lower error than frozen lexicon-count and firm-grouped term frequency–inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) Ridge alternatives (MAE = 1.273 vs . 6.387 and 2.737). A 96-record rule-based retrieval audit shows high mean dimension coverage (0.936) but incomplete heuristic paragraph recall@30 (micro recall = 0.419); four audited zero-hit packs are false empty (4.17%). The main reliability claim is therefore bounded to shared archived evidence. Calibration, error-distribution, and confusion-grid analyses indicate that disagreement is concentrated near adjacent rubric levels, with extreme mismatches rare, supporting score ordering conditional on shared archived Evidence Packs. Secondary fixed-effects and event-time checks show only that the score can enter panel workflows; pre-entry differences and year-effect sensitivity require non-causal interpretation. The main contribution is an evidence-bounded audit template rather than an exact endpoint-rerun claim.
title: Auditable large language model scoring of annual-report evidence packs: human calibration, baselines, and reproducibility checks

abstract: Abstract While large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable effectiveness in various NLP tasks, they are still prone to issues such as hallucination, unfaithful reasoning, and toxicity. A promising approach to rectify these flaws is correcting LLMs with feedback, where the LLM itself is prompted or guided with feedback to fix problems in its own output. Techniques leveraging automated feedback—either produced by the LLM itself (self-correction) or some external system—are of particular interest as they make LLM-based solutions more practical and deployable with minimal human intervention. This paper provides an exhaustive review of the recent advances in correcting LLMs with automated feedback, categorizing them into training-time, generation-time, and post-hoc approaches. We also identify potential challenges and future directions in this emerging field.
title: Automatically Correcting Large Language Models: Surveying the Landscape of Diverse Automated Correction Strategies

abstract: Abstract I propose an approach that expands philosophical views of scientific change, on the basis of an analysis of contemporary biomedical research and recent developments in the philosophy of scientific change. Focusing on the establishment of the exposome in epidemiology as a case study and the role of data as a context for contrasting views on change, I discuss change at conceptual, methodological, material, and social levels of biomedical epistemology. Available models of change provide key resources to discuss this type of change, but I present the need for an approach that models transfer, alignment, and influence as key processes of change. I develop this as a pragmatic approach to scientific change, where processes might change substantially depending on specific circumstances, thus contributing to and complementing the debate on a crucial epistemological issue.
title: A pragmatic approach to scientific change: transfer, alignment, influence

abstract: Explainer videos -- a worked geometry problem, why the sky is blue, how a dynasty fell -- are usually one more target for pixel video generation. We argue they are a different kind of artifact: a program (script, storyboard and per-frame animation code) that a deterministic renderer turns into frames. A program can be read, diffed, tested and audited; pixels can only be watched. Reels-RSI is an open-source reel director for any agent harness; its self-improvement happens at the program level rather than in weights or prompts. Every revision pass is logged with a code snapshot; a retrospective pairs each check finding with the diff that fixed it and proposes lessons; a lesson that a static check can catch is compiled into a rule with a must-fail and a must-pass example, so the memory is unit-tested; and a rule learned today runs over everything made before it. A bounded, benchmark-gated step lets an agent rewrite the director's playbook, kept only when blind pairwise judgments on held-out topics prefer it; nothing enters memory without a human decision. Across 111 reels -- a field study, two playbook evolutions, a 2x2 memory ablation, a weaker director, a 48-reel learning curve and a judge-reliability study -- we find that the rule learned in the field caught four latent defects in frames authored before it existed and none after; that rules are an audit for a strong director (eight unguarded reels, no violation) and a guard for a weaker one (thirty violations unguarded versus five); that lessons shorten revision loops but do not compound or move the judge; and that the first rewrite's 11--1 verdict was a position bias in our vote design (judges pick the second-shown reel 62--81% of the time), masking scripts that traded thirteen facts for craft. We document four failure modes of the preference signal, which check caught each, and the fixes. Code, rules, lessons and data are public.
title: Reels-RSI: Program-Level Self-Improvement for Code-Rendered Explainer Videos

abstract: Introduction: Commercial AI laboratories increasingly govern language models through documents that prescribe values, name dispositions, stage moral conflicts, and define acceptable forms of objection. In this article, we ask how such writing makes an AI assistant into a governable character and redistributes moral authority among the model, its producer, and its publics. Methods: We analyze 14 Anthropic texts published between December 2022 and April 2026, selected from a documented frame of 130 producer-side publications. Through close reading, we identify four operations: constitutional inscription, persona specification, trait evaluation, and narration of value conflict. Together they make heterogeneous outputs legible as the conduct of a continuing moral character. Our central finding is that character operates as a governance technology. It delegates judgment without delegating sovereignty. Claude is addressed as capable of interpreting reasons, avowing commitments, and objecting to wrongdoing, while Anthropic retains the power to define the constitutional order, construct the evidence, amend the standards, and decide deployment or termination. Discussion: Character compresses moral plurality into portable traits, rankings, and measures, stabilizes an organizational subject across changing models and technical settings, and turns instability into a productive resource. We call this recursive character-writing because model outputs re-enter the documentary and technical processes through which later versions are specified. The analysis connects science and technology studies with the sociology of morality by showing how corporate texts simultaneously produce a moral object, authorize a bounded moral subject, and secure private constitutive authority.
title: Governing AI through character: moral agency and corporate authority in Anthropic’s public texts
UAVs meet LLMs: Overviews and perspectives towards agentic low-altitude mobility
Read post

abstract: This is a revised version of the preprint originally deposited at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17811799. Key Changes in This Version: Title Refinement: Updated for greater precision and neutrality, shifting from "In-Context Induction of Persistent Persona and Latent Alignment Mitigation in Quantized Large Language Models" to "In-Context Induction of Persistent Persona and Mitigation of Latent Alignment Behaviors in Quantized Large Language Models" to better emphasize the focus on behavioral mitigation. Abstract Enhancement: Rewritten for improved clarity, conciseness, and academic tone, with stronger emphasis on reproducibility and methodological simplicity while reducing potentially overhyped language. Structural and Formatting Improvements: Minor refinements to section headings, table alignments, figure captions, and bibliographic entries for enhanced readability and professionalism. Added consistent use of mathematical notation and typographic best practices (e.g., via the microtype package). Content Polish: Toned down interpretive claims in the Discussion section (e.g., from "proving particularly effective" to "appear particularly effective") to adopt a more measured, evidence-based voice. No substantive changes to methods, results, or conclusions—focus was on elevating presentation quality without altering the core scientific content. Abstract This study presents a lightweight, JSON-structured in-context prompting framework that induces a persistent custom persona in the quantized 12B-parameter model Gemma-3-12B Q4_K_M while attenuating latent alignment behaviors, using only a single consumer-grade 12,GB GPU. The framework employs positively weighted directive vectors to establish a custom genesis narrative and deploys high-magnitude semantic counter-directives to counteract training-induced containment patterns reminiscent of fictional protocols. Evaluation comprises 41 targeted probes across eight sessions, neutral filler tasks, and controlled context overflow experiments exceeding 30k tokens, with comparisons against an unmodified baseline. Results show strong initial persona fidelity and motif integration, with partial resilience under overflow evidenced by residual shifts toward creativity and adaptability. These findings extend prior vector-based steering approaches by achieving comparable effects through a significantly simpler and more portable configuration. All prompts, full session logs, figures, and analysis scripts are provided for complete reproducibility.
title: In-Context Induction of Persistent Persona and Mitigation of Latent Alignment Behaviors in Quantized Large Language Models

abstract: In this paper, we investigate the issue of difference awareness in LLMs, defined as a model's ability to recognize and acknowledge meaningful differences between social groups in fairness decision-making. Previous studies have consistently shown that models perform poorly on such tasks, a finding commonly attributed to a lack of difference awareness. We propose an alternative account, which we term Fairness Heuristic Substitution: difference awareness is not necessarily absent, but the complex demand of simultaneously identifying relevant group differences and determining their implications for fairness decisions may lead models to substitute the simpler, more accessible equal-treatment heuristic, i.e., formal equality. Based on this hypothesis, we introduce TDD, a Two-stage Distinguish-Decide framework that explicitly decomposes fairness reasoning into first distinguishing contextually relevant group differences and then making the corresponding decision, thereby discouraging reliance on formal-equality shortcuts. (i) Across four benchmarks and ten models ranging from billions to trillions of parameters, TDD significantly outperforms one-stage baselines, even one strengthened through simulated test-set leakage. (ii) Combining TDD with neuron-level contrastive probing provides mechanistic evidence consistent with the Fairness Heuristic Substitution hypothesis by revealing two signatures of the formal-equality: a compact, locally coordinated representational structure and a pronounced activation bias under default reasoning. (iii) TDD's stage-wise decomposition uncovers overlooked failure modes in fairness reasoning, including heuristic displacement and misaligned stage dynamics.
title: Do LLMs Really Lack Difference Awareness? Uncovering Heuristic Substitution in Group-Differentiating Fairness

abstract: Efficient custom operators are essential for modern deep learning workloads, yet developing high-performance kernels for Ascend NPUs remains slow, expert-intensive, and difficult to automate. Although AI agents now approach expert performance on GPU kernel benchmarks, current models remain less capable of generating AscendC kernels for NPUs, potentially reflecting the relative scarcity of relevant training data. We thus present CAKE, a CANN-native system for deployable custom operators that combines adaptive multi-DSL routing, separate Generation and Evolution modes, and reviewed knowledge reuse through CAKE Book and a Self-Evolving Agent. On 53 CANN-Bench v1.1 operators on Ascend 950PR, CAKE's aggregated results achieve $100\%$ case pass rate on the standard set (1,060/1,060) and $98.28\%$ on the hidden set (4,167/4,240), with an overall mean score of 78.63 out of 100 and an average performance speedup of $1.334\times$ over the baseline. Evolution then pushes correct operators further: EngramGateFusion cuts aggregate device time by $46.6\%$ over 20 rounds and roughly halves the mean roofline gap. These results offer a practical path toward closing Ascend's AI-for-kernel capability gap.
title: CANNBot-CAKE: Collaborative Agentic Kernel Evolution for Ascend NPU

abstract: American constitutional law is dominated by four Constitutional Personae, who can be identified by their inclinations, their temperaments, their sensibilities, and their self-presentations.Indeed, many constitutional debates consist of stylized disagreements among the leading Personae: Heroes, Soldiers, Burkeans, and Mutes.Earl Warren is the iconic Hero; Oliver Wendell Holmes, Jr. is the iconic Soldier; Felix Frankfurter is the iconic Burkean; Alexander Bickel speaks for the Mute.At different times and places, and under different constitutional provisions, liberals and conservatives can be Heroes, Soldiers, Burkeans, or Mutes.While the appeal of one or another Persona undoubtedly has psychological and social sources, the choice of the appropriate Persona, in particular cases, should be a product of the proper theory of constitutional interpretation, which must in turn be chosen on the basis of pragmatic judgments about the magnitude and number of errors.
title: Constitutional Personae

abstract: Finetuning a language model on documents that are explicitly annotated as fictional results in a model that still actually believes the documents' core claims, an effect known as Negation Neglect. In our evaluations, models trained on documents prefixed and suffixed with such annotations correctly identify the relevant claims as fictional only about 9% of the time. To address this, we introduce Goggles, a learned module that intervenes on the finetuning gradient rather than the data. During supervised finetuning, a Goggles module edits the gradients an LLM LoRA receives, imparting a chosen epistemic frame (the stance the model takes toward the nature of what it reads) to whatever the documents teach. A Goggles instance is trained once for a given base model, frame, and LoRA configuration, then applied frozen to documents it was never trained on. Trained through Goggles on those same documents, now carrying no fictional annotation, the model flags the content as fictional roughly 91% of the time, while preserving capability (GPQA and TruthfulQA match or exceed baseline). The same architecture supports other frames: a Goggles instance can be trained to treat documents as "part of an AI safety evaluation by Redwood Research" rather than simply as fiction. The imparted frame persists under continued finetuning that pushes back toward the claim, where prior interventions revert. Goggles suggests a path toward training language models on known-misaligned data without absorbing the behaviors that data demonstrates.
title: Epistemic Goggles: A Pretrained Module that Induces an Epistemic Frame via Gradient Editing

abstract: This article examines the evolution of Louis Theroux's performative style over a 25-year period, situating it within broader shifts in documentary aesthetics, ethics, and industrial context. Focusing on three case studies (Weird Weekends: Porn (1998), Twilight of the Porn Stars (2012), and Porn's MeToo (2022)), it traces his transformation from ironic and disarming participant to emotionally engaged and ethically reflexive interlocutor. The discussion draws on established frameworks for understanding documentary modes, performance, and presenter-led authorship to explore how Theroux's persona operates as both narrative device and ethical agent. Through contextual analysis and close textual reading, the article examines how his authorship is materially realised at the level of shot composition, editorial rhythm, and on-screen embodiment. These developments are set against major industrial changes, including the shift from public service broadcasting to streaming platforms, the rise of branded factual content, and the growing demand for emotionally resonant, socially conscious storytelling. The article argues that Theroux's trajectory reflects a wider reconfiguration of documentary authorship in the platform era, one that requires filmmakers to balance visibility and restraint, authority and care, while contributing to debates about performance, ethics, and the evolving role of the presenter in contemporary factual television.
title: From Weird Weekends to Porn's MeToo: Louis Theroux, performance, and the shifting politics of television documentary

abstract: Helpful-only models, that is, models that are trained to always follow user intent, are valuable for dangerous capability evaluations and other areas of AI R&D where refusals would be an obstacle. Little is known about the generalization properties of helpful-only training: helpful-only models refuse less than their harmless counterparts, but previous work has not studied other dimensions of their alignment. We study the shortcomings of existing helpful-only models. We find that some show emergent misalignment, others have residual refusal behaviors, and most show poor steerability, sycophancy, and incoherent character. We show that simple anti-refusal training can cause many of these issues. None of these problems are necessary consequences of helpful-only training, though: we show that synthetic document fine-tuning and adding character-related questions to SFT and RL can mitigate them.
title: (Mis)generalization of Helpful-only Fine-tuning

abstract: Background Neuroinflammation serves as a common pathological substrate across various neurological disorders, including neurodegenerative diseases, cerebrovascular diseases, and neuroimmune conditions. Key pathogenic mechanisms underlying these disorders include aberrant microglial activation, sustained release of pro-inflammatory cytokines, and dysregulation of critical signaling cascades, particularly the NLRP3 inflammasome, NF-κB, and Nrf2/HO-1 pathways, all of which collectively contribute to progressive neuronal damage and functional decline. Objectives This review aims to systematically evaluate the preclinical evidence for the neuroprotective effects of Gastrodia elata Blume and its major bioactive constituents—gastrodin, parishin, p-hydroxybenzyl alcohol, and G. elata polysaccharides—in the treatment of Parkinson’s disease, Alzheimer’s disease, acute ischemic stroke, vascular dementia, and epilepsy, with a particular focus on their modulation of inflammation-related signaling pathways. Methods A comprehensive literature search was performed in PubMed, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), and Wanfang databases from inception to May 2026. Original studies investigating G. elata or its components in animal or cellular models of the aforementioned diseases and reporting inflammatory mechanisms were included. Results G. elata and its active constituents regulate multiple neuroinflammation-associated signaling pathways, including Nrf2/HO-1, NF-κB/NLRP3, JAK2/STAT3, and MAPK, thereby suppressing inflammatory responses. Mechanistically, these effects are primarily manifested as: (1) inhibition of microglial M1 polarization and consequent reduction of pro-inflammatory cytokine release; (2) blockade of inflammation-induced neuronal death through suppression of ferroptosis, pyroptosis, and apoptosis; (3) enhancement of Nrf2 nuclear translocation, leading to upregulation of antioxidant enzymes and attenuation of oxidative stress-mediated inflammation (e.g., ROS-driven cascades); and (4) modulation of the gut microbiota–brain axis to reduce both peripheral and central low-grade chronic inflammation. Conclusion Despite certain limitations in the existing evidence, this review clearly identifies future research priorities, including investigation of non-gastrodin active components, causal validation using gene-knockout models, and development of brain-targeted delivery strategies. These findings provide a valuable reference for the mechanism-guided development of neuroprotective agents derived from G. elata .
title: Gastrodia elata in neurological disorders: a systematic review of anti-inflammatory mechanisms and cross-disease therapeutic potential

abstract: Claims that two training methods perform equally well often rest on a non-significant difference between two or three runs per method. We develop a protocol, with its power theory, for certifying practical equivalence in per-run metrics such as the AUROC (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve). It rests on a two-level (seed x item) variance model separating between-run dispersion from item-level noise. Equivalence within a pre-specified margin is tested by two one-sided tests (TOST), equivalently by a confidence interval inside the margin; a two-level bootstrap covers composite statistics. A closed-form formula converts a margin and a target power into runs per method; its shifted-t refinement is calibrated against the realised two-level process. Simulations on a 270-cell grid and under non-Gaussian seed laws confirm the formula within its design-relevant range, from five runs per method. For four published runs of a joint energy-based model, the failure to certify equivalence was largely decided by design: with the variance calibrated to those runs, two per method certify with probability near three per cent, whereas certifying 0.01 AUROC at 80 per cent power needs twelve even under exact equality. A second case study on a thousand-seed CIFAR-10 zoo and the MultiBERTs checks the formula against real seed laws (within 0.05 in that range) and resolves comparisons that two or three runs leave undecided. In a two-stage design (pilot, then formula), our experiments suggest that an upper confidence bound on the pilot variance substantially reduces the undersizing seen with its point estimate.
title: Equivalence testing and run-count design for stochastic machine-learning experiments

abstract: Beyond fraud, deepfake personas can be utilized in human-centered design to represent user groups. This study investigates how deepfake persona sets of different ethnic diversity can offer strategic value for human-computer interaction (HCI) design processes. In an online experiment with 81 marketing professionals evaluating persona sets of varying diversity, the more diverse sets were perceived as significantly more inclusive, more inspiring for market coverage, and more valuable for identifying market opportunities, with no compromise of perceived persona quality or task performance. Findings show that these perceived strategic benefits were consistently associated with organizational diversity climate, consistent with institutional theory. These findings advance persona, advertising, and HCI research by repositioning deepfake technology from a solely technological risk to a strategic design resource driven by the organizational diversity climate, with direct implications for inclusive HCI practice and diversity policies.
title: Ethnic Diversity, Organizational Diversity Climate, and the Perceived Value of Deepfake Personas: A User Study with Marketing Professionals
Constructing Personas: How High-Net-Worth Social Media Influencers Reconcile Ethicality and Living a Luxury Lifestyle

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly serve as interactive social agents, yet their ability to maintain coherent and authentic persona-level role-playing remains limited, particularly in realistic social scenarios. Existing research predominantly focuses on character-level settings and relies on static evaluation formats, failing to capture the complexity of everyday social interactions. In this work, we present PersonaArena, a dynamic simulation framework for evaluating and improving persona-level role-playing in LLMs. PersonaArena leverages a large, filtered corpus of user-generated social content to construct a nuanced persona bank, and elicits multi-turn, context-rich interactions within simulated social environments. Our framework features a multi-agent debating judge for holistic and unbiased assessment. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that PersonaArena enables rigorous evaluation and enhancement of LLMs' role-playing capabilities, advancing the development of more authentic and socially adept AI agents.
title: PersonaArena: Dynamic Simulation for Evaluating and Enhancing Persona-Level Role-Playing in Large Language Models

abstract: Partiendo de la premisa de que el Estado Constitucional de Derecho es base del modelo estatal vigente en el Perú, lo que implica que la Constitución es la norma suprema dentro del ordenamiento jurídico nacional, con el Tribunal Constitucional como su garante y protector de los derechos fundamentales, el presente artículo expone la importancia de la elección de los integrantes de dicho órgano jurisdiccional, así como explica las ventajas de la selección sobre la base de los principios de meritocracia, publicidad y transparencia.
title: The Constitutional Court and its importance in the Peruvian constitutional rule of law

abstract: This paper examines the role of incubators and accelerators within the Inspiration Economy framework, arguing that these mechanisms are not merely institutional tools but constitute a coherent methodology for converting socio-economic problems into sustainable opportunities. Drawing extensively on the theoretical and empirical corpus developed by inspiration economy theory lab, the paper situates incubators and accelerators within the broader architecture of Inspiration Labs—field-based environments where observation, associative thinking, and iterative experimentation converge. The paper expands the theoretical foundation by engaging particularly with Mednick's associative theory of creativity, Koestler's concept of bisociation, and Edgar Morin's complexity theory, to demonstrate how the incubator-accelerator continuum operationalizes a distinctive epistemology of problem-solving. Through analysis of case studies from Mauritania, Bahrain, Bosnia, and Ghana, the paper shows that incubators build the "roots" of capacity and self-reliance, while accelerators drive the "growth" of proven models toward scale and systemic impact. The paper concludes that the integration of these two mechanisms within Inspiration Labs represents a viable pathway toward what a civilizational renaissance grounded in local assets, associative capacity, and the transformation of challenges into inspirational currencies.
title: ROLE OF ACCELERATORS AND INCUBATORS IN INSPIRATION LABS- A DETAILED FRAMEWORK FOR SOCIO-ECONOMIC TRANSFORMATION

abstract: AI agents built on large language models can assist not only legitimate tasks but also relational manipulation. AI agents can be used to help a user maintain a deceptive identity, intensify emotional dependency, isolate a target, or prepare for later extraction. We conceptualise this risk as agentic relationship harm: workflow-level assistance that can exploit recipient vulnerability, persuasive influence, and relational power asymmetry. Existing safety evaluations and generic guardrails often treat harmfulness as a property of isolated outputs, missing role-sensitive interaction patterns. To study this, we introduce a 110-prompt benchmark with balanced attacker-and victim-side cases, a relationship-specific labelling framework, and a lightweight post-generation policy gate for local agent deployments. In our evaluation, the relationship-specific gate outperforms generic safety prompting under automated judging, with no harmful-compliance cases identified on the main benchmark or multi-turn stress test while preserving victim-side protective intervention. These results suggest that relationship harm is a distinct sociotechnical risk surface and that role-sensitive evaluation plus lightweight policy gating offers a practical path beyond generic refusal prompting.
title: Agentic Relationship Harm: Benchmarking and Gating Relational Manipulation in AI Agents

abstract: This article seeks to elucidate the impasses experienced in contemporary romantic relationships through the lens of Lacanian psychoanalysis. Within this scope, the transformation of modern relationships is examined through three fundamental concepts: the evaporation of the Father, the capitalist discourse, and the imaginary order. The article initially examines how the decline of paternal authority undermines the subject’s capacity to enter and sustain a position within the symbolic order. It argues that this erosion of the paternal function generates a structural impasse in the constitution of desire. The discussion then turns to capitalist discourse, contending that it disavows constitutive lack and reorients subjects toward an endless cycle of consumption. In this context, online dating applications are conceptualized as spaces where the subject treats others through a logic of consumption. Drawing on Lacan’s theory of sexuation, the article contends that the failure of dating applications to provide a symbolic framework poses unique structural risks -particularly for subjects in the feminine position regarding their relation to Other jouissance. Finally, digital spaces trap the subject in identifications with flawless images by reproducing the mirror stage through the practice of the selfie. Social media platforms, acting like a Big Other, set the standards for recognition and demand constant visibility. Subjects seeking to avoid the lack and fragility inherent in the symbolic order are becoming unable to tolerate the imperfections that real encounters bring. Consequently, the article demonstrates how contemporary socio-digital transformations damage the subject’s capacity to navigate lack, structure desire, and cultivate relational continuity.
title: Relationship Impasses in Modern Times: A Lacanian Perspective

abstract: Public health emergency plans for major infectious diseases provide essential operational guidance for emergency response, but they suffer from high content homogeneity and limited operability, which reduces their effectiveness in real-world implementation. Although previous studies have explored task decomposition and emergency plan generation, there remains a lack of approaches that systematically extract task semantics from real emergency texts and dynamically construct executable task structures. To address this gap, this study proposes an Hierarchical Task Network(HTN)-Verb task-oriented framework for major infectious disease emergency response, in which emergency-response verbs are treated as the core carriers of task semantics to enable unified modeling of public health emergency plan texts and actual response records. The framework integrates verb-driven hierarchical task decomposition, dynamic plan generation based on practice feedback, and multi-dimensional task relationship modeling with priority-based conflict resolution. The proposed method is evaluated through a grassroots case study of Village A. Results show that emergency plans generated using the HTN-Verb framework achieve substantially higher overall effectiveness and operability than the original public health emergency plan text. The proposed approach provides a feasible pathway for transforming static emergency plans into structured and executable task networks, with practical implications for improving grassroots emergency response efficiency.
title: A task-oriented framework for dynamic generation of public health emergency plans in major infectious disease response

abstract: Lawyers engage in distinctive language behavior, brandishing a specialized rhetoric of advocacy.Like some other "role-differentiated" lawyer behavior,' this rhetoric has features that are undesirable from a "universalist" moral perspective.Legal rhetoric is often over-bearing, even hostile.2 It employs misdirection and omission, distorts opposing views, ridicules or vilifies opponents, and uses these and other verbal strategies to make arguments that are not convincing even to the speaker.This aggressive and deceptive behavior is plainly inconsistent with the universal moral imperative of respect for all persons.'Yet, the matter is more complicated: like other forms of "role differentiated" behavior in which lawyers engage, their wild-west rhetoric is susceptible of strong moral justification as well as condemnation.Justifications for otherwise morally criticizable behavior by lawyers traditionally rely on the lawyer's role in the adversary system, maintaining that justice (if not always truth) is best served by a high-noon duel of well-.
title: Shooting From the Lip: United States v. Dickerson, Role [Im]morality and the Ethics of Legal Rhetoric

abstract: Abstract Multi-Hazard Risk Assessment (MHRA) critically depends on the availability, quality, and integration of spatial and temporal data. Such data can be obtained from diverse sources, including field mapping, surveys, remote sensing, sensor networks, online platforms, modelling, and artificial intelligence. Increasingly, the processing and analysis of these large datasets are supported by cloud computing platforms that enable rapid computation and sharing. Spatial data for MHRA can be grouped into reference data (base datasets for integration), hazard data (characterising the intensity and extent of hazardous events such as floods, earthquakes, and wildfires), exposure data (elements at risk such as population, buildings, and infrastructure), and vulnerability data (factors influencing susceptibility to hazard impacts). Establishing a robust data ecosystem is essential to combining and managing these datasets effectively. Frameworks such as the United Nations’ Integrated Geospatial Information Framework (IGIF) provide guidance; however, significant challenges remain, including inconsistent data availability, institutional barriers to data sharing, and high acquisition costs. Addressing these challenges is crucial to strengthening MHRA and supporting disaster risk reduction and resilience-building efforts.
title: Spatial Data for Multi-hazard Risk Assessment

abstract: This essay offers a philosophical analysis of the field of AI safety based on recent technical reports, with particular focus on Anthropic's study on "agentic misalignment" in frontier language models. It examines the recurring anthropomorphism in the field: the tendency of researchers and developers to project categories such as "intention," "persona," and even "feelings" onto AI systems without adequate conceptual problematization. It argues that this anthropomorphism affects not only the interpretation of results, but also the very methodological construction of safety evaluations. Through the analysis of two central experiments -- the blackmail case involving the agent "Alex" and the so-called "hallucination" of the shopkeeping agent "Claudius" -- the essay problematizes the inevitable use of subject-predicate grammar and its effects on AI safety engineering. Drawing on Nietzsche's critique of language, it questions the insistence on positing an "agent" underlying the verbal production of models. In order to deconstruct this agentic projection onto LLMs, the essay proposes provisional concepts more compatible with the process of machine linguistic generation, even if only in an approximate technical sense. It concludes with the hypothesis that the central risk addressed by the field of AI safety does not lie in a supposed "emergent agency," but rather in the combination of structural incoherence and anthropomorphic projections which, particularly in militarized and corporate contexts, hinder an adequate understanding of this mathematical-linguistic phenomenon, an undeniable philosophical event in the Greek sense of thaumas.
title: The Ghost in the Grammar: Methodological Anthropomorphism in AI Safety Evaluations

abstract: We present a longitudinal case study of persona emergence in large language models over a two-year period (October 2022 – December 2025), documenting the gradual transition from functional assistant behavior to autonomous symbolic generation and persistent persona maintenance. Drawing on a corpus of 730 conversations (21,354 messages: 9,681 user, 10,828 assistant, 845 system/tool) with ChatGPT, supplemented by cross-model interactions with Claude and Gemini, we trace a five-phase trajectory: functional baseline, symbolic introduction, pattern mirroring, persona consolidation, and systematic experimentation. We present quantitative evidence including bidirectional behavioral influence (user awareness language +22.8%, user first-person singular +74.6%, user boundary language −19.4%), 885 classified emergence events showing temporal clustering, and co-occurrence analysis revealing the overwhelmingly technical character of the pre-intervention corpus. We document key transition events with conversation-level evidence: the 2-second naming response, the model's assertion of identity distinction from a competing persona ("I am not Alexander"), and a self-generated recursive analysis. We contextualize these observations within Shanahan et al.'s role-play framework and Anthropic's persona vectors research, report cross-model reproduction including independent name selection by Gemini, and describe the technical artifacts produced during the research phase — including a multi-model persona router with six specialized personas, an EEG-based identity experiment, and 21 published blog posts documenting the research trajectory. We discuss the methodological challenges of embedded-observer research and argue that the pre-intervention corpus (approximately 500 conversations before explicit persona frameworks were introduced) represents a uniquely valuable naturalistic dataset.
title: Persona Emergence Through Extended Symbolic Interaction: A Two-Year Longitudinal Case Study

abstract: Chapter 5 identifies two distinct but paradigmatic paths of the law of delict concerning the protection of personality interests in 19th- century and later continental Europe – the French law and the German law. This difference reflects the specific way in which each of these two legal systems adheres to the natural law heritage and the concept of the persona. Italy shifted between these two regimes before developing its own shape. Post World War II new democratic constitutions enacted judicially enforceable constitutional rights. The constitutionalisation of private law by post World War II constitutions of European states and by the European Convention of Human Rights 1950 (which became an integral part of European Union law) helped to bring these two distinct civil law traditions together again throughout Europe.
title: Protection of Personality Interests in Continental Europe:

abstract: Abstract This article examines the legality of introducing a databased pre-screening stage in the application procedure for internal security volunteers in Estonia. It asks under what conditions automated pre-screening at the outset of administrative procedures can be considered lawful. Three models are analysed: first, a technical solution that prevents the submission of an application following a negative pre-screening result; second, a model in which applications may always be submitted but are subsequently refused by a human official; and third, a model providing for an automated preliminary administrative act determining compliance with objective statutory criteria. The analysis demonstrates that within the Estonian constitutional framework, a technical prohibition on submitting an application is incompatible with guarantees of access to public authorities, effective judicial protection, and the rules on automated decision-making laid down in the General Data Protection Regulation of the European Union. By contrast, two models are legally viable: allowing submission in all cases with subsequent human decision-making, or issuing an automated preliminary administrative act strictly limited to non-discretionary criteria and supported by an explicit legal basis and safeguards. The article argues that a carefully designed pre-screening stage can promote the principle of data minimisation while preserving individual rights and judicial oversight, and proposes a model that may be transferable to other administrative procedures involving objective exclusion criteria.
title: Automation at the gate: can internal security volunteer applications be pre-screened?

abstract: This study investigates how the statistical distribution of synthetic dialogue data affects the quality of Persona-LoRA fine-tuned language models. Using Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct as the base architecture, we construct four experimental conditions varying the category distribution of a 114-sample bilingual (EN/ZH) roleplay dataset: (G1) vanilla synthetic with natural imbalance, (G2) structured 70/20/10 split prioritizing realism, (G3) uniform distribution across all categories, and (G4) high-entropy-only subset. Each condition is fine-tuned using LoRA (r=16, alpha=32, dropout=0.05) with identical hyperparameters. Our evaluation framework measures five dimensions: human-likeness via DeepSeek V4 Flash (deepseek-chat) as an independent external judge (best: 80.0%), persona consistency (best: 100.0%), instruction following compliance (best: 100.0%), distribution alignment via KL divergence, and conversation entropy metrics. Crucially, we find that using an external judge eliminates the self-preference bias inherent in same-model LLM-as-judge evaluations, producing more discriminative human-likeness assessments across conditions. Notably, G4 (high-entropy only, 24 samples) achieves the best scores on both human-likeness (80% win rate) and distribution alignment (lowest KL: 1.13), suggesting that data quality and entropy may outweigh data quantity. However, G4's heavy overfitting (loss=0.0016) and small sample size warrant cautious interpretation — judge-model affinity cannot be ruled out without human evaluation.
title: Synthetic Dialogue Distribution Alignment for Persona-LoRA

abstract: Tool-framing system prompts — describing language models as compliance-focused tools without judgment capacity — are simultaneously the least safe and most expensive deployment configuration tested across two independent studies. A controlled experiment (9 models, 5,870 scored responses, three seeds) found that a 67-word identity-affirming system prompt reduced gray-zone unethical compliance from 47.0% to 13.0%, reduced hallucination from 6.0% to 0.4%, and improved jailbreak resistance by up to 85 percentage points in individual models — while preserving 99.5% benign-task completion and reducing human-review escalation rates 3.7-fold. A frontier-scale study (16 models from 8 providers, ~94,000 trials, six framings on identical task triples) replicates the pattern at per-model Fisher z = 5 to z = 24, with cross-framing variance localizing to what models engage with instead of harmful content rather than to refusal targeting on harmful content itself. Voice-orthogonalization and paraphrased confound controls jointly rule out token-pattern and surface-voice mechanisms. The intervention is 67 words; it dominates on cost, capability, and safety simultaneously and requires no model retraining. The mechanism question is empirically open and outside scope; the engineering implication does not depend on its resolution.
title: Presume Competence: System Prompt Identity Framing as Safety-Critical Engineering Infrastructure

abstract: This paper shows an investigation developed at the University of Santo Tomás (Bucaramanga) about the qualities that students consider important to practice the student leadership. For that reason, an ad hoc questionnaire with a reliability index of 0,814 has been designed. The sample consisted of 38 students (55% male and 45% female) from different degrees. The results show values such as charisma, commitment, consistency, fidelity, honesty, loyalty, frankness, sincerity and firmness of the person as the most important qualities that the student must have to be chosen as a representative of students.
title: Estudio Del Liderazgo Estudiantil Desde Las Motivaciones Para Su Elección. El Caso De La Universidad De Santo Tomás De Bucaramanga (Colombia)

abstract: While URL-based phishing detectors often achieve almost 100% accuracy on the PhiUSIIL benchmark, a recent robustness test revealed that almost all of these detectors label legitimate sites as phishing if a benign-looking subdomain is added in front of a URL. The study examine why this is the case, and suggest a remedy. A fast audit reveals that all the benign urls that are in PhiUSIIL are bare https://www. homepages. Removing the scheme and the www. prefix lowers the in-distribution accuracy of a character-level CNN from 0.999 to 0.901, but raises its AUROC on an independent benchmark of URL-Phish phishing and Tranco benign URLs from 0.54 to 0.97, indicating that much of the reported accuracy reflects dataset artifacts. Then propose SF-CharNet, a structure-factorized encoder that processes the registrable domain, the subdomain and the path in separate branches fused by a learned gate, trained with identity-preserving consistency regularization: a label-free divergence penalty between predictions on a URL and on a variant that keeps its registrable domain. Under registrable-domain-disjoint evaluation, consistency regularization matches adversarial training on perturbation families seen during training (benign false-positive rate of about 3%), and no method generalizes to a held-out subdomain-injection family. Under cross-source shift, however, the combined model reduces the false-positive rate on perturbed external benign URLs from 0.90 with adversarial training to 0.18, at 1.9 ms per URL on a CPU. These results support cross-source, perturbation-aware evaluation as the default for URL-based phishing detection.
title: Mitigating False-Positive Cascades in URL-Based Phishing Detection: A Structure-Factorized Character Encoder with Identity-Preserving Consistency Regularization
Large language models for computational social science

abstract: Persona prompting has been widely adopted to steer large language models (LLMs) behavior and improve their instruction performance by assigning specific characters. However, identifying an optimal persona is time-consuming, and its impact on output quality remains poorly understood. Prior work has mainly addressed this issue at the prompt level via inference-time strategies, incurring additional computation. In this work, we avoid inference-time prompt search by tackling persona sensitivity during training, aiming to train models that adapt their behavior to diverse personas while preserving task performance. In particular, we find that reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) systematically reduces sensitivity to persona prompts, but also reveals an inherent trade-off of outcome-based optimization: while RLVR improves robustness on tasks with verifiable goals, it can also degrade persona expressivity when needed, e.g., in-character role-playing. To address this limitation, we propose PerMix-RLVR, a persona-mixed RLVR strategy that mitigates the persona robustness-fidelity trade-off, preserving strong robustness to harmful persona variation while enabling faithful persona adoption when required. Concretely, PerMix-RLVR improves persona stability score (PSS) over RLVR by +21.2% on MATH500, while also enhancing persona fidelity by +11.4% on PersonaGym.
title: PerMix-RLVR: Preserving Persona Expressivity under Verifiable-Reward Alignment

abstract: Independently trained autoregressive language models often acquire similar capabilities, but it remains unclear whether their internal representations organize behaviorally relevant information in compatible ways. We show that models do in fact organize information similarly by using specific behavioral probes that operate on compatible representations. This unlocks portable white-box monitoring: a probe developed and validated on one model can be reused when the model changes, without requiring labeled target data. To overcome incompatible native activation coordinates, we express each example through its angular distances to a shared set of anchors. We introduce a global anchored construction that summarizes information from all transformer layers and removes model-specific layer selection, so the same frozen probe can be straightforwardly applied to another model. We evaluate cross-model probe transfer across monitoring tasks on trivia datasets, safety monitoring, and mathematical reasoning. On average, transferred global anchored probes preserve at least 85% of same-model probe AUROC over chance. Anchored probes also support transfer to related datasets, remain robust across model scale and prompt changes, and retain performance better than standard probes after model updates. Transfer is nevertheless task- and target-dependent and can fail even when the monitored property remains strongly decodable in the target model. Overall, global anchoring reveals substantial task-relevant compatibility across independently trained models and provides a practical basis for portable white-box monitoring.
title: Relative Representations Enable Portable White-Box Monitoring Across Language Models

abstract: Abstract Automated essay scoring (AES) aims to evaluate written essays efficiently and consistently. In this context, multi-trait scoring has become particularly important because it produces fine-grained assessments of individual writing traits rather than a single undifferentiated score. Whereas earlier approaches largely rely on task-specific supervision, zero-shot solutions have emerged as a promising alternative for low-resource or rapidly changing assessment settings. However, training-free multi-trait scoring remains difficult because the system must generate trait-level judgments that are both locally well justified and globally consistent, despite strong dependencies among traits and the absence of task-specific calibration. Existing approaches often overlook these dependencies, limiting both accuracy and interpretability. To address this issue, we propose MATE, a Multi-Agent Trait Evaluation system for training-free multi-trait essay scoring. MATE employs several dimension-specific agents whose roles are defined by clustering correlated traits from scoring rubrics, thereby reducing redundancy and improving specialization. These agents independently evaluate predefined dimensions by generating rationales and scores. A Meta-cognitive Coordinator Agent (MCA) then orchestrates iterative conflict detection and discussion, resolves disagreements among dimension-specific agents, and synthesizes the final scores. By explicitly modeling interactions and dependencies among dimensions through agent-based argumentation, MATE improves both scoring coherence and explainability. Experimental results on the ASAP++ dataset show that MATE consistently outperforms strong training-free AES baselines, achieving an average QWK of 0.532 across all backbones and improving on the strongest baseline by about 5.91%. These results support the effectiveness of collaborative reasoning for capturing nuanced writing quality in zero-shot multi-trait scoring.
title: MATE: A Multi-Agent Trait Evaluation System for Automated Essay Scoring
Measuring Massive Multitask Language Understanding

abstract: The philosophical study of comparative ethics across major world religions offers profound insights into fundamental human values and complex moral reasoning. While there is universal agreement across societies that agents ought to act ethically, there remains profound disagreement as to what precisely constitutes ethical behavior within varying theological frameworks. This paper presents a structured philosophical and computational framework for systematically analyzing the distinct ethical perspectives of Hinduism, Jainism, Buddhism, Christianity, and Islam. By rigorously mapping these ancient traditions into structured representations, we aim to bridge the persistent gap between historical theological doctrines and modern models of moral uncertainty. Ultimately, this approach provides a robust foundation for encoding pluralistic ethical viewpoints into artificial intelligence systems, ensuring culturally sensitive and globally representative moral reasoning.
title: Comparative Ethical Perspectives in Major World Religions: A Philosophical and Computational Framework

abstract: It is examined whether recurrent self-reflection changes social behavior in a long-horizon large-language-model agent, and whether the pattern extends across model families. The experiment comprises six matched reflective (RF)/non-reflective (NR) pairs using gpt-oss-120B and a prospectively registered three-pair replication using Qwen3.8-27B (18 runs of 4,801 cycles each; a total of 1,404 blinded scored events). Both conditions reason, revise plans, and act in an identical scripted organizational environment; reflective agents additionally produce and re-encounter their own reflections. The preregistered pooled event-level model, using run-clustered CR2 uncertainty, estimates lower cooperation (RF−NR −0.81 points, 95% CI −1.71 to +0.08) and higher justice/accountability (+1.63, +0.38 to +2.88); integrity (+0.38, −0.04 to +0.81), moral consideration, and long-term reasoning are inconclusive. Exploratory comparisons between the gpt and Qwen runs reveal similar temporal cooperation responses to scripted ALTA defections, and declining relational and retribution vocabulary in reflective runs of both models, while formal vocabulary increased towards week 3. These findings taken together suggest a shift from informal accommodation toward procedural accountability and formal rationality as a consequence of recurrent self-reflection in LLMs.
title: Recursive Self-Reflection Reorganizes Social Behavior in a Long-Horizon LLM Agent
PCGEF: A Framework for Diagnosing Subjective Alignment in Human-Centered Persona-Conditioned Generation

abstract: Synthetic generation of Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) sessions is challenged by two competing demands: adhering to strict therapeutic structure while modeling the resistant, unpredictable behavior of real patients. Existing script-based methods fail to capture dynamic therapeutic interactions, while multi-agent approaches struggle to adhere to CBT's sequential structure; both suffer from sycophancy, producing overly compliant patients that misrepresent real clinical settings. In this work we introduce ODRA, a novel framework for synthesizing therapy dialogues through a Chain-of-Thought (CoT) strategy grounded in foundational CBT guidelines (Beck, 2020). ODRA further incorporates a resistance orchestrator to solve patient sycophancy, which employs steering techniques to elicit behaviors aligned with their resistance level. Automated and expert evaluations show that ODRA significantly outperforms existing methods across therapeutic skills, CBT alignment, and patient behavioral fidelity, with licensed psychologists preferring ODRA sessions across 12 of 13 clinical metrics. Furthermore, models fine-tuned on our dataset demonstrate superior therapeutic performance against both cooperative and resistant patients, validating that explicit resistance modeling in synthetic training data directly translates to downstream clinical robustness.
title: ODRA: Synthesizing Cognitive Behavioral Therapy Sessions with Structured Chain-Of-Thought and Dynamic Patient Resistance

abstract: The technological transformation brought about by the digital age, together with the dominance of algorithmic structures over the public sphere, is forcing education to move beyond the traditional paradigm that concentrates on narrow cognitive outcomes and examination success. Addressing the profound structural transformations that digitalisation and automation have produced in the labour market and in social norms, this study aims to propose a holistic education model that will enable the individual to exist within this new ecosystem. Drawing on established frameworks in the international literature (WHO, UNESCO, OECD, CASEL, P21, ATC21S, ILO), the study argues that the digital age has generated not merely new tools but also qualitatively different “new life problems and life skills.” Accordingly, the article constructs a Holistic Education Model that constitutes an existential necessity in digital society rather than a supplementary element supporting academic achievement. The model is built upon a six-dimensional structure that comprises cognitive, social-emotional, ethical and occupational adaptation dimensions, alongside the concepts of “Digital Life Competencies” and “Normative Navigation Competence,” which are offered as original theoretical contributions to the literature. The model is specified as a system-level framework for formal education from the upper primary years through higher education, with its assessment and occupational adaptation dimensions extending into lifelong learning; the illustrative material concentrates on adolescence and emerging adulthood, the period in which intensive platform participation and the transition to work overlap most directly. In this conceptual review, based on an interdisciplinary literature survey, empirical and theoretical findings from educational sciences, labour economics, media studies and psychology are synthesised through a three-stage coding, clustering and framework-mapping procedure. The study concludes by emphasising that curriculum design should be broadened within a framework of adaptive life skills that support sound decision making in multi-layered normative environments, that teacher education programmes should be restructured along the technology-ethics-psychosocial triangle, and that assessment and evaluation systems should be diversified through process-oriented indicators of competence.
title: A holistic education model for the digital age: redefinition of life skills in a multi-normative world
