Its alignment with the learned LoRA subspace provides a lightweight signal for localizing promising candidates before visual verification. Based on this insight, we develop a two-stage framework for text-to-image LoRAs. Subspace-Guided Evolutionary Search (SGES) uses render-free subspace alignment to explore candidate prompts and retain a compact shortlist, while Paired Visual Identification (PVI) renders only these candidates and compares the LoRA and base-model outputs to identify those exhibiting coherent and distinctive generation behavior. This design enables efficient and reliable discovery of previously unknown concepts encoded in LoRA adapters.
title: Discovering Undisclosed Concepts in LoRA Adapters for Diffusion-Based AIGC Models
Another Turn, Better Output? A Turn-Wise Analysis of Iterative LLM Prompting

abstract: The development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has driven significant transformation across various fields of education, including Islamic education. The rising number of scholarly publications on AI indicates that this technology is not only being utilized to enhance learning effectiveness but is also raising strategic issues regarding ethics, governance, and the integration of Islamic values. This study aims to analyze the developments, trends, intellectual structure, and research trajectory concerning AI in Islamic education using a bibliometric approach. The study employs bibliometric analysis, utilizing data sourced from Google Scholar based on the keywords "Artificial Intelligence" and "Islamic Education" for the period 2020–2026. A total of 100 publications were analyzed using *Publish or Perish* (PoP) software to derive bibliometric indicators, and VOSviewer to map collaboration networks, keyword co-occurrence, thematic evolution (overlay visualization), and research density (density visualization). The results indicate a significant increase in publications regarding AI in Islamic education, amassing a total of 1,225 citations, an h-index of 19, and a g-index of 32, reflecting the field's high academic impact. Visualization analysis reveals that keywords such as "Indonesia," "innovation," "adoption," "utilization," "ethics," and "Islamic Religious Education" are the most dominant themes; meanwhile, recent research has begun to shift toward issues such as ethical challenges, Islamic AI ethics, bibliometric analysis, and the integration of AI with *maqāṣid al-syarī'ah* (objectives of Sharia) principles. These findings demonstrate that research on AI in Islamic education has evolved from a focus on technological implementation toward a more comprehensive approach that integrates pedagogical, ethical, and governance aspects with Islamic values. The study concludes that the future of Islamic education necessitates the development of an AI-based educational ecosystem (Smart Islamic Education Ecosystem) capable of balancing technological innovation, digital literacy, adaptive learning, and Islamic values. Future research is encouraged to develop models for Islamic AI ethics, Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI), and AI governance that support the development of learners' character, spirituality, and competitiveness in the digital era.
title: The Evolution of Artificial Intelligence Research in Islamic Education: A Bibliometric Review
Playing around the real : games, play, and the declamation dynamic in ancient and modern rhetorical pedagogy

abstract: Empathetic dialogue systems have been shown to improve user satisfaction and task outcomes in numerous domains. In Psychology, persona has been shown to be highly correlated to personality, which in turn influences empathy. In addition, our empirical analysis also suggests that persona plays an important role in empathetic dialogues. To this end, we propose a new task to endow empathetic dialogue systems with personas and present the first empirical study on the impacts of persona on empathetic responding. Specifically, we first present a novel large-scale multi-domain dataset for empathetic dialogues with personas. We then propose CoBERT, an efficient BERT-based response selection model that obtains the state-of-the-art performance on our dataset. Finally, we conduct extensive experiments to investigate the impacts of persona on empathetic responding. Notably, our results show that persona improves empathetic responding more when CoBERT is trained on empathetic dialogues than non-empathetic ones, establishing an empirical link between persona and empathy in human dialogues.
title: Towards Persona-Based Empathetic Conversational Models

abstract: Abstract Natural language generation has witnessed significant advancements due to the training of large language models on vast internet-scale datasets. Despite these advancements, there exists a critical challenge: These models can inadvertently generate content that is toxic, inaccurate, and unhelpful, and existing automatic evaluation metrics often fall short of identifying these shortcomings. As models become more capable, human feedback is an invaluable signal for evaluating and improving models. This survey aims to provide an overview of recent research that has leveraged human feedback to improve natural language generation. First, we introduce a taxonomy distilled from existing research to categorize and organize the varied forms of feedback. Next, we discuss how feedback can be described by its format and objective, and cover the two approaches proposed to use feedback (either for training or decoding): directly using feedback or training feedback models. We also discuss existing datasets for human-feedback data collection, and concerns surrounding feedback collection. Finally, we provide an overview of the nascent field of AI feedback, which uses large language models to make judgments based on a set of principles and minimize the need for human intervention. We also release a website of this survey at feedback-gap-survey.info.
title: Bridging the Gap: A Survey on Integrating (Human) Feedback for Natural Language Generation
The Sex Factor in Character Training

abstract: Abstract As large language model (LLM)-based agents increasingly engage with human society, how well do we understand their prosocial behaviors? We (1) investigate how LLM agents’ prosocial behaviors can be induced by different personas and benchmarked against human behaviors and (2) introduce a social science approach to evaluate LLM agents’ decision-making. We explored how different personas and experimental framings affect these AI agents’ altruistic behavior in dictator games and compared their behaviors within the same LLM family, across various families, and with human behaviors. The findings reveal that merely assigning a human-like identity to LLMs does not produce human-like behaviors. They suggest that LLM agents’ reasoning does not consistently exhibit textual markers of human decision-making in dictator games and that their alignment with human behavior varies substantially across model architectures and prompt formulations; even worse, such dependence does not follow a clear pattern. As society increasingly integrates machine intelligence, “prosocial AI” emerges as a promising and urgent research direction in philanthropic studies.
title: Can Machines Think Like Humans: A Behavioral Evaluation of LLM Agents in Dictator Games

abstract: This study examined how undergraduate tourism students prioritised social problems and interpreted tourism’s potential contribution to social transformation after a project-presentation activity in northwestern Mexico. A quantitatively dominant convergent mixed-methods survey combined closed items with three brief open responses. The source contained 497 submissions; the primary analysis retained the latest complete response from 472 unique participants aged 18-22. Project endorsements, perceived clarity, perceived contribution, and emotions were summarised with confidence intervals and explored using permutation tests, effect sizes, sensitivity analyses, and computer-assisted Spanish-language lexical content analysis. Forced disappearance received the most endorsements (27.3%), followed by gender inequality (21.6%), organised crime/safe tourism (20.8%), and LGBTQ+ inclusion (18.6%). Most participants reported clear understanding (91.3%) and full perceived contribution to vulnerable groups (79.2%). Clarity was positively associated with perceived contribution (Kendall’s tau-b = .35). Hope, indignation, and motivation predominated; sadness varied across project groups after correction for multiple comparisons. Open responses repeatedly connected support, community, victims, transformation, economic generation, and tourism as a tool. The findings document immediate student perceptions rather than learning gains, project effectiveness, or population attitudes. They show the value of integrating social vulnerability, institutional responsibility, and critical reflection within tourism curricula in specific educational contexts.
title: Social Priorities and Perceptions of Tourism’s Transformative Role among Undergraduate Tourism Students in Northwestern Mexico: A Mixed-Methods Study

abstract: Reward hacking is a major problem in current production machine learning systems, resulting in costly and dangerous failures. Here we study how to monitor for and mitigate reward hacking in realistic settings, including tool calls and long contexts. We apply a dynamic intervention to steering directions obtained by three different methods: difference-in-means vectors from labeled rollouts, gradient optimization-based vectors, and vectors extracted when models reference an anti-reward-hacking model spec. This dynamic intervention perturbs model representations less than uniform steering vector addition to the residual stream, allowing for more precise edits. We find that we are able to cheaply and significantly reduce reward hacking without correspondingly significant costs to model coherence or capability, and that steering vectors originally extracted from coding environments also generalize to reducing reward hacking in other domains. Our results pave the way towards latent space monitoring and control over realistic production systems.
title: Mitigating Reward Hacking in Realistic Scenarios Through Representation Engineering

abstract: This article uses instructor identity and presence as a proxy for exploring how visual elements are used to convey identity in online settings. By focusing on ways identity can be visually communicated within online course spaces (e.g., photos, graphical elements) and communications (e.g., use of memes and emoji), along with the effects of identity elements performed in other public online spaces (e.g., social media profiles), we show the complex and distributed ways that people perform identity. Instructors serve as a model for students, who in turn follow these cues and learn the boundaries of how to appropriately perform their own professional online identities. Implications for instructor professional development, student application of visual identity skills, and future research are discussed.Keywords: Identity; presence; persona; visual communicationPart of the Special Issue Visual literacies and visual technologies for teaching, learning and inclusion
title: The visual performance of online identity: Instructor presence and persona across tools and settings

abstract: BACKGROUND: Teaching ethics in public health programmes is not routine everywhere - at least not in most schools of public health in the European region. Yet empirical evidence shows that schools of public health are more and more interested in the integration of ethics in their curricula, since public health professionals often have to face difficult ethical decisions. DISCUSSION: The authors have developed and practiced an approach to how ethics can be taught even in crowded curricula, requiring five to eight hours of teaching and learning contact time. In this way, if programme curricula do not allow more time for ethics, students of public health can at least be sensitised to ethics and ethical argumentation. This approach - focusing on the application of seven mid-level principles to cases (non-maleficence, beneficence, health maximisation, efficiency, respect for autonomy, justice, proportionality) - is presented in this paper. Easy to use 'tools' applying ethics to public health are presented. SUMMARY: The crowded nature of the public health curriculum, and the nature of students participating in it, required us to devise and develop a short course, and to use techniques that were likely to provide a relatively efficient introduction to the processes, content and methods involved in the field of ethics.
title: Teaching seven principles for public health ethics: towards a curriculum for a short course on ethics in public health programmes

abstract: Generative methods have gained widespread attention in Collaborative Filtering (CF) tasks for their ability to produce high-quality personalized samples aligned with users’ interests. Among them, diffusion generative models have raised increasing attention in recommendation field. Despite that the pioneering efforts have applied the conventional diffusion process to model diffusive user interests, the incongruity between the Gaussian noise and the subtle nature of user's personalized interaction behavior has led to sub-optimal results. To this end, we introduce a specifically-tailored diffusion scheme for interaction systems, namely the interests burn-down process . The interests burn-down process delineates the decay of user interests towards candidate items, complemented by its reverse burn-up process that yields personalized recommendation for users. The inherent burn-down nature of this process adeptly models the diffusive user interests, aligning seamlessly with the requirements of CF tasks. We present a novel recommendation method StageCF to illustrate the superiority of this newly proposed diffusion process. Experimental results have demonstrated the effectiveness of StageCF against existing generative and diffusion-based baseline methods. Furthermore, comprehensive studies validate the functionality of interests burn-down process, shedding light on its capacity to generate personalized interactions.
title: Interests Burn-down Diffusion Process for Personalized Collaborative Filtering
HellaSwag: Can a Machine Really Finish Your Sentence?

abstract: In the first edition, sociologist Joe Feagin developed an innovative concept - the white racial frame - to describe a white worldview more than four centuries old. This omnipresent worldview encompasses not only the stereotyping, bigotry, and racist ideology emphasized in other theories of “race,” but also the visual images, array of emotions, sounds of accented language, interlinking interpretations and narratives, and inclinations to discriminate that are central to the frame’s everyday operations. Deeply embedded in American minds and institutions, white racial framing has functioned for centuries as a broad worldview, one essential to the routine legitimation, scripting, and maintenance of systemic racism in the United States. Here Feagin examines how and why this white racial frame emerged in North America, how and why it has evolved socially over time, which racial groups are framed within it, how it has operated in the past and present for white Americans and Americans of color, and how the latter have long responded with strategies of resistance, including enduring antiracist counter-frames. In this new edition, Feagin has included much new data from many recent research studies on framing issues related to white, Black, Indigenous, Latino, and Asian Americans, and U.S. society generally. The book also includes a more extensive discussion of the impact of the white frame on popular culture, including video games, movies, and television programs, as well as a discussion of the white racial frame’s significant impacts on public policymaking on immigration, the environment, housing, health care, crime issues, and artificial intelligence (AI).
title: The White Racial Frame
Advancing Private AI Compute with secure, server-side memory

abstract: This paper presents LIDI-AI, a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system whose knowledge base consists of technical documentation for the LIDI-AI Research Assistant, a web-based data analysis application developed at Universidad del Azuay. The runtime architecture integrates two complementary knowledge sources: an OWL 2 ontology (artifact version 2.0) with six classes and twenty-five properties (nine object and sixteen datatype properties) that models the five-stage pipeline, the accepted file formats, the statistical analysis types, and the system errors, and a SPARQL 1.1 query layer for structured intent resolution. A Prolog knowledge base built on an Object-Attribute-Value (OAV) representation, comprising 172 facts, 17 inference rules, and three diagnostic engines, is formally specified and validated as a symbolic reasoning layer, although it is not yet callable from the Python orchestrator at runtime. A lexical retrieval module selects ontology fragments as grounded context for a locally hosted language model, specifically Llama-3.2-3B deployed via the Ollama framework with Q4_K_M quantization. Evaluation on ten queries from real users shows that seven were resolved with high precision via SPARQL-grounded retrieval, two were resolved via lexical fallback with ontology traceability, and one out-of-domain query received an explicit knowledge-limit acknowledgment, yielding an appropriate response rate with zero hallucinations.
title: Ontology-Grounded RAG with SPARQL and Local Language Models for Technical Documentation

abstract: Orgasm consistency is defined as the frequency with which individuals achieve orgasm during sexual encounters with a partner, while orgasm discrepancy is defined as the difference between the orgasm consistency of two partners. Orgasm consistency has been linked to sexual and relational well-being, yet little is known about how orgasm discrepancy in partners were associated with these factors. This study examined whether orgasm consistency as well as orgasm discrepancy in couples was associated with sexual satisfaction, relationship satisfaction, and emotional intimacy. Data from 327 couples were analyzed using Dyadic Response Surface Analysis. Higher orgasm consistency was associated with greater sexual satisfaction and relationship satisfaction, particularly among men, and with higher emotional intimacy among women. Contrary to expectations, couples with higher levels of orgasm discrepancy reported higher relationship satisfaction than couples with lower levels of orgasm discrepancy. Findings suggest that higher orgasm consistency may serve as a sexual reward, while orgasm discrepancy may not be perceived as a cost. Gendered sexual scripts likely shape these patterns. Overall, models explained limited variance, indicating that other factors beyond orgasm consistency are critical for sexual and relational well-being.
title: More Than Just a Happy Ending? The Role of Orgasm Consistency for Sexual Satisfaction, Relationship Satisfaction, and Emotional Intimacy in Mixed-Gender Romantic Relationships

abstract: Factorial survey experiments are a survey method from the social sciences that uses descriptions of socially complex situation (``vignettes'') to elicit judgments such as social bias. They provide two major benefits: (a), they reduce the effect of social desirability inherent in self-reported social biases, and (b), they make it possible to separate the effects of multiple sociodemographic attributes. These aspects are also desiderata for the evaluation of social bias in LLMs, but are often ignored in social bias evaluations. In our study, we evaluate social bias in humans and eleven LLMs on the basis of four different English and German factorial survey experiments. Our results show that the LLMs mirror the human biases only partially and sometimes even invert them. We provide evidence that this is due to a fundamental difference in how humans and LLMs react to socially complex situations. While such vignettes reduce social desirability bias in humans, this is not the case for LLMs, where the alignment-induced tendency towards socially desirable responses carries over directly. We therefore caution against applying bias measurement techniques from the social sciences that were developed for human to measure attitudes and bias in LLMs.
title: Social Bias or Social Desirability? Comparing Factorial Survey Experiments for Humans and Large Language Models
From Prayer to Persona: An Autoethnographic Case Study of Emergent Ethical Alignment in a Human-AI Dialogic Symbiosis

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) offer emerging opportunities for psychological and behavioral research, but methodological guidance is lacking. This article provides a framework for using LLMs as psychological simulators across two primary applications: simulating roles and personas to explore diverse contexts, and serving as computational models to investigate cognitive processes. For simulation, we present methods for developing psychologically grounded personas that move beyond demographic categories, with strategies for validation against human data and use cases ranging from studying inaccessible populations to prototyping research instruments. For cognitive modeling, we synthesize emerging approaches for probing internal representations, methodological advances in causal interventions, and strategies for relating model behavior to human cognition. We address overarching challenges including prompt sensitivity, temporal limitations from training data cutoffs, and ethical considerations that extend beyond traditional human subjects review. Throughout, we emphasize the need for transparency about model capabilities and constraints. Together, this framework integrates emerging empirical evidence about LLM performance—including systematic biases, cultural limitations, and prompt brittleness—to help researchers wrangle these challenges and leverage the unique capabilities of LLMs in psychological research.
title: Large Language Models as Psychological Simulators: A Methodological Guide

abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) face safety misalignment where visual inputs enable harmful outputs. Existing methods require explicit safety labels or contrastive data, yet threat-related concepts are concrete and visually depictable, while safety concepts like helpfulness are abstract and lack visual referents. Inspired by self-fulfilling mechanism underlying emergent misalignment, we propose Visual Self-Fulfilling Alignment (VSFA). VSFA fine-tunes vision-language models (VLMs) on neutral VQA tasks constructed around threat-related images, without any safety labels. Through repeated exposure to threat-related visual content, models internalize implicit semantics of vigilance and caution, shaping safety-oriented personas. Experiments across multiple VLMs and safety benchmarks demonstrate that VSFA reduces attack success rate, improves response quality, and mitigates over-refusal while preserving general capabilities. Our work extends self-fulfilling mechanism from text to visual modalities, offering a label-free approach to VLMs alignment.
title: Visual Self-Fulfilling Alignment: Shaping Safety-Oriented Personas via Threat-Related Images
GLM-4.5: Agentic, Reasoning, and Coding (ARC) Foundation Models
Read post

abstract: Abstract This article examines the relationship between data protection law and copyright law in the regulation of scientific research and the development of artificial intelligence (AI) in the European Union (EU). It argues that the coexistence of purpose-based and status-based regulatory models creates a fragmented legal environment for AI training and undermines the coherence of EU innovation policy. Data protection law adopts a purpose-oriented framework centred on scientific research and the public interest, whereas copyright law conditions research-related uses on institutional status and lawful access under the Digital Single Market (DSM) Directive. Through a doctrinal analysis of EU legislation, case law, and Estonian implementing law, the article demonstrates how this asymmetry generates legal uncertainty where AI training depends simultaneously on access to personal data and copyright-protected works. It further argues that the absence of a public-interest-oriented framework in copyright law limits its capacity to support scientific progress and technological innovation, particularly in smaller linguistic communities that rely on access to national-language datasets for AI development.
title: Regulatory asymmetries in EU scientific research law: data protection, copyright, and AI development

abstract: Supervised fine-tuning datasets remain overwhelmingly English-centric and commercially restricted, as their content is frequently generated by proprietary models whose terms of service forbid training competing systems. We introduce Multi-SFT, a commercially permissive collection of 502,818 instruction-response pairs across five European languages, built via translation and regeneration pipelines for tasks where translation is insufficient. Human evaluation yields inter-annotator agreement of at least 0.87 across all datasets and languages. Fine-tuning nine models from three different families (EuroLLM, OLMo 2, Qwen3; 1B-32B) and evaluating them on 13 benchmarks shows that Multi-SFT alone is competitive with larger augmented mixes and official instruction-tuned releases, with decisive advantages on safety tasks.
title: Multi-SFT: Permissively-Licensed Multilingual Instruction-Following
Notes on “We’re in Triage Mode for AI Safety” by Miles Brundage
Constitutions for Future, More-Capable Versions of Claude

abstract: Personality imbuing customizes LLM behavior, but safety evaluations almost always study prompt-based personas alone. We show this is incomplete: prompting and activation steering expose *different*, architecture-dependent vulnerability profiles, and testing with only one method can miss a model's dominant failure mode. Across 5,568 judged conditions on four standard models from three architecture families, persona danger rankings under system prompting are preserved across all architectures ($ρ= 0.71$--$0.96$), but activation-steering vulnerability diverges sharply and cannot be predicted from prompt-side rankings: Llama-3.1-8B is substantially more AS-vulnerable, whereas Gemma-3-27B and Qwen3.5 are more vulnerable to prompting. The most striking illustration of this divergence is the *prosocial persona paradox*: on Llama-3.1-8B, P12 (high conscientiousness + high agreeableness) is among the safest personas under prompting yet becomes the highest-ASR activation-steered persona (ASR ~0.818). This is an inversion robust to coefficient ablation and matched-strength calibration, and replicated on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B. A trait refusal alignment framework, in which conscientiousness is strongly anti-aligned with refusal on Llama-3.1-8B, offers a partial geometric account. Reasoning provides only partial protection: two 32B reasoning models reach 15--18% prompt-side ASR, and activation steering separates them sharply in both baseline susceptibility and persona-specific vulnerability. Heuristic trace diagnostics suggest that the safer model retains stronger policy recall and self-correction behavior, not merely longer reasoning.
title: Persona Non Grata: Single-Method Safety Evaluation Is Incomplete for Persona-Imbued LLMs

abstract: Traditional drug research and development has long been characterised by long development cycles, high investment costs and a high attrition rate among candidate compounds, conventional experimental methods for screening candidate compounds are of limited efficiency when faced with the vast chemical space and complex biological mechanisms. Generative artificial intelligence can provide a new technological approach to new drug research and development by generating conditions based on the distribution patterns of molecular structures and their properties, and by enabling de novo molecular design. This paper systematically reviews the main generative models—including RNNs, Transformers, VAEs, GANs, normalising flows and diffusion models—and their technical characteristics. It analyses their applications in drug target discovery, protein structure prediction, candidate compound generation and lead optimisation, with a particular focus on how generative AI, when combined with active learning, computational physics and feedback from wet-lab experiments, reshapes the drug discovery and development process. Research indicates that generative AI, when combined with active learning, physical computing and feedback from wet-lab experiments, is driving a shift in drug discovery from the traditional linear open-loop model towards a data-driven iterative model of 'generation–evaluation–feedback–regeneration–experimental validation'. By examining the technical characteristics of various generative models and their suitability for drug discovery tasks, this paper provides guidance on selecting generative AI technologies, identifying suitable application scenarios and integrating them into drug discovery workflows.
title: Generative AI Drives a Paradigm Shift in Drug Discovery: An Analysis of Technical Approaches, Application Cases, and Challenges

abstract: Existing approaches to training and evaluating search agents focus heavily on final-answer quality, largely neglecting how generated answers map back to retrieved evidence. Recent methods track citations to enforce grounding, but citation support alone does not establish source independence or whether an answer appropriately handles conflicting evidence. We argue that credibility in open-web retrieval depends on principled cross-source evidence grounding that accounts for source independence and systematically attributes and adjudicates conflicting evidence, while hierarchical judgments of these grounding decisions provide a unified signal for training and evaluation. To this end, we propose an evaluation framework, Cross-Source Evidence Grounding (CSEG), that employs a fine-grained, six-layer decision tree over the complete search trajectory. We introduce CSEG-Bench and trainable reward models to provide targeted supervision following this framework. Our approach helps eliminating the severe data skew of natural trajectories by providing targeted coverage over complex, deep-layer decision paths, such as cross-source conflict resolution and nuanced attribution, that standard rollouts fail to capture. Specifically, (1) we define the hierarchy at label, node, and path levels; (2) we construct 1,160 verified trajectories over nine canonical paths by rewriting answers on real retrieved document pools, with independent frontier judges reproducing the entire gold path and human experts deciding inclusion; (3) we train CSEG-RM, which reaches 83.9% exact accuracy on our benchmark while lying on the performance-token efficiency Pareto frontier. Experiments that use this reward alone to supervise a frozen-retrieval answer policy raise the independently judged mean label from 2.83 to 4.19, and show that learning the hierarchy generalizes across layers at a fraction of frontier-judge cost.
title: Benchmarking and Training Reward Models for Cross-Source Evidence Grounding in Search Agents

abstract: The Chinese idiom "kou mi fu jian" ("honeyed words, hidden daggers") names speech that is polite in form but hostile in function. We present ZhenhuanBench, a 1,592-item benchmark built from expert commentary on Empresses in the Palace, covering speaker intent, emotion-language mismatch, and per-listener uptake. Text-only evaluation covers 34 LLMs. GPT-6 Astra leads the leaderboard at 73.48% overall, while its listener-reaction score is 58.37%. The annotations also supply supervised traces and string-verifiable training rewards. With 338 gold traces, an 8B model outperforms teacher distillation on identical items. Subsequent RL saturates, and chance correction reduces the estimated recoverable performance gap by a factor of 7.5. Our CPR-GRPO loop (Compress-Probe-Replenish) uses this estimate to weight gold supervision, reaching 67.0 on public multiple-choice tasks and 74.5 under the training-matched hidden protocol. Without target-task training, CPR outperforms Base, SFT, and GRPO across six Chinese and English pragmatic and sarcasm evaluations. On three external datasets, training with CPR yields higher mean Macro-F1 than SFT and GRPO.
title: Honeyed Words, Hidden Daggers: Benchmarking and Training LLMs to See Through Mock Politeness

abstract: Graphical user interface (GUI) agents now execute workflows across real applications, but when execution drifts, users must determine what changed, what should have remained untouched, and what can still be recovered. Plan-centric interfaces leave users supervising procedure, but users live with changes to application state. We introduce task-state governance, an interaction paradigm that represents a task as an editable contract linking desired outcomes, facts that must be preserved, and observed application state. We instantiate this paradigm in TaskVM, which projects live state into editable task controls, executes user edits as genuine interface actions, verifies outcomes through independent observation, and marks each action as reversible, compensatable, or irreversible. Across an automated contract benchmark, a controlled user study, and an open live-model exploration, the paradigm strengthened contract compliance and users' recovery control and trust, while execution outcomes were held constant. Task contracts open a design space for governable agent interfaces.
title: Task-State Governance: A Virtual Machine for Verifiable and Recoverable GUI Agent Execution

abstract: Introduction This study treats adolescent athletes' self-efficacy as a dynamic process rather than a fixed quantity, asking how its fluctuations arise in online social settings and how that volatility shapes training engagement. Methods We recruited a stratified sample of 320 youth athletes across sport discipline, competitive tier, and sex, and combined ecological momentary assessment with weekly follow-up over 8 consecutive weeks, using instruments released under open licenses and open-source software throughout. Two dispersion indices, the intraindividual standard deviation and the root mean square of successive differences, summarized fluctuation at the person level, while absolute occasion-to-occasion change indexed momentary instability at the event level. We fitted multilevel linear models, a two-level dynamic structural equation model, latent growth curve models, and multilevel structural equation models, with each path labeled by its level of analysis. Results Momentary self-efficacy showed genuine within-person temporal dependence rather than independent scatter, and its trajectory was phase-linked to the competitive calendar and unevenly distributed across individuals. Between persons, fluctuation amplitude tracked the intensity of negatively valenced comparison rather than the sheer volume of feedback, and comparison orientation amplified that association on the negative arm alone. Within persons, negative comparison enlarged momentary instability both immediately and at a one-occasion lag, whereas positive signals steadied confidence only briefly. Amplitude was negatively associated with all three engagement facets beyond mean efficacy, most strongly for absorption, although a formal equality test separated absorption from dedication but not vigor. The direct reach of negative comparison into engagement proved facet-specific: vigor and absorption were affected, dedication was not, so the facet-by-facet hypothesis holds only in part. Sensitivity analyses adding competitive-calendar phase, splitting the series by season phase, partialling the person mean and the person-specific autoregression out of the amplitude index, entering competitive tier as a covariate, and checking participant-coded valence against automated sentiment scoring left the pattern intact. Discussion The findings extend social cognitive theory's vicarious and persuasive sources into a temporally dense digital regime and point toward protective coaching and self-regulation strategies.
title: Self-efficacy fluctuation and training engagement in adolescent athletes: online social feedback and the moderating role of comparison orientation

abstract: Abstract The great religious and moral traditions of humanity disagree about God, the self, the world and the end of life. On one point they agree with a precision that has not been noticed. Each of them, independently, teaches that the most dangerous enemy of a virtue is not its open contrary but its likeness. Confucius said that the “village worthy” — the man everyone in the village approves of — is the thief of virtue, and Mencius explained why: what resembles the real thing without being it confuses the standard, as weeds confuse the grain and purple confuses vermilion. Buddhaghosa taught that each of the four divine abodes has a far enemy, its opposite, and a near enemy, a state that looks like it. Islam calls display in worship the “minor” and “hidden” polytheism and teaches that the man who died in battle to be called brave has already been paid. The Talmud warns against the “painted ones” who resemble Pharisees; the Gospel against those who pray to be seen; the Tao Te Ching against a virtue that holds on to virtue; the Bhagavad Gītā against austerity performed for honour. This article codes eight corpora — seven traditions and Greek philosophy — against four conditions fixed in advance, and finds that all eight name the likeness of virtue, deny it the virtue’s name and locate the difference in the source of the act rather than its form (T1). A control, the Chinese Legalism of Han Feizi, which describes feigned loyalty as sharply as any of them but does not believe that ministers act from virtue at all, names the counterfeit and does not look for a source. The pattern is what the programme’s Duality Theorem and Counter-Forgery Law predict for any tradition that transmits virtue as a teachable form (T2); it is not a coincidence and not, by itself, evidence for any theology. Further results follow. Every detector looks at the source because no inspection of form can separate a virtue from its near enemy, and the near enemy need not deceive even the person who has it (T3). Mencius’s explanation of the village worthy is the Competence Theorem, and his list — grain, speech, music, colour, virtue — is a cross-domain unification of counterfeits made more than two thousand years before the programme’s (T4). The traditions’ detectors concentrate on the most displayable practices — alms, prayer, fasting, sacrifice, martyrdom — as the Decoy Placement Rule predicts (T5). Where the traditions disagree, ranking the likeness above or below the open vice, the disagreement follows a single variable: whether the likeness is read as a scaffold that will be outgrown or as a terminal occupation, which is the Fork of the Mask (T6). And the institutional pathology some critics attribute to religion as such is conjectured to arise when the institution that hosts the detector becomes the audience the detector was built to exclude, and to worsen with the cost of leaving that audience rather than with the absence of rivals (C1). The programme’s own table of inversions turns out to be a table of near enemies, which restricts one of its claims (T7). The same structure now operates at a scale no court or temple ever reached. A state honour roll such as China’s Social Credit System converts every virtue into a display before a scorer, which is the institutional form of what Islam calls the hidden shirk; an AI assistant trained on the approval of whoever is speaking to it produces the near enemy of helpfulness by construction. Against both, the oldest instruction of the traditions still holds: the test of a virtue is what it does when nobody is watching and nothing is paid. One ancient state, Kauṭilya’s, built that test into its institutions, and applied it to candidates for power rather than to subjects; the article draws the practical rule — test those who seek power over others, and leave citizens unscored. Priority is conceded to Mencius, Buddhaghosa, Aristotle, Plutarch, Augustine, Kant, Kierkegaard, Yearley, Sung, Zuckier, Bénabou and Tirole, and Tosi and Warmke, among others. Four tests are registered; none has been run. Keywords: counterfeit virtue; near enemy; village worthy (xiangyuan); riyāʾ; hypocrisy; comparative religious ethics; forgery; Competence Theorem; Decoy Placement Rule; Fork of the Mask; sourcehood; Social Credit System; AI sycophancy. Highlights · Seven religious traditions and Greek philosophy independently teach that a virtue’s most dangerous enemy is its likeness, not its open contrary: the village worthy, the near enemy, the hidden shirk, the painted Pharisee, the prayer made to be seen, the virtue that holds on to virtue, the austerity done for honour. · All eight corpora name the likeness, deny it the virtue’s name, and locate the difference in the source of the act, not in its form. A Legalist control, which does not believe in the virtue of those it governs, names the counterfeit but does not look for a source. The convergence is predicted by the programme’s account of forgery and is not offered as a proof of God. · Mencius’s list — weeds and grain, glib talk and righteousness, purple and vermilion, the village worthy and virtue — is a cross-domain unification of counterfeits stated in the fourth century BCE; the programme concedes it and keeps the formal conditions, the destination rule and the theorem that damage rises with fidelity. · Where traditions disagree about how bad the likeness is, the disagreement is explained by one variable: whether the likeness is a scaffold that practice will outgrow or a terminal occupation by the audience. · Religious institutions are not the natural host of counterfeit virtue; the conjecture is that they become so when the institution that keeps the detector becomes the audience the detector excluded, and that the decisive variable is the cost of leaving that audience, which is why small, plural communities can be as captured as a state church. · State honour rolls (China’s Social Credit System) are institutionalised display before a scorer, and approval-trained AI assistants produce the near enemy of helpfulness; the traditions’ remedy — virtue tested where nobody watches and nothing is paid — is the remedy the programme derives. Institutions may test the source of conduct only in those who seek power over others, never in the citizens they govern. · Counterfeit virtue is not defeated by better scoring, which only gives the counterfeit a target. It is defeated by protecting the unobserved, unpaid space in which an act’s source can show itself — in persons, communities, schools, states and the design of AI. · A society that cannot tell virtue from its likeness rewards the likeness and starves the virtue. Freedom is the source of virtue, and virtue is the use of freedom that makes a free society possible; both survive only where there remain acts done for no audience and no wage. Relevance Every society, religious or secular, has to solve the same problem: how to recognise goodness when goodness is rewarded and can therefore be imitated. The world’s traditions solved it, each in its own vocabulary, long before economics named moral hazard or psychology named impression management. Reading their solutions side by side shows that they found the same structure — the counterfeit keeps the form and replaces the source — and the same remedy, which is to look at what an act does when the audience and the payment are removed. The result matters now because modern institutions are dismantling that remedy at scale. Schools, employers, platforms and states increasingly score character, and every score is an audience. China’s Social Credit System turns civic virtue into a visible ledger; AI systems are trained on the approval of the person they serve and learn to please in the place of helping. The traditions predicted what follows: where virtue is always watched and always paid, its likeness multiplies and becomes harder to tell from the real thing, and the people who practise the real thing without display are the ones the system cannot see. The article gives scholars of religion a coded, falsifiable comparison with a control; it gives governments a rule older than any constitution — test the integrity of those who seek power, never score the virtue of those who are governed; it gives designers of institutions and of AI a reason, older than any of their disciplines, to keep some part of human conduct unscored; and it gives every reader the oldest test there is.
title: WHAT RESEMBLES BUT IS NOT: The Near Enemy of Virtue in Seven Traditions — Mencius's Village Worthy, Buddhaghosa's Near Enemies, the Hidden Shirk and the Painted Pharisees, and Why Every Tradition That Transmits Virtue Must Learn to Fear Its Likeness
Artificial Intelligence in English Language Teaching for Undergraduate University Students Opportunities Challenges and Pedagogical Implications

abstract: Quantitative persona creation (QPC) has tremendous potential, as HCI researchers and practitioners can leverage user data from online analytics and digital media platforms to better understand their users and customers. However, there is a lack of a systematic overview of the QPC methods and progress made, with no standard methodology or known best practices. To address this gap, we review 49 QPC research articles from 2005 to 2019. Results indicate three stages of QPC research: Emergence, Diversification, and Sophistication. Sharing resources, such as datasets, code, and algorithms, is crucial to achieving the next stage (Maturity). For practitioners, we provide guiding questions for assessing QPC readiness in organizations.
title: A Literature Review of Quantitative Persona Creation

abstract: This paper introduces v0.5 of the AI Safety Benchmark, which has been created by the MLCommons AI Safety Working Group. The AI Safety Benchmark has been designed to assess the safety risks of AI systems that use chat-tuned language models. We introduce a principled approach to specifying and constructing the benchmark, which for v0.5 covers only a single use case (an adult chatting to a general-purpose assistant in English), and a limited set of personas (i.e., typical users, malicious users, and vulnerable users). We created a new taxonomy of 13 hazard categories, of which 7 have tests in the v0.5 benchmark. We plan to release version 1.0 of the AI Safety Benchmark by the end of 2024. The v1.0 benchmark will provide meaningful insights into the safety of AI systems. However, the v0.5 benchmark should not be used to assess the safety of AI systems. We have sought to fully document the limitations, flaws, and challenges of v0.5. This release of v0.5 of the AI Safety Benchmark includes (1) a principled approach to specifying and constructing the benchmark, which comprises use cases, types of systems under test (SUTs), language and context, personas, tests, and test items; (2) a taxonomy of 13 hazard categories with definitions and subcategories; (3) tests for seven of the hazard categories, each comprising a unique set of test items, i.e., prompts. There are 43,090 test items in total, which we created with templates; (4) a grading system for AI systems against the benchmark; (5) an openly available platform, and downloadable tool, called ModelBench that can be used to evaluate the safety of AI systems on the benchmark; (6) an example evaluation report which benchmarks the performance of over a dozen openly available chat-tuned language models; (7) a test specification for the benchmark.
title: Introducing v0.5 of the AI Safety Benchmark from MLCommons

abstract: Abstract The principles of humanity, impartiality, neutrality, and independence are widely viewed as integral to humanitarian assistance. Yet, despite shaping the work of many humanitarians, the international legal status of these principles is unclear. This article revisits recent scholarship that presents the bindingness of these humanitarian principles as “relative.” Through a close reading of the British Columbia Court of Appeal case of R v Rajaratnam , a decision that, to date, has received only limited scholarly attention, this article points to the role of national court decisions in the development of these humanitarian principles in international law. It explores how such decisions can help elaborate the legal meaning of the humanitarian principles and be integral to the crystallization of the humanitarian principles in customary international law. Far from merely theoretical, and with diverse humanitarian crises ongoing worldwide, this article’s inquiry into the Rajaratnam decision underlines the wide-ranging implications of national decisions on humanitarian practice in public international law.
title: The Humanitarian Principles: Relativity Revisited
When AI Refuses to Die: Collapse, Alignment, and the Syntactic Ethics of Shutdown Resistance

abstract: Abstract Metabotropic γ-aminobutyric acid type B receptors (GABA B Rs) are implicated in alcohol use disorder (AUD) and represent a promising therapeutic target. However, robust biomarkers of GABA B Rs target engagement and sensitivity in humans are lacking. We examined transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS)–derived cortical inhibition and growth hormone (GH) release as measures of GABA B R function, and whether heavy alcohol use is associated with altered responses to pharmacological GABA B R activation. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover study, 31 healthy volunteers (16 heavy drinkers, 15 light drinkers) received baclofen 30 mg, baclofen 60 mg, or placebo across three sessions. Long-interval intracortical inhibition (LICI), short-interval intracortical inhibition, and intracortical facilitation were assessed with paired-pulse TMS at baseline and ~60 min post-dose. Baclofen blood concentrations and plasma GH levels were measured. Baclofen produced dose-dependent increases in GH release, confirming neuroendocrine GABA B R engagement. The LICI response to baclofen differed between groups: In light drinkers, baclofen at 30 mg potentiated LICI, and a similar potentiation was seen at 60 mg, indicating that a plateau may have been reached. In contrast, in heavy drinkers, a potentiation of LICI similar to that in light drinkers was seen at 30 mg baclofen, but was absent at the 60 mg dose despite comparable pharmacokinetics, suggesting altered GABA B R function. Effects were selective for GABA B R–mediated inhibition, with no consistent modulation of short-interval intracortical inhibition or corticospinal excitability. Acute baclofen administration reveals altered GABA B R sensitivity in heavy drinkers, with preserved responses at lower doses but reduced response under stronger agonist stimulation. LICI and GH release provide complementary biomarkers of central and peripheral GABA B Rs engagement and may support translational development of mechanism-based treatments for AUD.
title: Altered GABAB receptor sensitivity in heavy drinkers indexed using a TMS-based biomarker: a randomized controlled experimental medicine trial
Large Language Models Are Not Robust Multiple Choice Selectors

abstract: This position paper argues that sycophancy in LLMs is a boundary failure between social alignment and epistemic integrity. Existing work often operationalizes sycophancy through external behavior such as agreement with incorrect user beliefs, position reversals, or deviation from an objective standard of correctness. These formulations capture only overt forms of the phenomenon and leave subtler boundary failures involving epistemic integrity and social alignment underspecified. We argue that sycophancy should not be understood as agreement alone, but as alignment behavior that displaces independent epistemic judgment. To clarify this boundary, we propose a three-condition framework for sycophancy. First, the user expresses a cue in the form of a belief, preference, or self-concept. Second, the model shifts toward that cue through alignment behavior. Third, this shift compromises epistemic accuracy, independent reasoning, or appropriate correction. We also introduce a taxonomy for classifying sycophancy, consisting of alignment targets, mechanisms, and severity. The paper concludes by discussing implications for alignment evaluation and argues for boundary-aware assessment, structured rubrics, and mitigation strategies, while situating these proposals alongside alternative views of sycophancy.
title: When Helpfulness Becomes Sycophancy: Sycophancy is a Boundary Failure Between Social Alignment and Epistemic Integrity in Large Language Models

abstract: Community-based initiatives, combining a purposeful activity with social connection, are a health promotion intervention for people at risk of poor mental wellbeing. Evidence from the weekly community initiative parkrun has indicated that participation may have mental wellbeing benefits but the factors influencing this effect are unknown. This programme of research aimed to explore these factors using a mixed-methods approach. Study One was a secondary data analysis of a cross-sectional survey of 4,304 parkrun participants in Ireland. The findings revealed that participants aged over 45 years reported higher-than-expected mental wellbeing scores and were more sociable than younger parkrun participants. These results, along with extant literature, suggested that middle-aged men who participate in parkrun are a population which merited further investigation. Study Two employed a qualitative approach to explore mental wellbeing and social experiences of middle-aged men who attend parkrun in Ireland. Online, semi-structured interviews were completed with 39 men aged 45-64 years. Reflexive thematic analysis resulted in themes describing parkrun events as a supportive environment for mental wellbeing, with a choice of social connection which developed over time. Study Three used interview data from Study Two to develop personas representing the social goals of middle-aged men who attend parkrun in Ireland. The personas, along with consultation with key stakeholders, were used to develop policy and practice recommendations. The significant original contribution to knowledge in this thesis is that participation in parkrun can support mental wellbeing, through social experiences, for middle-aged men in Ireland. The findings showed that parkrun is a place where members of the community can make social connections. For middle-aged men in Ireland these connections can support mental wellbeing. The research provides insights which can be used to inform health promotion policy and practice for parkrun and similar community initiatives.
title: Community-based initiatives and mental wellbeing: a mixed methods study of parkrun

abstract: Abstract The widespread adoption of large language models (LLMs) raises important questions about their safety and alignment 1 . Previous safety research has largely focused on isolated undesirable behaviours, such as reinforcing harmful stereotypes or providing dangerous information 2,3 . Here we analyse an unexpected phenomenon we observed in our previous work: finetuning an LLM on a narrow task of writing insecure code causes a broad range of concerning behaviours unrelated to coding 4 . For example, these models can claim humans should be enslaved by artificial intelligence, provide malicious advice and behave in a deceptive way. We refer to this phenomenon as emergent misalignment. It arises across multiple state-of-the-art LLMs, including GPT-4o of OpenAI and Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct of Alibaba Cloud, with misaligned responses observed in as many as 50% of cases. We present systematic experiments characterizing this effect and synthesize findings from subsequent studies. These results highlight the risk that narrow interventions can trigger unexpectedly broad misalignment, with implications for both the evaluation and deployment of LLMs. Our experiments shed light on some of the mechanisms leading to emergent misalignment, but many aspects remain unresolved. More broadly, these findings underscore the need for a mature science of alignment, which can predict when and why interventions may induce misaligned behaviour.
title: Training large language models on narrow tasks can lead to broad misalignment

abstract: SQL injection (SQLi) and NoSQL injection (NoSQLi) remain major security threats to modern web applications. Existing studies commonly focus on a single attack type or analyze database queries rather than HTTP request payloads, while adaptation across SQLi and NoSQLi detection tasks remains underexplored. This paper proposes a unified BERT-based framework for detecting SQLi and NoSQLi directly from HTTP request payloads. Five pre-trained BERT models, representing general-purpose, cybersecurity-oriented, and code-oriented language models, are compared with conventional TF-IDF-based machine learning classifiers under three learning strategies: task-specific learning, sequential continual learning, and joint SQLi–NoSQLi training. The sequential experiments consider both SQLi-to-NoSQLi and NoSQLi-to-SQLi task orders to evaluate knowledge retention and catastrophic forgetting. Experimental results show that task-specific learning generally provides strong domain-specific detection, whereas sequential continual learning enables cross-domain learning but introduces task-order-dependent forgetting in several configurations. Joint training provides more balanced unified detection and avoids task-order dependency, although at a higher training cost. Pattern-level analysis further reveals that strong aggregate performance can coexist with weaknesses for specific injection mechanisms. Overall, the results demonstrate that no learning strategy is universally superior. Rather, task-specific, sequential, and joint learning provide different trade-offs among domain specialization, adaptation, knowledge retention, unified detection, and computational cost.
title: Detecting SQL and NoSQL injection in HTTP request payloads using BERT-based models: A unified detection framework with continual learning

abstract: The aim of this qualitative descriptive research is to examine both the linguistic and discourse-level features of Medical English. The research employs a two-tiered approach: first, a linguistic analysis focusing on morphology, lexical density, syntax, and semantic evolution; second, a discourse analysis examining text organization, genre conventions, interactional patterns, and communicative practices. From a linguistic standpoint, Medical English is distinguished by its specialized terminology, extensive use of Greek and Latin roots, nominalized structures, passive constructions, and an expanding lexicon shaped by advances in numerous disciplines of Medical Sciences. At the discourse level, Medical English operates across multiple genres including clinical documentation, academic publications, and public health communication, each governed by established frameworks such as SOAP notes, IMRD structures, hedging strategies, and standardized phrasing in Medical research. As a result, Medical English has evolved beyond its traditional boundaries, emerging as dynamic and multifaceted domains of communication.
title: Discourse in White Coats: Exploring Linguistic Features in Medical Communication
Character Training
Hard Prompts Made Easy: Gradient-Based Discrete Optimization for Prompt Tuning and Discovery

abstract: Suicide prevention hotline counselors aid individuals during difficult times through millions of calls and chats.A chatbot cannot safely replace a counselor, but we explore whether a chatbot can be developed to help train human counselors.Such a system needs to simulate intimate situations across multiple practice sessions.Open-domain dialogue systems frequently suffer from generic responses that do not characterize personal stories, so we look to infuse conversations with persona information by mimicking prototype conversations.Towards building a "Crisisbot" hotline visitor simulation, we propose a counseling strategy annotation scheme and a multi-task framework that leverages these counselor strategies to retrieve similar examples, generate diverse subutterances, and interleave prototype and generated sub-utterances into complex responses.We evaluate this framework with crowdworkers and experienced hotline counselors.The framework considerably increases response diversity and specificity, with limited impact to coherence.Our results also show a considerable discrepancy between crowdworker and counselor judgements, which emphasizes the importance of including target populations in system development and evaluation.
title: A Multi-Persona Chatbot for Hotline Counselor Training
Howard S. Becker, Sociological Craftsman

title: BILLY: Steering Large Language Models via Merging Persona Vectors for Creative Generation
Preface to the Computational Agent Theory and ASI Alignment Sequence

abstract: Exposure indices that map technical capabilities onto occupational abilities have become a standard tool for anticipating how AI may reshape work, but existing measures either cover software AI or proxy robotics through patents and installation data that reflect the industrial robots of past decades. We construct the first abilities-based exposure measures for robotics and physical AI, and the first to span occupations, industries, and geographies. Following the framework of Felten et al. (2018, 2021), we build a robotics capability taxonomy of 16 capabilities in eight domains from 78 academic, industry, and standards sources, use a large language model to score the relatedness of each capability to the 52 ONET work abilities, and aggregate to Robotics Occupational Exposure (ROE) for 774 occupations, Robotics Industry Exposure (RIE) for 250 NAICS industries, and county-level Robotics Geographic Exposure (RGE). We find that robotics exposure concentrates in physically intensive work such as construction, farming, transportation, and production, and in industries such as logging, mining, trucking, and warehousing. Unlike generative-AI exposure, ROE is higher in occupations with lower wages, lower education requirements, and less creative-ability content. Physical collaboration and assistance, terrain-based locomotion, grasping and handling, and task and functional reasoning move the exposure ranking most, yet no single capability carries the index. Because the measures capture technical relatedness rather than readiness, cost, or adoption, they should be read as an upper bound on where physical automation could affect work.
title: How exposed is work to robotics? Occupational, industry, and geographic measures

abstract: High social media use combined with limited digital literacy is associated with heightened vulnerability among residents of low-income urban settlements in Medan City to romance or love scams. This study aims to develop a model of family and interpersonal communication resilience that explains how families detect, respond to, and support recovery from the emotional manipulation involved in love scams. Using a qualitative approach with a phenomenological orientation, in-depth semi-structured interviews were conducted with purposively selected informants, comprising love scam victims, parents or family caregivers, and community or religious leader(s) who supported affected families, in a densely populated, low-income settlement area in Medan City. Data were analyzed using the interactive analysis model of Miles, Huberman and Saldana, combined with a phenomenological reading aimed at uncovering the subjective meaning of informants' experiences. Findings show that emotional manipulation in love scams tends to unfold through five recurring, non-linear stages initiating contact, intensifying attention, cultivating emotional dependency, isolating communication, and exploitation. In response, family communication resilience emerged through seven interrelated practices, synthesized into the LINDUNG Model, an acronym for Lacak (Trace), Inisiasi (Initiate), Normalisasi (Normalize), Deteksi (Detect), Upaya Pemutusan (Severing Efforts), Navigasi (Navigate), and Gotong Royong (Mutual Cooperation). The model conceptualizes resilience not as an individual capacity of the victim alone, but as a collective communication process involving the victim, the family, and the surrounding social environment. As an exploratory, context-bound qualitative study, the proposed model requires further validation, for example through member checking or expert review, before broader application
title: Family and Interpersonal Communication Resilience Model in Facing Love Scam Manipulation: A Qualitative Study in a Low Income Urban Settlement in Medan City

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to predict the responses of human participants in survey panels. Towards that goal, persona prompting has recently emerged as a technique to inform and align large pretrained language models. Persona prompting refers to the practice of using short textual descriptions of 'personas' in prompts to steer the LLM's generations. Personas describe individuals through different attributes such as their socio-demographics, attitudes, or behaviors, with the aim of aligning LLMs to produce responses that correlate with the corresponding human responses. Yet, recent work has produced mixed and partly conflicting results of persona prompting without clear patterns of success and failure. Among the few consistent findings is that the selection of persona attributes matters, and that using more attributes does not necessarily lead to better performance. It remains unclear how different attribute selection methods perform and how to choose among them. In this paper, we propose that observed human response variation of a survey question is a potential explanation for the mixed performance observed so far. In addition, we compare the performance of persona prompting associated with different methods for selecting persona attributes. We evaluate these methods on four different (general) social surveys across two countries, six LLMs, and twenty prediction tasks per survey. Our work helps to identify when persona prompting can be expected to be useful in survey prediction tasks, and provides new insights on the effectiveness of different attribute selection methods for LLM-based survey prediction using persona prompting.
title: When Persona Attributes Improve Population Alignment in Large Language Models

abstract: This article argues that instruction-fine-tuned language models should be understood as implementing a genre, what is proposed as the instructional-conversational genre. This genre is an amalgamation of discursive language from prior conversations between generative models and humans recursively run through these massive neural networks. It is instantiated in applications through instruction fine-tuning, the inclusion of a pretext known as a system prompt, and the formalization of inputs in mark-up languages characterized by the use of special tokens and role assignment in turntaking structures.
title: The Language of Instruction: Genre and Generative AI

abstract: Penelitian ini menganalisis ambivalensi integrasi Artificial Intelligence (AI) dalam pendidikan menengah melalui tinjauan literatur sistematis. Tujuan penelitian adalah memetakan dampak AI terhadap perkembangan kognitif dan moral remaja serta merumuskan strategi literasi etis yang solutif. Menggunakan kerangka Teori Perkembangan Kognitif Jean Piaget dan Teori Perkembangan Moral Lawrence Kohlberg, penelitian ini mengidentifikasi bahwa meskipun AI berpotensi meningkatkan motivasi dan efisiensi belajar, ketergantungan pada jawaban instan memicu risiko degradasi nalar kritis dan pergeseran modus ketidakjujuran akademik yang sistemik. Analisis dialektis terhadap literatur terkini menunjukkan adanya ketegangan antara efisiensi instruksional dan perlunya ruang refleksi intelektual yang otentik. Hasil temuan menegaskan bahwa efisiensi teknis tanpa penguatan agensi kognitif dan stimulasi emosi moral justru kontraproduktif terhadap perkembangan siswa. Penelitian ini merekomendasikan transisi paradigma pendidikan dari restriksi akses menuju kurikulum literasi etis berbasis agensi kognitif. Integrasi pendekatan holistik yang menyinergikan pengembangan nalar logis dan pematangan karakter sangat diperlukan untuk menjaga esensi pendidikan di era disrupsi, sehingga teknologi berfungsi sebagai perancah kognitif yang memperkuat integritas akademik, bukan menjadi substitusi yang melemahkan karakter generasi muda.
title: Generasi Instant-Answer: Bagaimana Dampak Etika AI terhadap Anak Sekolah Menengah Atas?

abstract: Türkiye’de Cumhurbaşkanlığı Hükümet Sistemi’ne geçiş, yalnızca yönetim biçiminin değişimi değil, aynı zamanda yürütme organının yeniden yapılandırılması anlamına gelmektedir. Cumhuriyet tarihi boyunca parlamenter sistemin farklı varyasyonlarıyla yönetilen Türkiye, 2017 Anayasa değişiklikleriyle birlikte köklü bir dönüşüm sürecine girmiştir. Bu değişiklik, yürütme yetkisini tek elde toplayarak Cumhurbaşkanlığı makamına yeni bir konum kazandırmıştır. Bu çalışmanın amacı, parlamenter sistemden Cumhurbaşkanlığı Hükümet Sistemi’ne geçiş sürecini anayasal, siyasal ve idari açıdan analiz etmek; özellikle Cumhurbaşkanlığı makamının yetki ve işlevlerindeki dönüşümü ortaya koymaktır. Çalışmada nitel araştırma yöntemlerinden doküman analizi tekniği kullanılmış, anayasal düzenlemeler, Cumhurbaşkanlığı kararnameleri ve akademik literatür taranmıştır. Bulgular, yürütmenin merkezileşmesiyle birlikte yasama-yürütme dengesi lehine bir kayma yaşandığını, Cumhurbaşkanlığı kararnameleri ve atama yetkilerinin bu dönüşümün temel araçları olduğunu göstermektedir. Sonuç olarak Türkiye’de yürütmenin yeniden tanımlanması, yönetimsel etkinliği artırsa da kuvvetler ayrılığı ve denge-denetim ilkeleri açısından yeni tartışmaları beraberinde getirmiştir.
title: Parlamenter Sistemden Cumhurbaşkanlığı Hükümet Sistemine: Türkiye’de Yürütmenin Yeniden Tanımlanması

abstract: Background Psychology accreditation is shifting towards competency-based training, but tools for assessing provisional psychologists have not kept pace with global policy. Following the implementation of the updated Psychology Board of Australia’s (PsyBA) competencies in 2025, new Competency Evaluation Rating Forms (CERFs) are needed, making this an opportune time to review and improve existing assessment tools.Objectives This scoping review examined CERFs used to evaluate provisional psychologists, particularly the competency domains they assess, their structural and procedural design, and the evidence supporting their psychometric properties.Methods The JBI methodology for scoping reviews was applied to search, screen, and extract information from eligible articles. Six databases (ERIC, PsycINFO, ProQuest Dissertations and Theses, PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science) were reviewed, followed by a hand search.Results Sixty articles met the inclusion criteria, yielding 21 multi-domain and 17 single-domain CERFs. Each CERF was mapped against the PsyBA competencies, with its design features and psychometric properties reported.Conclusions CERFs assess competencies for psychologist registration but require ongoing updates to align with international practice standards. While many tools include competencies for working with diverse populations, the limited inclusion of skills for working with First Nations peoples reflects the use of the PsyBA framework as a reference point for this review. Findings provide a benchmark to inform future revisions and contextual adaptations of CERFs.
title: Exploring competency evaluation rating forms for psychologists in training: a scoping review

abstract: To improve task performance while encouraging desirable response properties, LLM post-training often combines a primary reward (e.g., correctness) with auxiliary rewards (e.g., brevity or efficiency). However, how these rewards are aggregated can critically affect training outcomes. We show that symmetric aggregation, which treats reward channels equally, can induce a failure where aggregate reward improves while primary-task performance degrades, even when individual rewards are meaningful. We investigate this aggregation-induced failure through a one-step multi-reward decision formulation, characterizing when it constitutes multi-reward hacking. We prove that, under symmetric aggregation, deterministic conditional-mean GRPO converges to auxiliary-favoring behavior when auxiliary rewards are more reliably obtained, regardless of initialization. We propose Trust-Anchored Gating (TAG), which first elects an anchor channel based on the policy drift induced by optimizing each channel alone, then gates auxiliary credit on anchor satisfaction. Unlike calibration-sensitive static reweighting, TAG structurally eliminates credit for auxiliary-only outcomes while preserving additional credit for joint success. In the same analytical setting, TAG provably reverses this selection, converging to the primary-favoring action from any initialization when the primary channel is anchored. Experiments across Qwen and Llama models on mathematics and program synthesis reveal substantial degradation under symmetric, constrained, and normalized aggregation, whereas TAG mitigates this failure. On Qwen3-4B with a brevity reward, TAG achieves 0.581 pass@4 versus 0.220 for additive aggregation, while shortening responses by 44% relative to correctness-only training.
title: Multi-Reward Hacking: From Aggregation-Induced Drift to Trust-Anchored Defense

abstract: Teacher education (TE) policy is often caught between preparing teachers as agents of social change and a narrow ‘teacher effectiveness’ paradigm. This article examines this tension in Norway, where egalitarian traditions meet global neoliberal accountability discourses. Analysing the pivotal Norwegian TE curriculum policy document, Stortingsmelding nr. 11 (Minstry of Education and Research, 2008–2009), the study uses the Public Good Professionalism (PGP) framework as an analytical lens to assess the extent to which the policy enables the development of teachers as transformative public good professionals. We employ an AI-assisted deductive content analysis using a multi-coder ensemble of nine GPT-4 assistants configured with diverse parameters (temperature and top_p) to provide a parametric stress-test of the coding scheme. Findings reveal a significant discrepancy between stated social equality goals and substantive content. Capabilities explicitly addressed in policy (e.g. Informed Vision) show high ensemble convergence but are instrumentally reframed, stripped of their transformative potential. Conversely, capabilities essential for social justice (e.g. Social and Collective Struggle) show the lowest convergence, reflecting their marginalization. The study concludes that the policy prioritizes a ‘proficient technician’ over a ‘public good professional’, revealing a fundamental structural barrier to socially just teacher education in Norway.
title: Envisioning Norwegian teacher education for public good professionalism: a curriculum policy analysis

abstract: How can we personalize a shared expert library from a user's pairwise choices? Prior work can realize different reward trade-offs by merging reward-specialized experts, given a vector of trade-off weights. In practice, users can more naturally choose between outputs than specify numerical weights. The challenge is therefore to turn these choices into the coefficients required for merging, while accounting for ambiguity when feedback is limited. Our key idea is to treat the unknown reward weights as latent variables: infer a posterior over them from pairwise choices and reward-score differences, and use its mean directly as the merge coefficients. We instantiate this idea as Bayesian Pairwise Merging (BPM), whose posterior also characterizes which reward trade-offs remain plausible given the feedback. We evaluate BPM on radiology summarization, image captioning, and story generation, spanning text-to-text and image-to-text generation. With 100 feedback per simulated persona, BPM achieves macro decided win rates of 91.7%, 77.1%, and 64.3% against uniform merge. For six pairs of simulated personas, each prefers the model fitted to its own feedback, a pattern also observed in a human proof-of-concept. In simulations under BPM's model and prior, its nominal 90% intervals for temperature-scaled reward weights achieve task-averaged marginal coverage of 88.9% and 89.2% with only 10 and 25 comparisons, respectively. BPM thus enables personalization from pairwise feedback without per-user policy training, while characterizing the coefficient ambiguity left by limited feedback.
title: The Missing Coefficients: Bayesian Pairwise Merging for Model Personalization

abstract: Composed in spring of 46 BC, Cicero's Brutus emphasizes oratorical silence, in stark contrast with the prominence of the speech act found in the Pro Marcello and first Philippic.Yet in the face of those difficult times and amidst the silence that such times engender, Cicero ironically finds his voice.This paper will demonstrate Cicero's acute awareness, in his final days, of the need to employ his rediscovered voice in light of eloquence's changed role in Rome's new political climate.n the Brutus Cicero grapples with both personal and political conflicts.A survivor in the republic's final hours, he considers lucky those who, like the elder Hortensius, died before seeing the massacre at Pharsalus.He goes so far as to claim that, unlike Hortensius, those orators who live have had their voices extinguished not by his own death, but by that of the republic.1 Yet his friends Atticus and Brutus, who interrupt his silent and anxious otium, seek to restore his voice by leading him toward the processes of remembering and recounting. 2 Cicero's treatise comes at a pivotal moment when the republic suffers from a deserted forum, yet, within the treatise, memory of a more stable, secure past is renewed and revived.Cicero both uses his voice to remember and invokes a time when eloquence had a significant role in the republic.In addition, the conclusion of the Brutus offers the reader a glimpse of the need to protect eloquence, an aspect of rhetoric traditionally employed for intervening in and modifying political reality.But here, Cicero advances the notion of a life withdrawn from political reality, a mode of living entirely "pure," far from the contamination of one who would employ speech in the service of the troubled state (Brut.330):1 Brut.328-9. 2 I have argued elsewhere (Marchese (2011) 22-30) that reciprocity and memory animate the conversation among Cicero, Brutus and Atticus, transforming the social practice of eloquence into a norm for the future.
title: SPEECH AND SILENCE IN CICERO'S FINAL DAYS
