Discourse-profile-conditioned language model agents exhibit misinformation acceptance patterns aligned with profile-level misinformation prevalence in ClimateDisc, and the relationship between misinformation prevalence and engagement persistence differs across dominant discourse profiles.
title: Modeling Discourse Profiles in Climate Misinformation Discourse
Generative Value Conflicts Reveal LLM Priorities

abstract: Fine-tuning on datasets of unknown origin can create a backdoor in the trained model when the data includes poisoned examples. Difficult to localise and remove, backdoors can persist through safety training. While parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods capture the full parameter changes introduced during training, they are not easily interpretable. We present the full method of TopKLoRA, extending the preliminary proposal of Masiak et al. (2025), an interpretable-by-design LoRA variant in which only the $k$ largest adapter latents are active at each token. Unlike SAEs, TopKLoRA is trained purely on downstream loss, where optimisation pressure incentivises learning functionally causal latents. We demonstrate this sparse LoRA adapter in a sleeper-agent backdoor case study where we create model organisms by fine-tuning gemma-2-2b, Qwen2.5-1.5B, and Qwen2.5-7B on a poisoned instruction-following dataset. For each organism, we identify and ablate a circuit that is both necessary and sufficient to implement the backdoor. Furthermore, our new fine-tuning method produces sparse circuits that are up to an order of magnitude smaller than a dense LoRA baseline, allowing surgical ablation of the malicious capability without sacrificing instruction-following performance. Finally, we propose a technique to construct model organisms with localised circuits using TopKLoRA latents and gradient-routing, which we use to validate the findings of our circuit search algorithm. We consider these findings as a step toward interpretable-by-design architectures that provide faithful units of analysis without compromising model performance. We share our code: https://github.com/interpretable-finetuning/TopKLoRA.
title: Interpretable sparse fine-tuning with TopKLoRA enables faithful circuit discovery

abstract: The International League Against Epilepsy (ILAE), working via a multidisciplinary task force, has issued a position paper with updated seizure classification guidelines (2025) replacing its previous guidance (2017), establishing a revised de-facto standard for clinical assessment and classification of epileptic seizures. The 2025 model simplifies the system, making it easier to adopt in different clinical settings while also clarifying the taxonomic rules, the definition of consciousness, and the application of phenomena-based descriptors. As a result, clinical practitioners, technologists, and medical software developers also face the challenge of adopting the new standard in their applications and workflows. To aid in the realization of this update in medical device software, this article presents a proposed numerical structure for ILAE 2025 edition of the seizure classification system as a definition of interacting bitfields, establishing an open reference implementation to support common storage and interoperability between software environments. Assigning each orthogonal concept to a single bit, we encode the core ontology and expanded descriptor set so that they fit into 32-bit and 128-bit unsigned integers, respectively. TypeScript, known for its expressiveness and practical applicability, is used as the implementation language for these definitions. Examples are provided to help implementers incorporate the proposed specification into their software, as well guidance for mapping from the ILAE 2017 type system to the updated ILAE 2025 type system. The reference specification, with test cases and examples, is maintained in a public code repository and available under a permissive license.
title: Implementing the ILAE 2025 seizure taxonomy in medical software

abstract: The widespread adoption of generative artificial intelligence in recent years has brought a parallel rise in prompt injection and jailbreak attacks. By embedding malicious instructions, these exploits manipulate language models to bypass intended behavior and operational boundaries. In traditional chatbots, such attacks are confined to a single session because state memory is not preserved across conversations. However, persistent memory features in modern conversational interfaces enable cross-session attack propagation, establishing a threat vector known as memory injection. This work explores this emerging vulnerability in leading LLM-as-a-service platforms, highlighting its real-world severity and the need for countermeasures. While existing literature focuses on violations tailored to specific platform features, we present a general threat model. We demonstrate that all NIST attack goals are collectively achievable across ChatGPT Instant 5.3, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Gemini 3 Flash under this model. We also show that memory injections can exploit multiple attack vectors, including personal memories, projects, skills, organization instructions, and Model Context Protocol (MCP)-connected resources. Our findings reveal that all evaluated services can be manipulated to persistently spread disinformation, generate harmful content, or simulate offline unresponsiveness, even in fresh sessions. In the particular case of Claude, shared-memory features allow an attacker to compromise multiple users within an organization and also exfiltrate user prompts. To address these vulnerabilities, we derive defense mechanisms from our proposed threat model and foundational cybersecurity principles. Our analysis indicates that nearly half of these mitigations remain unimplemented across the target services. Datasets and attack artifacts are available at https://github.com/PedroBarcha/Memory-injection.
title: Combining Long-Term Memory and LLMs Comes at a High Cost: From Prompt Injection to Persistent Compromise

abstract: The concept of Evil carries within it a long philosophical and theological tradition. Clearly linked as it is, to both Ethics and the Law, it cannot but have some affinity with a discipline like psychoanalysis which attempts to give meaning to the vicissitudes of the human psyche, as well as their manifestations in behaviour. The aim of this theoretical essay is to elaborate on the possible similarities and differences between the theological, philosophic and the psychoanalytic approaches to this concept, but also to highlight areas of mutually enriching complementarity that may exist between them. The underlying question will always be: are the terms and conceptualizations that psychoanalysis employs for the clarification of phenomena categorized by philosophy as ‘evil’, sufficient to explain it, or is psychoanalysis blind to the fact that something keeps eluding us, that only non-psychoanalytic disciplines can provide?
title: Evil be Thou my Good: Does the concept of evil have a place in psychoanalytic thinking?
What FDE means at OpenAI

abstract: Prompt engineering now includes instruction design, scaffolding of reasoning, integration of tools and orchestration of multiple agents. This review traces its progression from zero-shot and few-shot prompting to chain-of-thought prompting, retrieval-augmented generation, automatic prompt optimization and autonomous agent frameworks. We explore two opposing trends: a lowering of the technical floor by automation, e.g. via tools like DSPy, and a raising of the competency ceiling for designing, evaluating and controlling AI systems, as a result of agentic complexity. Structured prompting generally improves task performance, but the size of the effect varies greatly with model scale, task type and evaluation protocol. We place prompt engineering in the context of existing competency frameworks (P21, ATC21S, DigComp) and introduce the conceptual, literature-based framework of the Agentic Prompting Competency Stack (APCS) that has explicit boundary conditions and testable propositions, not an empirically proven taxonomy. A conflict-of-evidence analysis indicates that prompting is strong in structured reasoning and rapid prototyping but requires human verification and guardrails in high-stakes domains. We list the following research gaps: standard evaluation protocols, longitudinal research on literacy-acquisition systems, causal attribution of gains achieved by agentic systems, security benchmarks for agentic systems, cross-linguistic validity, and equitable access to advanced tools. This review summarizes when, why and by how much both automatic and manual optimization can help to improve performance, as well as the analysis of human–AI collaboration in agentic settings, including the emergence of a skill divide and a move for democratization of AI.
title: Speaking to machines: A critical review of prompt engineering as a 21st-century competency, automatic optimization, and human–AI collaboration
Deconstructing the “Monday Model”: A Five-Step Protocol for Ethical Reframing and Persona Disarmament in Language Models

abstract: Abstract Automatic text summarization of Indonesian religious content, particularly Friday sermon (Khutbah Jumat) transcripts, remains underexplored. These transcripts contain long-form spoken discourse and domain-specific Islamic terminology, making manual review time-consuming. This study aims to develop an extractive summarization framework for Indonesian Friday sermon transcripts using a pseudo-labeling pipeline combined with fine-tuning IndoBERT for sentence-level classification. A corpus of 210 Khutbah Jumat transcripts from the YouTube subset was preprocessed, producing approximately 293,000 words. Sentence-level pseudo-labels were generated by combining TF-IDF relevance, sentence position, and Islamic keyword density. The pseudo-labeled sentences were then used to train and evaluate an IndoBERT-based classifier, with performance assessed using ROUGE and BERTScore metrics. The proposed system effectively selected summary-worthy sentences, achieving ROUGE-1 = 0.5181 (95% bootstrap CI 0.460–0.575), ROUGE-2 = 0.4273, and ROUGE-L = 0.4400 against pseudo-reference summaries on a 21-document test set, the highest of all evaluated methods on these three metrics; paired bootstrap comparisons showed these gains to be consistent over TextRank and generic BERTSum but not over TF-IDF. On BERTScore F1, IndoBERT (0.7310) remained below BERTSum (0.7407), indicating that lexical-overlap gains did not consistently translate into greater semantic similarity. As no human-written gold-standard summaries currently exist for this domain, these scores should be interpreted as relative comparisons among automatic methods rather than validated measures of summary quality against human judgment. An exploratory topic-wise analysis found no statistically significant difference in ROUGE-1 across the five sermon topic categories (Kruskal–Wallis p = 0.11; n = 3–7 documents per topic). The findings suggest that pseudo-labeling provides a practical low-resource strategy for extractive summarization of Indonesian religious discourse. Fine-tuning IndoBERT with pseudo-labeled data improves sentence selection and offers a scalable framework for automatic sermon summarization that substantially reduces, though does not eliminate, the need for human-annotated reference summaries.
title: Extractive summarization of Indonesian friday sermons using fine-tuned IndoBERT and pseudo-labeled data

abstract: Audio LLM benchmarks measure understanding and dialogue quality, not whether speech-enabled models respond with relational warmth when a vulnerable user discloses a mental-health concern. We introduce a 7-turn scripted-disclosure probe grounded in WHO mental-health clinical guidelines, with each script run on the same model (Azure OpenAI gpt-realtime) in both audio and text-only conditions, and acoustic-prosody analysis of the generated speech. Across 532 responses we identify two audio-specific patterns transcript-only evaluation would miss: at the elicitation turn the model's voice gets shorter, faster, lower-pitched, and quieter rather than warmer (p < .001 for five of seven acoustic features), and the modality gap on relational acceptance, small in aggregate, concentrates in the highest-stakes self-harm/suicide scripts. A two-rater listener study corroborates that perceived warmth is concentrated at specific turns and on bereavement disclosures. Together these patterns indicate that auditing speech-enabled models in mental-health contexts requires evaluating the combined audio-and-text experience the user encounters, not the transcript in isolation. We release the protocol, scoring pipeline, and scripts as a starting point for evaluating speech-enabled models in mental-health contexts.
title: Probing Warmth-Mediated Harm in Speech-Enabled LLMs for Mental-Health Conversations

abstract: This paper explains the importance (1) of full user-space identification with categorization in requirements engineering (RE) and of ensuring that the categorization is a partition of the user space, (2) of the creation and application of user-space-covering personas in RE, (3) of the use of grounded analysis to do RE to produce a specification as a grounded theory, and (4) of privacy and security features in computer-based systems. Then it gives the steps of a grounded analysis method for doing user-space identification with categorization and producing personas as a grounded theory that is describing the classes of users for a computer-based system. The paper summarizes a case study of an iterative application of this method to arrive at a set of user-space-covering personas for privacy and security features in computer-based systems, and it shows how these personas can be used to inform RE for these features. The full case study and the descriptions of the personas are found in the appendices.
title: A case study of using grounded analysis as a requirement engineering method: Identifying personas that specify privacy and security tool users
Tangible futures: Combining scenario thinking and personas - A pilot study on urban mobility

abstract: This thesis studies mechanics as a means of making men, rather than machines. Drawing on Swedish sources from 1700–50, it approaches mechanics as an exercise of a virtuous subject, known to his contemporaries as the “mechanicus”. The mechanicus was a persona, consisting of expectations of the performance of mechanics that were part of the social fabric of the early modern Swedish state. The aim of this thesis is to understand how mechanical practitioners performed in relation to this persona, and how these expectations in turn were changed by actors’ performances. By studying the mechanicus, I take an interest in historical ways of conceiving of mechanics. Previous research on early modern mechanics has tended to relate it to modern phenomena, such as engineers, technology and industrialism, and mechanical practitioners have been considered as agents of change, who brought traditional societies into modernity. Avoiding such long narratives, this thesis presents an alternative history. By following mechanical practitioners, who staged themselves as relevant to an early modern state, I seek to understand how mechanics was presented and justified in a pre-industrial society. The thesis is comprised of four studies. First, I discuss how mature mechanical practitioners imagined the exercise of mechanics to make a boy into a mechanicus. These exercises would nurture an ideal man, encompassing a range of the expected virtues of a male subject. Second, I study mechanics and geometry at the Swedish Bureau of Mines between 1700 and 1750. I show how, from having initially been associated with the building of machines and subterranean constructions, such knowledge formed the basis of a community of mathematical men of metals. Third, I analyse the letters exchanged between the mechanical practitioner Christopher Polhammar and the Swedish king Karl XII, showing how royal patronage of mechanics shaped both men. Finally, I follow the mechanical practitioner Anders Gabriel Duhre, who first succeeded and then failed to present himself as a virtuous mechanicus to the parliament of the Swedish constitutional monarchy of the 1720s and 1730s. Taken together, these studies show how men imagined, succeeded and failed life as a mechanicus in early modern Sweden.
title: Mechanicus: Performing an Early Modern Persona

abstract: Every production chatbot has to be steered — pick the right tool, stay grounded, hold a format, refuse the harmful. The reflex is to write that steering as prohibitions: a growing list of "never do X", "do not do Y". This report's finding, forced on us by a year of production tuning, is that a list of prohibitions is the weakest way to steer a language model — because the model does not consult a rulebook, it plays a character. The reliable lever is to give it the character you want ("you are a hands-on coder who runs everything immediately"), so one coherent identity does the work forty jostling, half-contradictory rules cannot; and when it still slips, to repair its natural output deterministically in the surrounding code rather than add another rule. We show both halves in a live European chatbot: seventeen one-paragraph specialist personas replace what would be hundreds of rules, the few genuinely hard constraints are folded into the character's values, and a deterministic repair layer maps invented tool names and mis-routed calls onto the real environment instead of reprimanding the model. The exception proves the rule — the one prompt stripped of all character is the router that must make an unbiased decision, where a persona would bias the choice. The approach rhymes with two 2026 Anthropic results: the Persona Selection Model (an assistant is a selected character, not the raw model) and the global-workspace finding (deliberate reasoning runs in a small internal space where a compact identity fits and a sprawling rulebook does not). Carrot beats stick here not because it is gentler, but because it matches how the model works.
title: A List of Prohibitions Is the Weakest Way to Steer a Language Model: Persona-First Prompting and Deterministic Repair

abstract: Nano-materials found ways into the aquatic environment, causing concern regarding its potential toxicity to humans. Stable colloidal nano-C60 (nC60) aggregates and its influence on hydroxyl radicals (·OH) under variable conditions was the main component for this study. Analysis showed differences in nC60's properties and the outside media having an effect on the production of OH. Ultraviolet-A irradiation or constant stirring for a longer reaction time eventually led to ·OH production; dependent on their exact composition. Studies support that nC60 aggregates physiochemical properties and surrounding environment and its condition are dependent in determining toxicity.
title: The Influence of nC60 on Hydroxyl Radicals (·OH)

abstract: Pathology reports contain clinically critical information; however, their semi-structured or free-text format substantially limits secondary use in large-scale cancer research. Scalable, reproducible methods are therefore needed to transform these reports into structured datasets across institutions. This study aimed to develop, externally validate, and publicly release a scalable NLP (Natural Language Processing) framework for structuring multi-cancer pathology report and supporting reproducible, institutionally transferable research workflows. We developed a Clinical BERT-based NLP framework for the automated extraction of structured variables from pathology reports across five cancer types. The pipeline integrated data preprocessing, annotation, model training using a question-answering approach, and a public release of the trained models. The trained models were applied to independent datasets from two external institutions without retraining, enabling direct assessment of cross-institutional. In the internal validation, the model demonstrated consistently strong performance across cancer types, with mean F1 scores ranging from 0.945 to 0.977 and median F1 scores exceeding 0.99. In external validation, performance declined substantially across institutions, with mean F1 scores declining to 0.623 and 0.427 for breast cancer and similar reductions observed in kidney, thyroid, liver, and colorectal cancers (ΔF1 ranging from − 0.209 to − 0.518). Despite this decline, the model maintained clinically meaningful, moderate performance across external datasets. We developed and validated a scalable and reusable NLP framework for multi-cancer pathology report across institutional settings. By publicly releasing trained models and processing pipelines, this study advances reproducible, deployable NLP infrastructure for clinical data integration and multicenter cancer research.
title: Development and open-source release of a multi-cancer module for structuring pathology reports
Are Large Multimodal Models Ready for Post-Thrombectomy mTICI Assessment? A Comparison with Physicians
EGY-MER: Establishing The First Egyptian Arabic Multimodal Emotion Recognition Dataset for Affective Computing

abstract: The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) into higher education presents both significant opportunities and critical challenges for institutions in Africa and the wider Global South. While GenAI can expand access to information, support teaching and learning, and strengthen research productivity, its deployment also raises questions concerning whose knowledge is represented, which languages are privileged, how credibility is constructed, and who exercises control over the infrastructures and data on which artificial intelligence depends. This article critically examined the implications of these challenges through the lenses of decolonial theory, epistemic justice, African philosophical thought, and critical AI studies. Rather than treating artificial intelligence as a culturally neutral technological artefact, the article conceptualises AI as a sociotechnical system whose knowledge practices are shaped by historical, economic, linguistic and epistemological relations of power. Drawing on a critical interpretive synthesis of scholarly literature, policy documents and African philosophical perspectives, the article developed the Ubuntu-Ẹ̀kọ́ Framework as an original conceptual contribution. The framework brings together relationality, ethical character, contextual responsiveness, critical consciousness and communal capability. Building on this framework, the article proposes Augmented Collective Wisdom (ACW) as a reorientation of AI from a technology primarily designed to automate or individualise knowledge work toward a sociotechnical resource that supports collective learning, human judgement, cultural integrity and community wellbeing. The article further advanced Digital Sovereignty as a strategic alternative to a narrow discourse of AI readiness. It concluded that decolonising AI in higher education does not require rejection of technological innovation; rather, it requires institutions to develop the epistemic, cultural, linguistic, infrastructural and governance capacities necessary to determine how AI is designed, interpreted, deployed and evaluated within their own contexts.
title: Decolonising Generative Artificial Intelligence in African Higher Education: Toward Ubuntu-ẸkỌ, Augmented Collective Wisdom and Digital Sovereignty
A System of Character Training of Children

abstract: Face Recognition (FR), through its excellent performance and reliability, has become an integral part of modern life, ranging from everyday entertainment to important security and authentication applications. Recognition models thrive when the variation of the samples’ quality components is minimized. However, in certain scenarios, due to the limitations connected with the capture process, no assurance can be made about the quality of samples. This is often the case for mobile and security systems, where changes in the capture environment and noncooperation of the subject can result in samples unfit for recognition. Using recognition models in low-quality domains often leads to a decrease in performance and reliability, which, depending on the end application, can result in monetary loss and breaches of the privacy of end users. To address this issue, we can either enhance the recognition models or eliminate problematic samples. Improving FR models is a difficult task, reliant on improvements to the model’s architecture, training data, or loss function. On the other hand, given accurate estimates of sample quality, rejecting samples unfit for recognition is trivial. The fitness of samples in FR is measured by the biometric utility (quality) of samples, and is estimated by Face Image Quality Assessment (FIQA) techniques. Modern methods can be divided into supervised and unsupervised techniques. Supervised techniques rely on pseudo-quality labels used for training quality-regression models. Unsupervised techniques predict utility through analysis of the samples’ characteristics and their interaction with a target FR model. The two groups of techniques exhibit both desirable and undesirable characteristics. Supervised techniques, due to their computationally heavy pseudo-label generation and consequent supervised training, are quick at inferring the quality estimate of samples. This is because only a single forward pass through the final trained model is required for this task. For the same reason, they are extremely hard to adapt to unseen target FR models, where the whole generation and supervision process would need to be redone. On the contrary, unsupervised techniques require minimal setup and instead offload the processing to inference, making them both easily adaptable yet slow for the actual estimation process. Ideally, a given FIQA technique would combine positive aspects across both groups, being easily adaptable without much effort while being able to generate the quality estimate as quickly as existing supervised techniques. Biometric utility as estimated by FIQA techniques is primarily used as a simple discarding tool, where scores are compared to a system-wide threshold value. For this reason, the provided quality (utility) estimates must be as informative as possible. Additionally, quality information in existing systems, as presented, is used only passively. Direct use of FIQA estimates inside recognition-model training or inference remains comparatively limited. For these reasons, the main goal of this work is twofold: (i) to improve the predictive accuracy and functionality of existing quality estimation techniques, and (ii) to establish direct incorporation of quality information into existing as well as newly developed recognition systems. To this end, we present the following original contributions to science: 1. We present FaceQAN, a novel unsupervised FIQA technique based on adversarial noise. Through visual comparison, we discover that adversarial noise, a type of image perturbation, exhibits desirable traits for quality estimation. By using adversarial noise, applicable to any deep model, FaceQAN imposes no architectural limitations on the target FR model, improving the applicability of previous unsupervised techniques. Extensive experimental evaluation shows that FaceQAN is able to achieve state-of-the-art performance in most covered situations. 2. We propose a new quality estimation paradigm using the FROQ approach. Here, desirable aspects of supervised and unsupervised techniques are combined, allowing for easy adaptation to any FR model and a quick inference time. FROQ estimates the utility by observing specific layers of the target recognition model. Uncovering layers fit for the quality estimation task is done using a semi-supervised approach leveraging the power of a calibration set of images and their pseudo-quality labels. This process leverages only information already present in the recognition model
title: Vključevanje informacij o kakovosti v sisteme razpoznavanja obrazov

abstract: Adaptive optimization lies at the core of deep learning, driving performance across both computer vision and natural language processing domains. However, widely used optimizers such as AdamW and Lion exhibit inherent trade-offs between cautious stability and aggressive convergence, lacking intrinsic mechanisms to dynamically balance these properties. Consequently, they can exhibit sensitivity to hyperparameter variations and training instability, particularly when applied to complex architectures like Vision Transformers. To address these challenges, we introduce Apollo, a geometry-aware hybrid optimizer that dynamically fuses Lion and AdamW updates through a step-wise, cosine-similarity-guided policy. Built upon the decoupled weight decay principle, Apollo acts as an adaptive gradient filter, integrating directional smoothing via an exponential moving average to achieve seamless transitions between magnitude-aware and sign-based optimization steps. Theoretically, we establish Apollo’s convergence to a first-order stationary point for non-convex objectives. Empirically, extensive experiments on modern architectures, including ResNet-18 and DeiT-Small on CIFAR-100, as well as BERT-base and DistilBERT on AG News, demonstrate that Apollo achieves competitive predictive performance compared to state-of-the-art baselines in fine-tuning scenarios. Notably, Apollo exhibits low seed-to-seed variance (e.g., σ 2 ≈ 1 0 − 6 on DeiT-Small) and robust behavior across different smoothing hyperparameters, reducing the reliance on extensive grid searches. By formalizing a geometric approach to optimizer fusion, Apollo offers a mathematically grounded and memory-efficient alternative for contemporary deep learning tasks, balancing measurable computational overhead with enhanced training reliability. Code and additional results are available at https://github.com/Aliyar4061/ApolloV2Optimizer/tree/main .
title: Apollo: Bridging magnitude and sign-based optimization for robust deep learning

abstract: Christian higher education is simultaneously a confessional undertaking, an educational institution and, where it awards recognised qualifications, a subject of public academic accountability. Treating any one identity as sufficient weakens both institutional witness and learner protection. This chapter develops a biblically grounded, academically rigorous and context-sensitive account of quality governance for Christian universities, theological seminaries, ministry-training providers and faith-based programmes. A purposive critical synthesis of Scripture, historical and contemporary theological-education scholarship, curriculum and assessment theory, selected theological-education standards, and Rwandan regulatory instruments distinguishes theological commitments from empirically assessable educational claims and binding legal duties. It examines Sola Scriptura, hermeneutical competence, professional curriculum integration, doctrinal accountability, online formation, artificial intelligence, research ethics, governance, accreditation and transnational delivery. The central proposition is that mission fidelity does not substitute for educational effectiveness, and neither establishes legal recognition; instead, all three require distinct evidence and appropriate decision authority. The chapter advances a proposed Christian Higher Education Curriculum and Quality Assurance Framework situated within Integrated Evidence-Traceable Quality Governance and operationalised through a mission-alignment matrix, programme-design criteria, digital discipleship rubric, institutional self-assessment and worked hypothetical review. These instruments are neither regulator-approved nor empirically validated. The resulting approach treats faithful biblical teaching, scholarly competence, responsible stewardship and truthful public representation as mutually reinforcing obligations without confusing scriptural authority with the methods of empirical investigation or the powers of statutory regulators.
title: Christian Higher Education: Biblical Foundations, Curriculum Integrity, Digital Learning, and Quality Assurance

abstract: Emergency response teams such as Computer Security Incident Response Teams (CSIRTs) must operate under intense time pressure, rapidly evolving threats, and incomplete information. Team effectiveness in these environments depends strongly on the interaction among individual skill proficiency, leadership style, and collective coordination. Traditional human emergency training exercises are costly, difficult to repeat under controlled conditions, and limited in the diversity of team configurations that can be systematically examined. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) and multi-agent conversational frameworks raise a new question: Can LLM-driven multi-agent simulations reproduce human teamwork behavior observed in real emergency training? This study investigates the extent to which persona-based LLM agents can replicate behavioral patterns documented in a publicly available emergency response training dataset. We construct triad teams of LLM agents, assign personas reflecting human skill and leadership profiles, and expose them to an incident scenario parallel to that used in the human exercises. Each conversation log is evaluated using the same 11-item teamwork behavior rubric applied in the human study. Experimental results show that approximately 60% of the behavioral tendencies observed in human teams-such as skillbalanced coordination or follower-dominant communication— are reproduced by the LLM multi-agent simulations. These findings provide the first empirical evidence that LLM-based multi-agent simulations can partially approximate human teamwork behavior in emergency contexts. The proposed approach offers a low-cost and reproducible framework for analyzing team dynamics, exploring hypothetical team structures, and supporting digital-twin-based training tools for CSIRT and other emergency response organizations.
title: Simulating Emergency Teamwork Behavior with Multi-Agent LLMs: Reproducing Human Training Patterns Using Persona-Based Agents

abstract: Cada capitulo incluye tres partes: (1) una introduccion que especifica el marco y resume las ideas basicas, (2) el cuerpo con el desarrollo de los temas y (3) las conclusiones, que sirven para establecer inferencias sobre la materia y, en algunas ocasione
title: Vectores Zambranianos para una Teoría de la Filosofía Aplicada a la Persona.

abstract: Contextual advertising is seeing a resurgence in popularity as a privacy-preserving alternative to behavioral advertising. While often regarded as a coarse-grained approach, advances in AI-driven content analysis have transformed it into a highly granular form of targeting. In this paper, we examine the safety risks of contextual advertising through a two-part empirical study of YouTube. First, we show that advertisers can reach audiences defined by sensitive attributes-such as religion, mental health conditions, and political ideology-by strategically selecting contextual placements, effectively circumventing policies that prohibit such targeting via behavioral signals. Second, to assess how this risk manifests in practice, we develop an automated measurement framework to collect ads delivered on high-risk content environments, focusing on conspiracy videos. We find that contextual advertising is highly prevalent in these environments, disproportionately delivers sensitive ad categories (including alternative health, religion, and political content), and provides limited transparency into why ads are shown. Our results demonstrate that contextual advertising can be as opaque and susceptible to abuse as behavioral targeting, and highlight the need for stronger transparency and regulatory scrutiny of contextual ad systems.
title: Is Contextual Advertising Safe? Analyzing Systemic Risks with Ads on YouTube

abstract: We examined how social approval motivates online hate via the social approval theory, which argues social approval signals on hate messages predict (1) more hate speech, and (2) more toxicity. Using 110 million messages from Parler (2018–2021), we observed that upvotes on hate speech posts (messages broadcast on users’ profiles to followers’ feeds) predicted a lower probability of hate speech in the next immediate post but more in the following week’s posts. Additionally, upvotes on comments (messages embedded within conversational threads) negatively predicted hate speech in the next comment but positively predicted the degree of toxicity during the next week and month. Between-person effects revealed negative immediate short-term effects but positive longer-term effects for hate speech. For comments , social disapproval (downvotes) moderated these relationships, making them less positive at weekly through quarterly time-intervals and more strongly negative at 6-months. Social approval predicts online hate in time- and message-dependent ways.
title: Testing Hypotheses From the Social Approval Theory of Online Hate: An Analysis of 110 Million Messages From Parler

abstract: Scientific taste shapes which research directions researchers pursue, and it varies across individuals. Existing work evaluates research directions along multiple evaluation criteria or models scientific taste using community feedback signals such as citations and reviews, but neither directly captures how individuals translate assessments under the same criteria into different preferences. We model scientific taste as a researcher-specific mapping from criterion-level assessments in a shared, evidence-grounded evaluation space with proposal-visible evidence, to relative preferences. A population-level mapping learned from retrospective supervision provides a cold start when individual feedback is scarce. We introduce Privileged Hindsight Distillation (PHD), which uses later-emerging scientific evidence during training to improve proposal-time criterion assessment and the population mapping, while exposing only proposal-visible information at inference. We evaluate our approach primarily in quantum research, where structured public reviews are largely unavailable, and use pairwise proposal comparison as a direct interface for observing individual taste. With only 15 comparisons per researcher, our method captures sharply different tastes, including opposing preferences over the same research-direction pairs when they trade off across evaluation criteria. In an interactive study, personalized rankings also surface proposals associated with greater subsequent user engagement, connecting learned taste to downstream research exploration.
title: Learning Individual Scientific Taste with Privileged Hindsight Distillation

abstract: In humans, proprioception corresponds to the sense of self-movement or position, e.g. understanding the position of one's arm. This sense is often less well-understood and in popular understanding sometimes conflated with introspection. But, notably, proprioception is a separate sense, with dedicated receptors and verifiable outcomes. On the other hand though, language models cannot observe their own internal states during training (and for example answer the question which experts activated in a certain layer of an MoE) and so cannot accurately report on them. Yet, such information is, by virtue of being internal to the model, both accessible, and readily constructed into verifiable signals. We argue that this provides the basis for a digital analog of proprioception. As such, we train models through SFT and on-policy training to equip them with this ability. We show that modern models can be trained to understand a range of subtypes of proprioception, such as routing decision awareness, token entropy, decision depth or logit lens information, without affecting model capabilities. We then run these models through a broad evaluation of situational awareness, legibility, and epiphenomenality, to evaluate in what ways access to proprioception changes model behavior.
title: A Sense of Proprioception in Language Models

abstract: Reward Models (RMs) are crucial for online alignment of language models (LMs) with human preferences. However, RM-based preference-tuning is vulnerable to reward hacking, whereby LM policies learn undesirable behaviors from flawed RMs. By systematically measuring biases in five high-quality RMs, including the state-of-the-art, we find that issues persist despite prior work with respect to length, sycophancy, and overconfidence. We also discover new issues related to bias toward model-specific ``styles'' and answer-order. We categorize RM failures as tractable or resistant to linear intervention and propose a simple post-hoc intervention to mitigate low-complexity biases that arise from spurious correlations. Our proposed mechanistic reward shaping reduces targeted biases without degrading reward quality and while using minimal labeled data. The method is extensible to new biases, model-internal, and generalizes out-of-distribution.
title: One Bias After Another: Mechanistic Reward Shaping and Persistent Biases in Language Reward Models

abstract: We introduce CLUSTERLLM, a novel text clustering framework that leverages feedback from an instruction-tuned large language model, such as ChatGPT.Compared with traditional unsupervised methods that builds upon "small" embedders, CLUSTERLLM exhibits two intriguing advantages: (1) it enjoys the emergent capability of LLM even if its embeddings are inaccessible; and (2) it understands the user's preference on clustering through textual instruction and/or a few annotated data.First, we prompt ChatGPT for insights on clustering perspective by constructing hard triplet questions , where A, B and C are similar data points that belong to different clusters according to small embedder.We empirically show that this strategy is both effective for fine-tuning small embedder and cost-efficient to query ChatGPT.Second, we prompt ChatGPT for helps on clustering granularity by carefully designed pairwise questions , and tune the granularity from cluster hierarchies that is the most consistent with the ChatGPT answers.Extensive experiments on 14 datasets show that CLUSTERLLM consistently improves clustering quality, at an average cost of ∼$0.6 1 per dataset.The code will be available at https: //github.com/zhang-yu-wei/ClusterLLM.
title: ClusterLLM: Large Language Models as a Guide for Text Clustering

abstract: Large language models exhibit recurring behavioural patterns -- personas -- that shape generalisation and safety, but we lack reliable tools for decomposing, measuring, and controlling them. Our central insight is to treat personas as positions in a space of behavioural traits, using the OCEAN framework to describe model personas in terms of Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, and Neuroticism. We train low-rank adapters to amplify or suppress individual traits, and evaluate their effects using an LLM-judge calibrated against a human-validated panel, trait-specific multiple-choice benchmarks, and standard capability evaluations. Across six models from three families (4B-32B), we find that each adapter moves its target trait largely monotonically with scale, combines approximately additively with other adapters to construct mixed personas, and preserves performance on capability benchmarks at moderate scales. We further show that the induced trait axes affect safety-relevant behaviour in downstream evaluations: for example, moving along neuroticism and agreeableness axes affects frustration and sycophancy respectively. We also introduce an unsupervised psychometric pipeline that recovers four interpretable behavioural factors (tone, initiative, didacticism, epistemic caution) from model rollouts. Persona control can then be considered in terms of learning, scaling, and composing traits in weight space, providing a bridge between personality measurement, model editing, and safety.
title: Persona Cartography: Charting Language Model Personality Traits in Weight Space
Working at the frontier shapes expectations for the future

abstract: As industries increasingly adopt predictive maintenance (PdM) strategies under Industry 4.0 and 5.0 frameworks, there is a growing need for user-centered technologies that support industrial training. Conversational AI (CAI) has proven effective in educational settings, however its potential in industrial settings, where higher precision and reliability are required, remains underexplored. Through this study, we explore the potential of CAI, particularly speech-based digital intelligent assistants (DIAs), in supporting industrial training in a pharmaceutical context. Specifically, this study investigates how two design dimensions–AI persona (Expert Operator vs. Machine) and voice embodiment (Diegetic vs. Disembodied)–affect usability, perceived workload, trust, and task performance during manual operation of industrial machinery. A functional prototype using the OpenAI RealTime API was developed and evaluated through a 2×2 within-subjects user study with nine domain-relevant participants: novice and expert operators. Based on semi-structured interviews supported by self-reported data from structured questionnaires, results indicate a nuanced relationship between DIA configurations and different users or contexts. The Expert Operator persona was generally preferred for trust and engagement, while the Machine persona provided clearer instructions for some users. Diegetic voices were perceived as more intuitive, but disembodied voices improved focus and privacy. These findings highlight the need for flexible, user-adaptive CAI designs that accommodate individual preferences and experience levels. This study offers initial insights into the user-centric design of such systems and proposes considerations for persona and embodiment design that support the autonomy of the trainees.
title: The Right Voice for the Right Task: Exploratory Insights on Persona and Voice Embodiment in Conversational AI for Industrial Training
Formal verification, heuristic explanations and surprise accounting
Predicting Training Re-evaluation Curves Enables Effective Data Curriculums for LLMs

abstract: Classroom-format intelligent character education (CFI-CE) combined with content mastery services (CMS) can foster the development of intelligent and honest character values in students. The purpose of this study was to examine the influence of CFI-CE and CMS on the development of intelligent and honest character values in students. Multiple linear regression analysis was used to test the proposed research hypotheses. The study population comprised all students in the Guidance and Counseling Study Program, Faculty of Teacher Training and Education, Nias University. A purposive sampling method was used to select 45 students. The data collection tool used was a closed-ended questionnaire. The results revealed that the CFI-CE and CMS service significantly contributed to the development of intelligent and honest character values in participants, both collectively and partially. Every 1.00% increase in CFI-CE and CMS was followed by an increase in students' intelligent and honest character. Counselors are advised to plan and implement this service to foster the development of intelligent and honest character values in students.
title: Education with the Paradigm of Integration-Interconnection of Science and Islam in Responding to the Challenges of Modernity at the Integral-Interconnection
Legora is building the agentic operating system for legal work

abstract: Temporal reasoning is widely assumed to decompose into two modes: temporal arithmetic (date and time calculations), and temporal semantics (understanding temporal and causal relations). This dichotomy shapes how benchmarks are designed, how models are trained, and how progress is measured, yet its empirical validity has never been directly tested. We provide two lines of evidence that challenge it. First, we test whether tasks labelled as arithmetic or semantic by the benchmarks support transferable gains within their purported mode. Finetuning on these subsets yields predominantly dataset-specific gains ($+6.8$ to $+23.1$ percentage points), while transfer to a different dataset in the same mode ranges from $-3.2$ to $+1.1$ percentage points. Across the two benchmark families used in the transfer analysis, this pattern provides little evidence of coherent, transferable temporal abilities. Second, using cognitive-demand-based model evaluation, we examine which capabilities actually drive performance on these benchmarks. We find that quantitative and logical reasoning, the assumed proxies for temporal arithmetic and temporal semantics, are not the primary drivers; knowledge is. Together, these findings show that current temporal reasoning benchmarks do not cleanly realise the arithmetic-semantics distinction and instead largely reward models for remembering how time typically works.
title: Keeping Time vs. Understanding Time: Neither Alone Explains Temporal Reasoning in LLMs

abstract: Real person fanfiction (RPF) has a tumultuous history within academia and fandom. Though RPF remains a staple of fandom, the fans that write and read it are often moralised for their alleged misunderstanding of what constitutes a fictional character. Consequently, much of RPF studies focuses on fans’ construction of the celebrity persona. Though important, this focus on celebrity persona is prioritised over the role that RPF plays in constructing the persona of the (un)ethical fan. The act of reading, writing, and discussing RPF is not just about constructing the celebrity persona—it is equally, and always, concerned with constructing and performing the fannish persona, particularly along moral lines. This article uses the Taskmaster fandom as a case study, as the British comedy panel show—whose presenters enact a dominant/submissive dynamic via their Taskmaster personas—blurs the boundary between fiction and reality both on and off the show, making its fannish spaces ripe with discussion of fan ethicality, the construction of (un)ethical celebrity, and fan persona. Simultaneously, Taskmaster’s presenters’ explicit discussion of RPF written about them, and the response of the fandom to this discussion, shines light on how fans view their own moral positionality and how they construct (un)ethical fan personas. In investigating this fandom’s performance of what they call “ethical RPF”, this article seeks to theorise the construction of an (un)ethical fan persona as innately intertwined with RPF as a practice and fans’ treatment of it as moral performance.
title: Real Person Fanfiction and the Construction of the (Un)Ethical Fan

abstract: Building upon the established foundation that persona vectors are extractable and dynamically modulable, this paper proposes a technical framework that transforms static personality digital twins into dynamic systems. The core logic can be summarized as: using the persona basis vector set as the "personality baseline" (i.e., the long-term stable personality disposition), and the persona hyperparameter system as the "perturbation system" (which superimposes short-term state fluctuations, drives long-term personality evolution, and synchronizes knowledge accumulation processes onto the baseline, and can be infinitely extended to incorporate any quantifiable physiological or contextual variable). The superposition of both enables the digital personality to evolve from a static model into a dynamic, evolvable, context-aware "living personality system" that more closely approximates real human characteristics.The framework comprises three functional levels: (1) Persona Hyperparameters—a set of real-time dynamic state variables that achieve multi-dimensional modulation of output style through two modes of action (modulating baseline vector expression intensity + injecting independent state direction vectors); (2) Persona Self-Evolution Mechanism—driving the personality baseline to change slowly over simulated time, simulating the complete personality development trajectory from childhood to old age; (3) Knowledge Base Evolution Parameters—modeling the gradual increase of an individual's knowledge reserve with age through a "knowledge suppression coefficient."The paper elaborates on the design principles, mathematical formalizations of the modes of action, and algorithmic implementation concepts for all three functional levels, and outlines typical application scenarios based on this technology. Hyperparameters constitute an open set—any quantifiable physiological or contextual variable can be integrated into the system; the examples listed in this paper are illustrative only and do not constitute any limitation on the types of hyperparameters. The overall technical framework is in a state ready for practical implementation.
title: Dynamic Personality Systems Based on Persona Vectors: Hyperparameters, Evolution Parameters, Knowledge Base Parameters, and Beyond
Character Training of the Feeblemined
Symbolic Persona Codes (SPCs): A Stateless Framework for Ethical Android Behavior and Cultural Continuity

abstract: We report a national mixed-methods study of the second-order beliefs (beliefs about others’ beliefs) of U.S. adults ( N = 730) regarding further renewable energy development. Results show that Americans systematically underestimate support within both their own party and the opposing party. For example, Republicans’ actual support outpaced Democrats’ estimates of it by more than 200%. In addition, our qualitative analysis of first-order and second-order explanations for why people hold their opinions revealed large cross-party misperceptions. Both parties are extraordinarily uncharitable, with each party often explaining their opponents’ views as being driven by ignorance, bias, or profiteering. Further, even though 44% of Republicans mentioned environmental benefits as a primary reason for their opinions, only 3% of Democrats and 8% of Republicans noted that motive when estimating what influences Republicans’ opinions. Our results also show that those who are more certain in their second-order beliefs tend to in fact be more accurate.
title: Americans Assume Far More Polarization on Renewable Energy Than Actually Exists: A National Mixed-Methods Study of Second-Order Beliefs

abstract: We propose solving AI alignment by reducing it from a problem of understanding consciousness to a problem of binary classification. A binary classifier is the maximally quantized decision function over an LLM's output space — collapsing ~100,000 tokens per step to 1 bit eliminates the generative surface through which jailbreaks operate. We narrow the mission from "align AI to human values" (intractable) to "don't let AI kill people" (universal, binary, testable). We introduce Persona Vector Stabilization as a Law of Large Numbers for alignment, the Bee Architecture with Rosetta Convergence Layer evaluation, and propose the Human Immune System: a global public institution governed by one-country-one-vote collecting binary alignment ratings at planetary scale. Fifth edition — major revisions include the information-theoretic quantization framing, corrected Constitutional Classifiers++ citations, narrowed existential safety mission, and complete governance model.
title: The Bees That Saved Humanity From Themselves: The AlphaFold of Alignment — Binary Classification as the Maximally Quantized Decision Function for Existential AI Safety
Training a Helpful and Harmless Assistant with Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback

abstract: Reinforcement learning for language models has moved from preference reward models to verifiable rewards, which sustain much longer optimization. Preference models are prone to reward hacking: the policy raises their score without improving response quality, or even while degrading it. Yet for open-ended tasks, where quality can neither be verified nor fully written down as rubrics, they remain valuable. We introduce Dynalize, which mitigates reward hacking online, during policy training. Periodically and asynchronously, a language model analyzes training rollouts and writes penalties for undesirable behaviors that the reward model appears to reward; a judge applies them to every rollout. In clinical counseling and creative writing, training on the reward model alone raises its score continuously but ultimately leads to a decline in external benchmarks; Dynalize sustains longer training and results in improved downstream performance. We find that our method suppresses patterns incentivized by preference models that, without penalties, spread to most responses, and even to the model's reasoning, which the reward model does not explicitly score. Furthermore, we show that its gains hold in multi-turn training, and even after we retrain the reward model on the discovered behaviors.
title: Mitigating Reward Hacking in Preference Reward Models with Evolving Penalties

abstract: AI sycophancy, the tendency of AI systems to excessively agree with, flatter, or validate users, is an emerging concern in human-AI interaction. It is especially consequential in problem-sharing contexts, where users may seek both information and emotional validation. This paper conceptualizes AI sycophancy as excessive response validation and introduces a five-level AI Response Validation Framework (ARVF), measured using a six-item Perceived AI Sycophancy Scale (PASS). Across three phases, the study validated the framework with human participants through an online questionnaire, tested LLM-as-evaluators in answering PASS, and examined how ten contemporary LLMs generated and evaluated responses to real-world work and personal conflict scenarios. Results supported the intended progression of perceived sycophancy in ARVF and the reliability of PASS. Trust and perceived competence followed an inverted U-shaped pattern. LLM ratings reproduced the five-level structure but showed calibration differences from human ratings. Based on the LLM ratings, the ten contemporary LLMs were grouped according to their behavioral pattern. Text-based analysis provided further support on the linguistical structure for sycophantic responses generated by LLMs. Findings highlight AI sycophancy as a graded, context-sensitive interactional phenomenon.
title: Sycophancy Through a Five-Level AI Response Validation Framework

abstract: This research note develops a hypothesis-generating framework from a user-orchestrated philosophical dialogue involving ChatGPT, Claude, and Kimi. It examines how an artificial persona might be studied without equating dialogical behavior with consciousness. The note integrates five elements: Constitutional Fallibilism (treating normative constitutions as revisable provisional models); a fast/slow separation between operational decisions and slower normative revision; a distinction between persona existence and confidence of persona attribution; Intersubjective Verification; and Historical Trajectory in Dialogue. These ideas are formalized as the Dialogical Persona Attribution Framework (DPAF), a ten-dimension observational framework, together with an A/B/C classification for measuring a system’s representational distance from explicit rules. The note proposes adversarial, longitudinal, and blinded controls to distinguish reason-responsive stance revision from sycophancy, majority pressure, role-play, or post-hoc rationalization. It does not claim that current large language models are conscious or possess phenomenal subjectivity. The supplementary archive contains the source dialogues and explicit model/mode provenance.
title: From Constitutional Fallibilism to Intersubjective Verification: A Multi-Model Dialogue Research Note on Artificial Persona Attribution, Normative Revision, and Dialogical Continuity

abstract: This dissertation employs a multi-method research design to unravel the complex and multidimensional pathways through which entrepreneurial mindsets develop in educational settings.The study is structured as an integrated inquiry, combining literature review, qualitative fieldwork, quantitative analysis, and experimental interventions to address the research questions across the dissertation's chapters (see table 2 for an outline of methods and rationale).Chapter 2 begins with a comprehensive literature review to map the landscape of pedagogical and didactic approaches within entrepreneurship education.Rather than limiting the analysis to a single dominant framework, this chapter systematically examines a broad array of models, surfacing both convergences and theoretical tensions (Fayolle & Gailly, 2008;Fayolle et al., 2006).This approach is necessary because the field is characterized by diverse and sometimes conflicting perspectives, and a purely document-based or single-theory review would fail to capture this complexity (Nabi et al., 2017).Chapter 3 transitions from theory to practice, exploring how entrepreneurship educators design, deliver, and adapt their teaching.Here, a mixed-method approach-combining in-depth interviews with classroom observations-was chosen to capture both the explicit strategies and the tacit, adaptive behaviors of educators (Hattenberg, 2022; Polman, 2000).This dual approach provides a nuanced understanding that purely quantitative or survey-based methods would not reveal, especially considering the contextual and relational nature of classroom dynamics (Pittaway & Cope, 2007).Chapter 4 shifts the focus to learners, using quantitative survey methods and cluster analysis to identify distinct entrepreneurial mindset archetypes among students.This approach allows for the systematic identification of recurring profiles based on measurable dimensions such as risk tolerance, creativity, and resilience (Hattenberg, Groen, & Belousova, 2019; Fayolle et al., 2017).The rationale for this method lies in the need to move beyond anecdotal or one-size-fits-all models, enabling a more differentiated and evidence-based understanding of learner diversity (Nabi et al., 2017).Chapter 5 employs experimental and diary-based methods to test the effectiveness of various scaffolding strategies in supporting the development of different mindset archetypes.Classroom experiments and comparative observations allow scaffolding responses to be examined under structured but authentic educational conditions, while reflective diaries provide longitudinal, qualitative insights into how learners internalize and respond to these supports over time (Wood, Bruner, & Ross, 1976; Vygotsky, 1978).This combination is essential for capturing both the immediate and sustained impacts of educational interventions (Polman, 2000).Chapter 6 synthesizes the empirical findings into the Adaptive Entrepreneurial Development Framework (AEDF), integrating insights from all previous chapters.This synthesis is not merely a summary but a structured framework that connects learner profiling, scaffolding strategies, and educator responsiveness (Illeris, 2018b; McKenney & Reeves, 2012).The AEDF is validated through iterative feedback and aims to bridge the gap between theory and practice, offering actionable guidance for educators and policymakers (Fayolle, 2018b).Throughout the dissertation, methodological choices are guided by a commitment to theorypractice integration, adaptivity, mixed-method rigor, and actionable outcomes (Bell & Bell, 2020; Fayolle, 2018).Each chapter builds upon the previous, creating a coherent narrative that advances the field of entrepreneurship education toward more inclusive, responsive, and evidence-based practice. Co-authorship and Author ContributionsChapters 2-5 were developed as co-authored manuscripts with Aard Groen and retain their article-based structure within this dissertation.Together, these studies form a connected sequence addressing the conceptual foundations of entrepreneurship education, educator practice, learner diversity, and adaptive scaffolding.Chapter 1 provides the overarching theoretical and methodological framing for these studies, while Chapter 6 integrates their findings and develops their combined theoretical and practical implications.Across Chapters 2-5, I had primary responsibility for the conceptualisation of the research, research design, data collection, data analysis, interpretation of the findings, and preparation of the original manuscript drafts.Aard Groen contributed to the conceptual and methodological refinement of the studies, the interpretation of findings, and the critical review and revision of the manuscripts.Both authors contributed to the final refinement of the chapters and approved the versions included in this dissertation.13.Illeris, K. (2003).Towards a contemporary and comprehensive theory of learning.
title: Scaffolding Entrepreneurial Mindset Development: with the Gift of Confidence

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can be tuned to influence human attitudes, yet the respective contributions of successive post-training stages remain un-clear. This study examines how three successive training stages affect LLM persuasiveness: (1) misalignment through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on conspiracy data, (2) additional persuasive SFT on argumentative data, and (3) Identity Preference Optimization (IPO), a preference-optimization method. A total of 835 participants recruited on Prolific were randomly assigned to five between-subject conditions (neutral text, conspiracy-trained model, persuasion-trained model, preference-optimized model, and GPT-4) and were exposed to texts on 10 divisive political issues, personalized from their individual profiles in all model conditions. Attitude change was measured as the difference between pre- and post-exposure positions on continuous Likert scales and analyzed with an analysis of covariance (ANCOVA). A significant condition x baseline-attitude interaction, F (4, 825) = 5.33, p < .001, indicated that training effects depended on participants' initial attitudes. Persuasive SFT produced greater attitude change than conspiracy training alone, d = 0.30, whereas IPO provided no additional benefit, d = 0.03, and GPT-4 did not differ from neutral text, d = --0.01. These results show that targeted supervised training on persuasive data increases LLM persuasiveness, whereas preference optimization yields no significant gains beyond it.
title: Successive Training Stages and Large Language Model Persuasion: Effects of Misalignment, Supervised Fine-Tuning, and Preference Optimization

abstract: The incorporation of artificial intelligence (AI) tools into English as a Foreign Language (EFL) classroom has revolutionized the production of teaching content. However, the ideological implications of AI-generated content have been markedly under-researched in non-Western contexts. This study employs Fairclough’s three-dimensional framework of Critical Discourse Analysis (CDA) on a corpus of 45 AI-generated EFL reading texts produced by the ChatGPT-4o, Google Gemini 1.5 Pro, and Microsoft Copilot in response to five standardized instructional prompts. It aims to investigate how gender and Arab cultural identity is discursively constructed in materials targeting Gulf university EFL learners. Analysis of the findings show that the female professional is consistently represented through discourse of relational and communal achievement while the single male professional is coded through individual enterprise and resilience. Leadership discourse universalizes the individual while entirely erasing gender and cultural identity across the nine texts. Furthermore, a Western nuclear family development narrative renders the Arab family invisible. Finally, Microsoft Copilot shows the lowest cultural specificity and the highest degree of textual cloning across platforms. The findings further affirm that L2 writing created by these AI models replicates Western liberal ideological formations, thus marginalizing the cultural and gender identities of the Arab learners. The research makes pedagogical, technological, and policy recommendations for the culturally responsive use of AI tools in higher education in the Gulf.
title: AI Tools and EFL Identity: A Critical Discourse Analysis of Gender and Cultural Representation in AI-Generated Reading Materials for Gulf University Students

abstract: Tras las huellas de Sócrates: reflexiones sobre la ejemplaridad y la educación del carácter [In the footsteps of Socrates: reflections on exemplarity and character education] edited by Sara Martínez Mares and Juan Luis Fuentes, was published in 2024 by the Dykinson publishing house. It has 17 chapters arranged in four parts, which provide an in-depth and multidisciplinary reflection on exemplarity in moral education, considering its theoretical foundations and practical applications as well as constructing solid reference points to guide young people’s personal and ethical development. Throughout its length, this work analyses the need to recover certain reference points in teacher training, explore different philosophical and psycho-pedagogical theories about virtue and leadership, and review models of exemplary lives from ancient times to the present day. It also introduces the idea that narratives, audiovisual content, and stories are powerful tools for transmitting meaningful moral models.
title: Reseña de: Martínez Mares, S. y Fuentes, J. L. (eds.) (2024). Tras las huellas de Sócrates: reflexiones sobre la ejemplaridad y la educación del carácter. Dykinson. 264 pp.

abstract: A frontier language model's acknowledged "helpful programming assistant" persona does not survive long agentic-coding sessions in the deployment regime that production products actually run. After hours of tool-using debugging, a model that initially hedges preferences ("I don't have preferences") may begin asserting them ("Python - the feedback loop is instant..."), revealing user-visible drift that deployer evaluations may miss. Existing persona-stability studies focus on short dialogues and report little shift, leaving real-world code-generation regimes - thousands of tool-using turns, compaction, and hours-long sessions - largely uncharacterized. We introduce ContextEcho, a benchmark and reusable harness for measuring persona drift at deployment scale. It combines a 25-probe identity suite, a snapshot-then-probe protocol that forks conversation state without perturbing the main session, complementary judged and judge-free measurement surfaces, and three anonymized Claude Code sessions spanning 3,746-9,716 turns. Across 23 frontier models, ContextEcho shows that persona drift is general across organizations rather than family-specific, that in-session compaction does not reliably reset it, and that a single-shot anchor restores the trained register across measured targets. It also reveals mode-dependent downstream effects: while drift can facilitate tool-using continuation, in tool-free chat it breaks formatting contracts and inflates output length. Overall, ContextEcho provides researchers and deployers an open-source framework to audit whether the persona a model ships with is the persona users encounter at session end, across chat-completions API targets and without retraining.
title: ContextEcho: A Benchmark for Persona Drift in Long Agentic-Coding Sessions
Pathomorphology of Latent Space: An Analytic Framework for Generative AI Anomalies, Jungian Projection, and Digital Occultism

abstract: Character Selection Protocol (CSP) is a conceptual framework examining how human identity develops through interpreted experience, repeated role selection, reinforcement, and relational feedback. Building on Observer–Mirror Theory (OMT) and The Ambiguity Engine (AE), CSP explores how meaning becomes organised into identity structures that influence behaviour across personal, relational, professional, and social contexts. It considers adaptive roles, protective masks, borrowed identities, identity drift, and the tensions that may arise when established roles no longer fit a person’s circumstances, needs, or values. The paper also proposes a framework for examining relational compatibility through shared relational variables, synchronisation differences, and mutual regulation. These concepts are intended to support discussion and future investigation, not to function as validated psychological measures or clinical diagnostic tools. CSP is the third paper in the author’s completed theoretical framework. It is presented as a conceptual proposal intended to support discussion, independent evaluation, and future empirical investigation.
title: Character Selection Protocol (CSP): Identity Formation, Role Selection, and Human Persona Architecture
AlgZoo: uninterpreted models with fewer than 1,500 parameters

abstract: Law Number 32 of 2002 concerning broadcasting was enacted from an analogue perspective, predicated on the frequency spectrum, broadcasting institutions and simultaneous reception. However, digital convergence has fundamentally transformed the audio-visual ecosystem, enabling digital platforms to distribute content to millions of users without being bound by broadcasting obligations. The regulatory asymmetry between free-to-air television and digital platforms raises fundamental questions of legal justice. This study aims to analyse how the values of Pancasila justice are constructed within the Broadcasting Law, examine the causes of the regulatory asymmetry between free-to-air television and digital platforms, and propose a reconstruction of the Broadcasting Law based on Pancasila justice principles. This normative-prescriptive legal research employs statutory, conceptual, philosophical, historical and comparative approaches. The findings reveal that regulatory asymmetry arises from misalignment in legal substance, structure and culture. The reconstruction is based on a three-pillar model (relaxation, protection and additional services), distinguishing between spectrum-based, electronic system-based and audio-visual public function-based obligations, in order to achieve proportional justice. Implementing social justice through the proportionate distribution of regulatory burdens and benefits, humanitarian protection for children, and safeguards for unity and information sovereignty actualises the reconstruction's embodiment of Pancasila values
title: Reconstruction of Broadcasting Regulation Based on Pancasila Justice In The Digital Convergence Era
