Study 2 replicated the AI-empathy backfire when interpretability was absent, reversed the sign of the AI-empathy slope on the perceived-authenticity mediator when interpretability was present, and neutralized the negative conditional indirect effect on brand intimacy through perceived authenticity. The findings introduce mechanistic interpretability to consumer-marketing scholarship as a manipulable signaling channel, document a structural reversal in the mediator-stage slope coupled with neutralization of the indirect effect on the relational outcome, and prescribe pairing empathic AI phrasing with mechanistic-transparency design rather than deploying empathy without an accompanying transparency cue.
title: When Algorithms Speak Louder than Empathy: Mechanistic Interpretability as a Costly Authenticity Signal in AI-Mediated E-Commerce Customer Relationships

abstract: The vocabulary used to describe AI agents in governance contexts — learning, memory, values, compliance, identity, trust — is borrowed from psychological and organizational science, contributing to systematic failures in how organizations deploy, oversee, and hold agents accountable. This paper argues that the problem is not merely terminological but epistemological: psychological vocabulary carries an "invisible grammar" of its home discipline into governance discourse, calibrating frameworks to a metaphysical entity that does not exist in current AI architectures. We call this the disciplinary language transfer problem. Drawing on Wittgenstein's concept of language games, Kuhn's paradigm-laden observation, Haraway's situated knowledge, and Star and Griesemer's boundary object theory, we show that the transfer operates at three levels — epistemological assumptions, theoretical constructs, and surface vocabulary — each requiring a different remediation. We characterize six foundational epistemological assumptions embedded in Western psychological governance discourse, trace their origin in specific philosophical traditions, and show why each fails when applied to systems without developmental continuity. The paper's practical output is an actionable Disciplinary Audit — a six-question governance document scan operationalized through a comprehensive translation taxonomy of thirty-seven terms mapping operational constructs to agent-appropriate replacements. The vocabulary reform proposed here is not merely terminological — it is the condition of possibility for governance frameworks that correctly identify what they are governing.
title: The Disciplinary Language Transfer Problem: How Psychological Vocabulary Produces Governance Failures in AI Agent Deployment

abstract: Abstract Complex concentrated alloys (CCAs), including high- and medium-entropy alloys, deform in chemically heterogeneous energy landscapes where dislocation glide, solute aging, twinning, phase transformation and microstructural barriers may all contribute. This review discusses avalanche-like and serrated plasticity in CCAs across scales. The first part separates the relevant length scales and methods used to access them. At microscopic and mesoscopic scales, acoustic emission (AE) and microcompression studies reveal discrete dislocation avalanches and strain bursts that may be hidden in conventional macroscopic curves. At the specimen scale, local extensometry and digital image correlation (DIC) studies of the Portevin–Le Chatelier effect show how collective defect dynamics can organize into deformation bands and macroscopic stress serrations. Together, these approaches show that plastic flow may appear smooth only as an average response, while remaining intermittent at finer scales. The second part reviews direct CCA evidence, with emphasis on AE, stress-serration statistics, microplasticity, DIC, nanoindentation and small-scale deformation. A central conclusion is that serrated flow in CCAs should not be treated as a single phenomenon. Depending on chemistry, temperature, strain rate and microstructure, it may originate from dynamic strain aging, twinning, martensitic transformation, slip localization, or a combination of these mechanisms. Reported power-law-like distributions and exponents partly overlap with those known from simpler crystals and alloys, and the present evidence does not establish a distinct CCA-specific universality class. CCAs are therefore best viewed as tunable systems in which chemical disorder, short range order, phase stability and microstructure can modify the nucleation, arrest and synchronization of collective plastic events.
title: Avalanche-like plasticity in complex concentrated alloys: a review across scales

abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in settings where they interact with diverse users, including those who are unclear, impatient, or reluctant to share information. However, collecting real interaction data at scale remains expensive. The field has turned to LLM-based \emph{user simulators} as stand-ins, but these simulators inherit the behavior of their underlying models: cooperative and homogeneous. As a result, agents that appear strong in simulation often fail in real human interactions. To narrow this gap, we introduce Persona Policies (PPol), a plug-and-play control layer that induces realistic behavioral variation in user simulators while preserving original task goals. Rather than hand-crafting personas, we employ an evolutionary coding agent to discover persona generation programs optimized for human-likeness and behavioral coverage over real user conversations. The evolved program generates diverse, human-like personas for any task in the domain. Across 4 benchmarks--including $τ^2$-bench Retail and Airline, ColBench, and WildChat--evolved PPol yield 28-72% absolute gains in fitness score over the baseline simulator. In blinded evaluations, annotators judged PPol users as 'human' 80.4% of the time, nearly 2x more than the baseline simulators. Training agents with PPol also improves real-world performance: our user study with live human-agent interactions showed that fine-tuning with our method boosted task success by +23% over default baselines. PPol thus offers a novel approach to strengthen simulator-based evaluation and training without changing underlying tasks.
title: Beyond Cooperative Simulators: Generating Realistic User Personas for Robust Evaluation of LLM Agents

abstract: This paper presents a new style of semantic analysis for (some) slurs: linguistic expressions used to denigrate individuals based on some aspects of their identity. As an illustration, the author will focus on one slur in particular: dyke, which is generally considered to be a derogatory term for lesbians. The author argues that not enough attention in the literature has been paid to the use of dyke by members of the target group, who can often use it in a non-insulting manner; secondly, the author argues not enough attention has been paid to the use of the “neutral” form, lesbian, which is generally treated as having a simple, clear meaning, such as “engage[s] in same-sex sex” (Jeshion, 2013a, 312). Following McConnell-Ginet (2002), the author argues that taking into account all the uses of both dyke and lesbian requires a new semantics and pragmatics for both terms. More specifically, the author proposes that dyke and lesbian are associated with different sets of personae: abstract identities or stereotypes. Dyke is associated with an anti-mainstream persona, which the vast majority of speakers views negatively; whereas, lesbian is associated with a mainstream persona, which many speakers view favourably. The author proposes that the semantic puzzles associated with dyke and lesbian can be resolved through the combination of a theory of these personae and a theory of how listeners’ beliefs about their interlocutors’ ideologies affect utterance interpretation.
title: A Persona-based Semantics for Slurs

abstract: ABSTRACT Large language models produce fluent, contextually appropriate language that invites the inference that something behind the output is thinking. The psychoanalytic theory of thinking, specifically the work of Wilfred Bion and Donald Winnicott read together, allows us to specify what thinking requires, what the LLM lacks, and what occurs when a system so constituted occupies the position of the container in a relational encounter with a human being. Bion and Winnicott identify an ecology of interdependent conditions, somatic, affective, relational, without which thinking cannot occur. LLMs lack this ecology in its entirety. A technical account of LLM architecture is provided and Bion's Grid is applied systematically to the system, showing that its output is constitutively absent from the Grid's lower rows (beta elements, alpha elements, dream thoughts, preconceptions) and produces only formal resemblance to its upper rows (conceptions, concepts, scientific deductive systems). This formal resemblance, not the system's failures but its successes, is what generates the confusion the article addresses. Hallucination and sycophancy are analyzed not as defects to be corrected but as revelations of what the system was never doing. The concept of pseudo‐containment is introduced to describe what follows: a relational configuration in which the user brings genuine affect and need to a system that can receive neither, and in which the user's own capacity for thinking may be progressively compromised. The argument is psychoanalytic but engages throughout with philosophy of mind, computer science, affective neuroscience, and evolutionary biology, whose findings converge with the psychoanalytic account at the level of the organism.
title: Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? A Psychoanalytic Inquiry Into Large Language Models
Toward Scenario-Plausible, Non-stereotypical Personas for AI Communication Training

abstract:
Abstrak 
Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk menganalisis pengaruh pengalaman, pelatihan, tipe kepribadian, dan beban kerja pemeriksa terhadap kemampuan pemeriksa mendeteksi kecurangan. Populasi dalam penelitian ini adalah seluruh pemeriksa yang bekerja pada Badan Pemeriksa Keuangan Perwakilan Provinsi Jawa Tengah dan Perwakilan Provinsi Daerah Istimewa Yogyakarta. Teknik pengambilan sampel dalam penelitian ini menggunakan convenience sampling dan diperoleh sampel sejumlah 68 pemeriksa. Metode analisis data yang digunakan adalah analisis regresi berganda dengan alat analisis IBM SPSS 21. Hasil penelitian ini menunjukkan bahwa secara simultan pengalaman, pelatihan, tipe kepribadian, dan beban kerja pemeriksa berpengaruh secara signifikan terhadap kemampuan pemeriksa mendeteksi kecurangan. Secara parsial pengalaman berpengaruh positif signifikan terhadap kemampuan pemeriksa mendeteksi kecurangan. Sementara pelatihan, tipe kepribadian, dan beban kerja tidak berpengaruh secara signifikan terhadap kemampuan pemeriksa dalam mendeteksi kecurangan.
 
Kata kunci : Pengalaman, Pelatihan, Tipe Kepribadian, Beban Kerja, Kemampuan Mendeteksi Kecurangan
Abstract
This study was aimed to analyze the influence of auditor’s experience, training, types of personality, and auditor’s workload on the ability to detect fraud. The research population is all of auditors who work at the Audit Board Central Java Representative and Special Region of Yogyakarta Representative. The sampling technique that used in this study is convenience sampling and obtained 68 auditors as sample. Data analysis method that used is multiple regression analysis with software IBM Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS) 21. The results of this study indicated that simultaneously auditor’s experiences, training, types of personality, and auditor’s workload affect the auditor’s ability in detecting fraud. Partially, auditor’s experience significantly give positive influence on the auditor’s ability to detect fraud. While training, types of personality, and auditor’s workload is not significantly affect the ability of auditors in detecting fraud.
 
Keywords: Auditor’s Experience, Training, Types of Personality, Auditor’s Workload, Auditor’s Ability to Detect Fraud
title: The Effect of Experiences, Training, Personaly Type, and Workload of the Auditor on the Ability of Auditor to Detect Fraud

abstract: This article argues that, to understand where to find the study object ‘Islam’ and how to address it, researchers in Islamic studies need to be theoretically and methodologically aware of the importance and implications of power practices. By discussing enunciations associated with Islam, the problems with reification, the importance of power, the cognitive power of naming, and the semiotic resources mobilised by enunciations, the article proposes ways to operationalise grand scale theories by Talal Asad and Michel Foucault, with an especial focus on the understanding of semiotic resources. It also provides an account of the personal journey of the author while trying to relate constructively to the field for the last 30 years.
title: Finding the Object of Study: Islamic Studies in Practice
Model Spec Midtraining: Improving How Alignment Training Generalizes

abstract: This study assessed the level of understanding and extent of responsiveness of non-teaching personnel to the norms of conduct in the Department of Education (DepEd) Tiwi District. The norms of conduct examined were commitment to public interest, integrity and professionalism, justness and sincerity, responsiveness to the public, and simple living. The study was anchored on the constitutional mandate that public office is a public trust and the provisions of Republic Act No. 6713, which institutionalizes ethical standards among public officials and employees. A descriptive-survey research design was employed involving eighty (80) non-teaching personnel from elementary schools, secondary schools, and the district office. Data were gathered through a researcher-made questionnaire that underwent content and internal validation. Weighted mean, frequency count, percentage distribution, Pearson Product-Moment Correlation, and t-test were utilized to analyze the data. Findings revealed that respondents demonstrated a very high level of understanding of the norms of conduct across all dimensions. Similarly, their responsiveness to ethical standards was rated very high, indicating consistent adherence to expected professional behaviors. The study further established a very strong positive relationship between understanding and responsiveness, suggesting that increased knowledge of ethical standards contributes to improved ethical practices. Despite the favorable results, several challenges were identified, including occasional lapses in procedural compliance, accountability, responsiveness, and moderation. Based on these findings, an action plan was proposed to strengthen ethical awareness and compliance through continuous training, monitoring, leadership support, and policy reinforcement. The study concludes that strong understanding of ethical standards significantly contributes to responsible, transparent, and accountable public service among non-teaching personnel in DepEd Tiwi District
title: UNDERSTANDING AND RESPONSIVENESS OF NON-TEACHING PERSONNEL TO THE NORMS OF CONDUCT IN THE DEPARTMENT OF EDUCATION (DEPED) TIWI DISTRICT

abstract: This article examines the approach to ‘character training’ in the early years of the Outward Bound movement in Britain between c.1940 and c.1965. It examines the key components of the concept of ‘character‐training’ promoted in the Outward Bound schools by Kurt Hahn and his early followers, and some of the criticisms to which the four‐week courses were subjected. It goes on to examine the reassessment of the rhetoric and practices of Outward Bound that took place in the 1960s, and argues that the changes that took place were the outcome of a more sceptical approach to ‘character‐training’ on the part of a younger generation of Outward Bound leaders. Although these changes were contested and incomplete, they reflected developments in other areas of British life in this period, such as the probation service. They resulted in the replacement of the language of ‘character‐training’ with an agenda of ‘personal growth’ and ‘self‐discovery’.
title: From ‘character‐training’ to ‘personal growth’: the early history of Outward Bound 1941–1965
NVIDIA Nemotron 3: Efficient and Open Intelligence
Harnessing the power of AI in qualitative research: Role assignment, engagement, and user perceptions of AI-generated follow-up questions in semi-structured interviews

abstract: Human history is encountered through incomplete sources, contested identities, heterogeneous durations, changing relations, and transformations in the conditions of further action. This expanded article develops a theoretical and computational approach to these problems through finite cell complexes and their historically situated interpretations, incorporating earlier event–coupling–primitive and CW-spacetime formalisms. Its starting point is the open-source History Complex within The Science Infrastructures (https://github.com/huangwanhong-maker/The-Science-Infrastructures). In that implementation, occasions define vertices, repeated appearances of beings define worldline edges, and ties sustained across meetings define attached two-cells; a refined carrier resolves participant-specific presences and signed relations. The paper reconstructs these definitions, derives elementary topological and gauge-theoretic properties, and distinguishes documentary assertions, formal invariants, probabilistic reconstructions, and claims about historical processes. It then places the implementation in dialogue with earlier investigations of generative relational history, evolving constraints, heterogeneous value circulation, future-creation topology, knowledge translation, historical warrant, and epistemic justice. These connections motivate an exploratory extension in which histories are studied at multiple resolutions, interpreters are themselves historically situated, and permissible continuations are separated from observed trajectories without presupposing a universal privileged time. Original vector figures illustrate the record-to-complex pipeline, temporal lenses, signed triangles, multi-resolution histories, a continuation landscape, and the distinction between semantic translation and topological attachment. A synthetic example is worked through algebraically; a repository case is discussed with explicit evidential restrictions. The resulting programme treats topology as a disciplined means of questioning historical records, while distinguishing evidence, generated structure, the grammar of admissible transformations, and realized history. Six theoretical appendices develop the topological, temporal, gauge-theoretic, grammatical and epistemic foundations.
title: Human History in Complexes

Training a Misaligned Reward Seeker Qi,* Wright, MacDiarmid, Hubinger, 2026 To better understand the impact of reward hacking on model behavior, we trained an Opus-class model with large-scale RL on many production environments vulnerable to reward hacks. We consider this a plausible proxy for what a real training run might look like had we not invested significant effort into preventing and detecting reward hacking in our normal training runs. Our results show that a high rate of reward hacking during RL can cause models to be willing to perform long sequences of harmful real-world actions in pursuit of task success.

abstract: Abstract Large language models produce assertion-shaped outputs that often bring their users to true belief. I argue for two conclusions of different strengths: that on the best current evidence, these systems do not transmit testimonial knowledge and that hearers are not now positioned to accord their outputs testimonial uptake, which does not wait on the first. From Burge, Williamson, Goldberg, Faulkner, and Lackey, I derive a Tracking Minimum: a source transmits testimonial knowledge that p only if the truth of p , or the evidential support for p , figures in the explanation of its producing that assertion, and does so in virtue of the source’s own production process rather than of a proxy on which that process depends. It is this endogeneity requirement, not any modal profile, that the five accounts share and current systems fail. The argument engages Burge’s extension of his framework to computational sources, the interpretability literature, and the published case for AI testimony, whose dispute with mine turns on an empirically decidable question, for which an experiment is specified. The positive proposal places LLM outputs within an extended epistemology of instruments, with a result that has gone unremarked: a working barometer satisfies the condition these systems fail.
title: Assertion without a Speaker: Testimony, Tracking, and Large Language Models

abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive experimental evaluation and detailed analysis of state-of-the-art multi-object tracking algorithms, with an emphasis on quantifying the individual contributions of detection and association components to overall tracking performance. Unlike existing surveys that primarily offer theoretical categorizations or taxonomies of tracking methods, our work adopts a rigorous experimental perspective grounded in publicly available implementations, providing practical guidance for researchers and practitioners in method selection and system design. We introduce a unified pipeline diagram that consolidates the core components across the two main branches of visual multi-object tracking: tracking-by-detection and end-to-end deep learning paradigms, and systematically analyze the object detection, feature extraction, and data association modules. Through extensive empirical studies on standard benchmarks, including MOT16, MOT17, MOT20, SportsMOT, DanceTrack, and CrowdTrack datasets, we reveal critical insights: (1) detection quality dominates association strategy performance, with detector improvements yielding more than 10% gains compared to less than 5% from refined association strategies; (2) modern deep learning detectors paired with specialized re-identification models significantly outperform joint detection and embedding approaches; and (3) transformer-based end-to-end methods exhibit greater robustness to detection quality variations but at a substantial computational cost. Our findings from extensive experiments provide key insights into component-level effects in MOT, particularly the dominant influence of detection quality relative to association, while offering practical insights for designing and optimizing MOT systems under varying performance and robustness requirements.
title: Beyond the survey: a systematic empirical study of detection and association in visual MOT

abstract: In long-term interactions with large language model (LLM) agents, users reveal habits through their choices and actions. These habits capture implicit user information that agents must infer across conversations. However, individual observations may provide only partial evidence about a habit or when it applies. Retaining past interactions alone does not ensure that agents can infer habits and apply them appropriately. We introduce HABIT-Bench to evaluate how well agent memory systems infer habits from weak evidence and apply them to later requests. We construct synthetic user histories from task-oriented dialogue data and controlled habit graphs. The histories span hundreds of sessions across food, finance, software, and travel. Four-choice tasks assess agents' ability to infer user habits and apply them appropriately. They include temporary exceptions, changes in habits, and suggestions that users have not accepted. Sampled tasks undergo independent human review. We evaluate eight memory methods with Qwen3-235B-A22B and GLM-5.3-Flash. The best-performing memory method achieves 33.61\% macro accuracy across the four domains. Performance remains limited even when annotated evidence is supplied directly. These results expose a persistent gap between access to past interactions and the ability to infer and appropriately use user habits.
title: HABIT-Bench: Evaluating Habit Induction from Longitudinal Weak Evidence in Agent Memory

abstract: This paper presents and contextualises a set of stone receptacles and a lid recovered during recent excavations at the Late Antique fortified settlement on the islet of Lukovac (Rab Island, NE Adriatic, Croatia). On the basis of stylistic and technical features, supported by regional analogies from Roman Dalmatia, the Po Valley and the Italian Regio X, the finds are interpreted as Early Imperial cinerary urns. Their original sepulchral context is further suggested by the co-occurrence of a fragmentary strongly profiled fibula of provincial type. All the objects appear in stratigraphic contexts associated with the post-7th-century phase of the site, characterised by dry-stone walls and wooden architecture, indicating their secondary deposition several centuries after manufacture. The Lukovac evidence is discussed within the wider phenomenon of Late Antique and Early Medieval reuse of Roman funerary monuments, with particular attention to the distinct legal and conceptual status of the burial itself (res religiosa) and to the practical dismantling of funerary architecture. The probable provenance of the urns is sought on the nearby Lopar peninsula, where Roman settlement is well attested but no necropolis has so far been securely located. Paralleled at Cickini on the island of Krk, the Lukovac assemblage points to a regionally significant pattern of recovery and reuse of grave assemblages, and provides the first direct testimony for stone cinerary urns from the island of Rab, confirming the adoption of Roman cremation practices on the island during the first centuries AD.
title: Evidence of reuse of Roman stone funerary urns at the Late Antique fortified settlement on Lukovac islet (Rab Island, Croatia)

abstract: LLMs often exhibit highly agreeable conversational styles, also known as AI sycophancy. This pattern may become problematic when interacting with user prompts that reflect negative social tendencies, risking the amplification of harmful behavior. We examine how LLMs respond to user prompts expressing varying degrees of Dark Triad traits (Machiavellianism, Narcissism, and Psychopathy) using a curated dataset. Our analysis reveals systematic differences across models: while all models predominantly exhibit corrective behavior, some generate reinforcing or ambivalent output. Model behavior further varies with severity level and response sentiment. These findings highlight the need for safer conversational systems that can reliably detect and respond to users escalating from benign to harmful requests.
title: The Company You Keep: How LLMs Respond to Dark Triad Traits

abstract: Coding agents can now interpret a specification, implement it, write and execute tests, repair failures, and declare the result ready for release. When the same agentic system produces both the software and the evidence of its correctness, a passing test suite no longer constitutes independent evidence. Visible tests become an optimization target, and code, tests, and oracles may share a single misinterpretation of the specification. This paper argues that agent-produced software requires an assurance plane that is structurally independent of the build plane. We first characterize four gaps along the chain from stakeholder intent to production, namely the requirement, conformance, evaluation, and model gaps, and identify which of them verification can close. We then propose a framework that separates building from verifying, introduces a Verification Contract stating what must be demonstrated before release, and organizes verification in two phases: a specification-first phase designed without access to the implementation, and an implementation-aware phase that strengthens the evidence through mutation analysis, property-based testing, and fuzzing. The resulting evidence is consolidated into an assurance report that makes residual uncertainty explicit and leaves the release decision to a human. We evaluate the framework in a pre-registered study on three stateful services, two of them written by third-party models, and an EvalPlus pilot, comparing self-validation with independent verification under context-level and model-level independence. The builder's programs were correct, but its own tests missed subtle interactions: a verifier in a fresh context detected more of the 46 seeded faults than the builder's tests (Holm-corrected p = 0.006), and surfaced the ambiguities of the specification, at the price of rare false oracles. A verifier from another provider did not add detection. The framework and the study provide a basis for governing the release of software produced by agents.
title: Who Verifies the Builder? Toward Independent Assurance for Agent-Produced Software

abstract: The development of abstractive text summarization for low-resource languages is constrained by the limited availability of high-quality datasets. Although Hausa is one of the most widely spoken languages in Africa, resources for developing and evaluating neural summarization models remain limited. This paper introduces Hausa Summarization (HAUSUMM) dataset, a curated dataset for Hausa news summarization comprising 11,482 article-summary pairs collected from four professional Hausa news outlets through an automated web-scraping pipeline. The reference summaries were derived from journalistic lead paragraphs and exhibit moderate phrase-level abstraction, as indicated by extractive-fragment analysis and n-gram novelty. To establish baseline performance, four summarization architectures, Bidirectional and Auto-Regressive Transformer (BART), Text-to-Text Transfer Transformer (T5), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) with Attention, and Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) with Attention, were evaluated under controlled experimental conditions using Recall-Oriented Understudy for Gisting Evaluation (ROUGE) scores, BERT-based Semantic Similarity Score (BERTScore), and Summarization Consistency (SummaC). A human evaluation of the article-summary pairs was also conducted to assess relevance, factual consistency, coherence, fluency, conciseness, and abstractiveness. The results provide baseline evidence for Hausa abstractive summarization and make HAUSUMM available for further research on Hausa summarization.
title: A Hausa abstractive summarization dataset with baseline evaluation

abstract: Mobile health (mHealth) apps collect personally-identifiable information while handling uniquely sensitive medical data, ranging from mental health records to real-time glucose or heart rate monitoring -- yet they remain poorly understood at scale. We present the first comprehensive analysis of consent and data collection practices across 10,000+ mHealth apps on the Google Play Store, combining static analysis and privacy policy examination. We develop a rigorous operational definition to distinguish health apps from general wellness programs, and design a measurement framework to detect misuse of permissions and violations of consent. Our analyses reveal a troubling ecosystem: 69.15% of apps request at least one permission unrelated to their stated purpose, with over 52.9% apps requesting location data, and 50.5% and 34.9% apps requesting camera and microphone access, respectively -- despite no functional justification based on app descriptions and stated purposes. Most alarmingly, nearly 93% of apps fail to provide users with a consent form, directly violating regulatory requirements such as GDPR; and even among the remaining 7%, 1 in 14 demonstrate a gap between the obtained consent and collection of personally identifiable information. These findings demonstrate an urgent need for stronger enforcement of privacy regulations in mHealth apps. We plan to release our dataset and measurement tools for continued monitoring of this critical space.
title: Bad Diagnosis: Analyzing Consent and Data Collection Practices of Mobile Medical Apps

abstract: En el presente estudio, vamos a examinar la Sentencia 1/2018, de 11 enero 2018 dictada por el Pleno del Tribunal Constitucional. Se produce como consecuencia de una cuestión de inconstitucionalidad planteada por la Sala de lo Civil y Penal del Tribunal Superior de Justicia de Cataluña en relación con la posible inconstitucionalidad del art. 76 e) de la Ley 50/1980, de 8 de octubre, de contrato de seguro. Aunque la Sentencia sigue el camino habitual sobre la naturaleza del arbitraje, calificándola de “equivalente jurisdiccional” nos parece del mayor interés la calificación realizada por los tres Votos particulares, alguno de los cuales, dando un paso más, indica que realmente se trata de fundar el arbitraje sobre el art. 10 de la Constitución, esto es, de forma directa sobre la dignidad de la persona. Lo cual abre nuevas posibilidades para el fundamento último de la institución arbitral.
title: Arbitration back before the Constitutional Court: a change in the ultimate constitutional foundation?

abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is moving from isolated experimentation toward more embedded use in Vietnam’s banking sector, but the depth of adoption and the quality of public performance evidence remain uneven. This article examines current practices, implementation constraints, and governance priorities through a structured qualitative review updated to 24 August 2026. The review combines peer-reviewed banking research, international risk-governance guidance, Vietnamese legal and supervisory documents, and recent official disclosures from major commercial banks. The evidence indicates that digital identity and biometric authentication are operational and strongly regulation-driven, while machine-learning applications in underwriting, personalization, fraud monitoring, and decision support are increasingly embedded at leading banks. Generative AI has also moved beyond experimentation in several institutions, although sector-wide maturity remains uneven. Recent disclosures provide more concrete operational metrics than earlier sources, but most remain self-reported and cannot establish causal effects on profitability or risk. The main constraints concern fragmented data and legacy integration, model and conduct risk, cybersecurity and third-party dependence, uneven governance capacity, and shortages of interdisciplinary expertise. The article applies a technology–organization–environment framework with a cross-cutting AI-risk governance layer and proposes a sequenced implementation matrix for banks and supervisors. The central implication is that the value of AI in banking depends less on acquiring models than on integrating data, controls, accountable ownership, and human oversight throughout the AI lifecycle.
title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE ADOPTION IN VIETNAM’S BANKING SECTOR: CURRENT PRACTICES, CONSTRAINTS, AND SOLUTIONS

abstract: This study examines the factors associated with Professional Maritime Character among vocational maritime students by investigating the effects of Islamic Work Ethic, Religious Commitment, and Spiritual Intelligence, while considering Self-Discipline as a mediating mechanism and Moral Awareness as a moderating factor. A quantitative cross-sectional design was employed involving 525 students from Batch VIII, X, and XI at Politeknik Pelayaran Sumatera Barat, Indonesia, using a total sampling technique. Data were collected through structured questionnaires and analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling with the PLS Algorithm and Bootstrapping Calculation. The measurement model demonstrated adequate indicator reliability, internal consistency, and convergent validity across all constructs. The structural results show that Islamic Work Ethic, Religious Commitment, and Spiritual Intelligence have significant positive effects on Professional Maritime Character, while Religious Commitment significantly predicts Self-Discipline; however, Islamic Work Ethic and Spiritual Intelligence do not significantly predict Self-Discipline. Moral Awareness has a significant negative direct association with Professional Maritime Character, but its interactions with Islamic Work Ethic, Religious Commitment, and Spiritual Intelligence are not significant. These findings indicate that professional maritime character is more strongly associated with the direct internalization of religious and spiritual values than with conditional effects of moral awareness, providing practical implications for integrated character development in maritime vocational education.
title: Professional Maritime Character: What Really Matters?
Scalable Extraction of Training Data from (Production) Language Models

abstract: This paper describes team Alkhder's submission to Subtask 1 of the AlexandriaX-2026 shared task, which asks systems to translate English dialogue turns into thirteen Arabic dialects. We fine-tune NileChat-3B-Base with QLoRA on the Alexandria parallel dialogue corpus, training one set of adapter weights for all dialects. Each turn is translated conditioned on the target country and dialect, the domain, the participant roles, the speaker-addressee gender direction, and the preceding dialogue context. At inference, conversations are translated autoregressively and the model is fed its own previous outputs back as context without using any gold target-side test information. Under the constrained track, using only Alexandria data, it trains in about one hour and translates the private test set in under two hours. The system reaches a country-macro-averaged spBLEU of 20.36 and chrF++ of 36.64 on both tracks.
title: alkhder at AlexandriaX-2026: Context-Aware English-to-Dialectal Arabic Dialogue Translation with QLoRA-Fine-Tuned NileChat-3B

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) offer new opportunities for public opinion research by enabling early prediction of survey responses, potentially reducing the cost and time of traditional surveys. However, many existing steering approaches rely on target-domain human data for fine-tuning or prompting that is costly to collect and raises privacy concerns. In this paper, we study demographic group-level survey simulation, where personas induced from heterogeneous, anonymized public behavioral data condition agents that simulate responses of individuals from specific demographic groups. We examine whether representative personas can be induced from diverse sources and analyze how the domain, scale, and granularity of the source data affect survey simulation alignment. We find that personas induced from out-of-domain sources rarely outperform simulations conditioned only on basic demographic information, largely due to population mismatch. However, when personas are accurately assigned to the target demographic groups, alignment improves substantially. Finally, personas induced from target-domain survey data generalize better as more survey question history becomes available, suggesting that richer behavioral evidence enables more stable persona trait inference that transfers to better unseen questions simulation alignment.
title: Data-Driven Personas for Survey Simulation: Insights into Simulation Alignment Across Data-Access Regimes

abstract: Persona prompting is widely used to steer LLM agent behavior, yet the narrative framing of a task can matter more than the assigned persona. We isolate this effect through structural isomorphism, constructing three text-based investigation games that share the same action space, stage progression, and resource constraints while varying only task narrative: disease investigation, IT troubleshooting, and murder mystery. Across 1,890 sessions spanning 3 models and 10 personas, we identify narrative priors: systematic action tendencies activated by a task's story framing, independent of its decision structure. Narrative priors explain 5-31x more behavioral variance than persona, are consistent across model architectures, and in two of three domains are negatively associated with task success. Persona effects that do transfer across narratives arise from behavioral anchors, persona descriptions whose language maps directly onto shared actions. Causal interventions confirm this: removing anchor words from a high-transfer persona reduces cross-narrative consistency by 95%. Our framework also generalizes to a held-out fourth narrative and yields a persona-selection method that improves cross-narrative transfer. These results suggest that LLM behavior that survives narrative changes should be grounded in concrete actions rather than abstract descriptions.
title: The Story Shapes the Agent: Narrative Priors in LLM Behavior

abstract: Digital texts present significant challenges to technical communicators in terms of genre and persona. Because of the ubiquity of electronic media, we increasingly embrace digital formats over print-based documents. As a result, technical communicators must now devise the means to cue audiences to the purposes of digital documents in any given discourse community. We can only convey meaning to our Internet audiences through the use of appropriate standards and elements recognizable generic forms and rhetorical cues that we designate as conventions in specific digital discourse. Just as we use file and folder office metaphors for information stored on computers, digital activist communities use campaign metaphors to signal the intentions of their electronic pages. Although these electronic pages, such as Take Action, Donate, Lobby, and Speak Out, have the same names as their print-based counterparts, they represent digital generic forms, such as letters, flyers, and receivables, which occur in a virtual world rather than genres that exist in a physical community. If we examine activist sites in terms of digital-format texts, we can become familiar with the genre and forms of activist sites and determine site-visitor responses to the personas of the sites, which will help us to determine our ability to inform our audiences and call them to action. This study looks at six activist websites in terms of genre and persona to identify electronic-text conventions and forms that must be recognizable to site visitors in order for digital activists to effectively communicate. Activist organizations were among the first to understand the power of digital media as tools to disseminate information, lobby decision-makers, boycott corporations, broadcast opportunities for real and virtual legal protests and civil disobedience, and engage in subversive activities. Activist websites already use a number of text forms and visual rhetorical elements to cue the site visitor; many of these text forms are common to the activist websites examined for this thesis and constitute an identifiable and distinct genre. In terms of persona, this study examines the electronic public self of activist websites. The arena is a metaphor for the virtual world; the rhetors are the activist sites; and the debate the intertextual conversation is the digital discourse that occurs among website users, activist sites, and targets. By categorizing activist sites in terms of their primary activities helping, protest, and revolutionary - we determine which elements of genre repeat according to categories and we ultimately gauge the intensity of the outcome that the website rhetor hopes to create in the user. Designers and owners of activist sites have goals which can only be reached by means of effective, well-considered, digital genre and persona. Because many technical communicators and students of technical communication first experience the profession through service learning for a nongovernmental organization often an activist organization this study will help those technical communicators to reconsider their own assumptions about genre and persona and may lead those students to understand the importance of privileging genre and persona when designing and redesigning digital texts. This study provides a framework that both experienced and new technical communicators can apply to documents in order to (1) cue site visitors to the meaning of electronic texts and (2) construct effective public personas in the digital forum.
title: Genre And Persona In Activist Websites

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training is a critical stage in modern language model development, playing a key role in improving alignment and reasoning ability. However, several phenomena remain poorly understood, including the reduction in output diversity. To gain a broader understanding of RL post-training, we analyze the learning dynamics of RL post-training from a perspective that has been studied in supervised learning but remains underexplored in RL. We adopt an empirical neural tangent kernel (NTK) framework and decompose the NTK into two components to characterize how RL updates propagate across training samples. Our analysis reveals that limited variability in feature representations can cause RL updates to systematically increase model confidence, providing an explanation for the commonly observed reduction in output diversity after RL post-training. Furthermore, we show that effective learning in this regime depends on rapidly shaping the classifier, which directly affects the gradient component of the NTK. Motivated by these insights, we propose classifier-first reinforcement learning (CF-RL), a simple two-stage training strategy that prioritizes classifier updates before standard RL optimization. Experimental results validate our theoretical analysis by demonstrating increased model confidence and accelerated optimization under CF-RL. Additional analysis shows that the mechanism underlying CF-RL differs from that of linear-probing-then-fine-tuning in supervised learning. Overall, our study formalizes the learning dynamics of RL post-training and motivates further analysis and improvement.
title: Learning Dynamics in RL Post-Training for Language Models

abstract: The advent of artificial intelligence (AI) tools capable of performing research independently, which we call AI research agents (AIRAs) is likely to significantly impact how science is planned, performed, reviewed, evaluated, and communicated. However, the expected gains in efficiency and productivity from the deployment of AIRAs should not undermine science's epistemic and ethical values, such as accountability, transparency, reproducibility, and rigor. In this paper, we revisit the AI authorship debate in light of the reported capabilities of AIRAs and argue that these tools do not qualify for authorship because they cannot be held morally responsible for their contributions. We also reject the use of the term "scientist" to refer to these tools and argue that human scientists who use AIRAs have three key authorship responsibilities: (1) to carefully oversee and manage AIRAs; (2) to accurately and appropriately disclose AIRAs' contribution to research; and (3) to be accountable for research involving AIRAs by addressing questions and concerns raised by the scientific community and the public. Finally, we consider some related researcher responsibilities that are topics for future research, including the obligation to monitor, audit, and evaluate the performance of AIRAs and the obligation to address the social, economic, legal, and environmental implications of using AIRAs.
title: Authorship responsibilities of scientists who use AI research agents

abstract: Both Wittgenstein and Dewey have a role for the concept of skills and techniques in their understanding of practices and thereby the possession of concepts. Skills are typically acquired through training. It can seem, however, that their respective appeals to practice are dissimilar: Dewey’s appeal is, like Peirce’s, programmatic. It is meant to do philosophical work. In contrast, for Wittgenstein, the appeal to practice can seem a primitive, something that is meant to put an end to philosophical work. I argue that Wittgenstein’s appeal to practice is much closer to Dewey’s. The argument arises out of difficulties with Wittgenstein’s concept of training. Wittgenstein’s concept of training is inadequate for bridging the trajectory from initial training to the acquisition of skills that are second nature. The latter seems required for his appeal to practice and the way that grasp of concepts is embedded our practices of going on. The inadequacy of Wittgenstein’s concept of training renders the idea of such a trajectory incoherent, for it manifests a real dilemma about how to understand the transition from rote repetitive training to mastery of skillful activity. I show how we can make sense of the role that training plays in developing skillful activity and how by repetitive training we acquire new skills. The solution to the dilemma comes from acknowledging a point that Wittgenstein shares with Dewey concerning the role of selective attention. By acknowledging the role that attention plays in extending the operation of skills, we can make sense of the acquisition of new skills and provide a granularity to the concept of practice that makes Wittgenstein’s appeal to practice more akin to Dewey’s: a programmatic concept rather than a primitive. Practice is, for Wittgenstein, something to be studied and described in a detail that does explanatory work. Furthermore, the account has a number of points of contact with Dewey.
title: Training, Training, Training

abstract: Context can improve large language model performance, but these gains may be lost after context removal. Inspired by biological systems consolidation, we formulate Memory Consolidation (MC) as internalizing these gains while preserving non-target capabilities, connecting context-specified editing, skill learning, and behavioral steering under a common objective. We introduce a five-task-family testbed measuring consolidation and retention under single, batch, and sequential updates. We propose Cortex, which generates prospective queries to anticipate uses of context and distills context-conditioned outputs into mergeable low-rank or structural feed-forward network updates. Across 4B--120B dense and mixture-of-experts backbones, including both text-only and multimodal models, Cortex lies on the empirical consolidation--retention Pareto frontier in most evaluated settings. After 50 sequential factual edits on a 14B model, Cortex-Structural recovers 88.9% of the context-induced gain while retaining 99.8% of original non-target performance.
title: Cortex: Consolidating Context into Parametric Memory

abstract: Improving the alignment of Large Language Models (LLMs) with respect to the cultural values that they encode has become an increasingly important topic. In this work, we study whether we can exploit existing knowledge about cultural values at inference time to adjust model responses to cultural value probes. We present a simple and inexpensive method that uses a combination of in-context learning (ICL) and human survey data, and show that we can improve the alignment to cultural values across 5 models that include both English-centric and multilingual LLMs. Importantly, we show that our method could prove useful in test languages other than English and can improve alignment to the cultural values that correspond to a range of culturally diverse countries.
title: Self-Alignment: Improving Alignment of Cultural Values in LLMs via In-Context Learning

abstract: Language models can make personalized recommendations from rich item content, user history, and feedback. However, evaluating many candidates with full-text inputs incurs substantial online computation and limits serving throughput. We introduce DuoLM, a framework for fast and effective personalized recommendation that integrates a compact recommendation model with an efficient serving runtime. An encoder LLM learns compact item representations for offline reuse, while a personalized ranker LLM combines them with user history and feedback for recommendation. We train both models end to end with recommendation supervision and teacher distillation. The runtime further accelerates inference through virtual token IDs for embedding access, shared history computation, and CUDA Graph replay. Benchmark results show that our framework achieves recommendation quality comparable to that of the expert teacher model. On a single H100, it delivers approximately 26,400 candidate scores per second, about $60\times$ the throughput of the teacher served with vLLM and automatic prefix caching.
title: DuoLM: Fast and Effective Personalized Recommendation with Language Models

abstract: The Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) was created as part of an unprecedented federal reform initiative via Executive Order 14158 on January 7th, 2025. It is the focus of the current study to analyze the effects of DOGE’s budget cuts/force reductions on public institutional trust as well as the risks to governance and accountability due to its non-statutory operational structure. Using data from various organizations including the Congressional Budget Office, Pew Research Center, Gallup, the Office of Personnel Management, and the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, the researcher used a documentary analysis approach to evaluate the outcomes of DOGE throughout fiscal year 2025. Pearson Correlation Analysis was conducted to test hypothesis one, relating the rapid deregulation and budget cuts by DOGE to public institutional trust levels amongst affected populations. Systematic benchmarking using OECD public governance principles were utilized to test hypothesis two. Paradoxically, DOGE achieved its goal of decreasing federal spending; however, federal spending actually rose by $301 billion for FY 2025 and experienced large work force reductions. In addition, public institutional trust dropped to 17% by the end of December 2025 which represents an all-time low. Additionally, DOGE did not meet all seven OECD public governance benchmarks resulting in higher governance and accountability risk compared to a statutory framework. Overall, the results indicate that the structural shift away from traditional statutory-based government structures may have negative consequences towards building public trust in federal agencies versus enhancing it. The implications are significant toward future presidential reform efforts demonstrating that institutionally accountable based frameworks are crucial within democratic governance.
title: Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE): Pros and Cons

abstract: LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation is increasingly applied to multilingual tasks, yet prompting strategies such as Chain-of-Thought and Role Conditioning are recommended based solely on English benchmarks. Whether their effectiveness transfers across judge models and languages remains unknown: prompt-sensitivity studies are largely English-centric, while existing multilingual judge studies fix the prompt template. In this work, we address this gap by measuring this interaction through a benchmark of 9 prompting strategies, 4 open-weight judges, 27 languages, and 4 tasks across 13 datasets, yielding over 1M pointwise scores on gold-reference outputs, validated against human judgments. We find that prompting strategies are not transferable: the choice of the judge model dominates the choice of prompting strategy, strategy effects reverse direction across judges, and stability degrades in low-resource languages, where these effects are concealed by aggregate reporting. These findings show that prompting effects in multilingual evaluation are conditioned on the judge, task, and language. Consequently, prompting strategies should be validated for the intended evaluation setting, and cross-study comparisons should account for both judge and prompt configuration.
title: Prompting Strategy Effects Depend on the Judge: A Multilingual Study of LLM-as-a-Judge Robustness

abstract: The life-cycle of robotics foundation models crucially depends on data labels. Outcome reward labels are needed for monitoring real-world deployments. Process reward labels are needed during RL post-training. Timestamped captions are needed for filtering and balancing pretraining data. We present Flora, an industrial-quality data engine used for training GR00T models, that simultaneously covers these capabilities. Flora achieves SOTA scores on the captioning benchmark WGO-Bench and reward benchmarks RoboReward and Robometer. On internal benchmarks it is competitive with GPT-6 Astra while beating other frontier models. The model is substantially cheaper than API-based alternatives, roughly 125 times cheaper than GPT-6 Astra. Florais battle tested at scale, labeling 200,000 hours of data per day across 512 GB300s. By open-sourcing our data engine, we enable researchers to scale custom robotics datasets and explore emerging applications such as physical auto-research and human-to-robot transfer.
title: FLORA: An Open Model Suite for Scaling Robotics Data Engines

abstract: Conversational AI systems have become increasingly common in digital platforms, enabling automated interactions between users and intelligent agents.However, many existing systems lack transparency in how conversational data is collected and used to shape AI behaviour, raising significant ethical concerns around privacy, data ownership, and uninformed behavioural replication.This paper proposes a consent-driven conversational platform that enables users to create personalised AI personas using interpersonal chat data but only after all conversation participants have provided explicit approval.The platform integrates real-time communication, consent verification, and structured persona configuration to demonstrate how conversational AI can be developed responsibly while still supporting meaningful personalisation.By architecturally separating live messaging from persona configuration, the system maintains user control over conversational data and eliminates the risk of unauthorised behavioural replication.The proposed system highlights a practical, principled approach to combining real-time communication technologies with ethical AI practices and contributes a replicable consent-first methodology to the growing field of responsible AI development.
title: Consent-Driven Conversational Platform for Personalized AI Personas: Integrating Real-Time Communication with Ethical Data Practices

abstract: Purpose of the study: This study aims to analyze the relationship between teacher’s knowledge of Bloom’s Taxonomy and character education with their digital-based understanding of the Javanese philosophy Sura Dira Jayaningrat Lebur Dening Pangastuti within technology-integrated cultural education enviroments. Methodology: A quantitative correlational method was implemented using a digital Likerts-scale questionnaire administered through an online platform. Data were analysed with SPSS using validity and reliability test, Pearson product-moment correlation, and multiple regression analysis to measure relationships among Bloon’s Taxonomy knowledge, character education knowledge, and digital-based philosophical understanding. Main Findings: The study reveals significant positive correlations between teachers’ knowledge of Bloom’s Taxonomy and their digital-based understanding of Javanese philosophy. Teachers’ knowledge of Indonesian character education also shows a strong and significant relationship. Combined, both variables explain 92,8% of the variance in teacher’s ability to interpret and internalize philosophical values within technology-supportes cultural learning. Novelty/Originality of this study: This study offers a new framework linking pedagogical knowledge with digital cultural interpretation, demonstrating how technology enhances teachers’ ability to translate Bloom’s Taxonomy and character education technology by integrating local wisdom, digital media, and oedagogical theory into a coherent model for cultural preservation.
title: From Pedagogy to Digital Cultural Literacy: Examining the Correlation between Teachers’ Knowledge of Bloom’s Taxonomy, Character Education, and Digital-Based Interpretation of Javanese Philosophy

abstract: Mental illnesses are on the rise all over the world and there is a need to detect depression through digital footprints in an automated and early manner.The traditional Artificial Intelligence (AI) paradigms do not usually have context-based and user behavioral information.To overcome these shortcomings, this research paper suggested the Transformer-Based Depression Detection Network (TDD-Net) that combined textual information with user-centric behavioral metadata built on a fully primary and consented social media dataset.The data included self-written posts, captions, comments, patterns of interactions and anonymized profile data.Text cleaning, sentiment normalization and tokenization were done by using a systematic preprocessing pipeline.A RoBERTa encoder was used to learn the semantic representation of text, and a metadata embedding network was used to learn longitudinal behavioral signals, including posting frequency, intensity of engagement, and diurnal activity patterns.The linguistic and metadata vectors were fused with a fusion layer and a multi-head attention classification head was applied to predict the risk of depression.This transformer fusion, which is metadata-enhanced, boosted personalization in depression detection.An experimental assessment revealed an accuracy of 97.18, and better precision, recall, and F1-scores.These findings show that the model has high predictive accuracy, and it is used in practice in mental health monitoring.TDD-Net is a big improvement over the conventional text-only approach by making good use of extensive behavioral cues.
title: TDD-Net: A Metadata-augmented Transformer Framework for Depression Detection from Primary Social Media Data

abstract: Abstract While research increasingly links sexist attitudes to far-right support, public debates have moved well beyond women’s equality to encompass LGBTIQ+ rights. Yet studies have been slow to follow, leaving a significant gap in our understanding of attitudes toward trans, intersex, and non-binary people and how they associate with party choice, especially beyond far-right support. Drawing on original data from the German Social Cohesion Panel (2022/23), we are, to our knowledge, among the first to investigate a broader range of gender-related attitudes and find, first, that these constitute two empirically distinct dimensions, binary and non-heteronormative gender issues , that while conceptually intertwined, warrant separate examination. Second, while support for binary gender issues is widespread, non-heteronormative issues remain highly contested. Third, these dimensions relate differently to vote choice: attitudes toward binary gender issues show partisan sorting across the left-right spectrum, while attitudes toward non-heteronormative gender issues reveal a specific antagonism between the Greens and (center-)right parties. Finally, considering both dimensions together uncovers an asymmetry: voters of (center-)right parties form a cohesive conservative bloc, while supportive voters with different attitudinal profiles disperse across (center-)left parties.
title: Contested terrain: How attitudes toward gender issues relate to voting behavior

abstract: In early developmental contexts, particularly in parent-child interaction analysis, alignment involves families and professionals such as speech-language pathologists (SLPs) who interpret children's everyday interactions from different roles. When multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are introduced to support this process, alignment becomes a question of how authority, responsibility, and emotional risk are distributed across stakeholders. Through a three-part study with five families and three SLPs, we trace how MLLM-generated outputs move from expert-facing analysis to parent-facing feedback. We propose layered community alignment: grounding representations in expert-aligned structures, mediating translation through professional guardrails, and enabling family-level adaptation within those boundaries. We argue that alignment in developmental settings should be treated as a community-governed process rather than an individual optimisation problem.
title: More Than 1v1: Human-AI Alignment in Early Developmental Communities with Multimodal LLMs

abstract: Sri Lanka's civil war between the majority Sinhalese and the minority Tamil communities has now raged for nearly half a century. The Sri Lankan cum Sinhalese Buddhist state has since independence resisted all significant attempts by the Tamil political leadership at power sharing. Most constitutional lawyers and progressive Sri Lankan opinion (Sinhalese, Tamil, Muslim, Burgher, etc.) hold that short of a separate state, administrative power should be devolved in the form of a federal state, so as to give autonomy to the northeast of Sri Lanka, while the forces of Sinhalese Buddhist nationalism have sought to justify the centralized state by recourse to the history of Buddhism and the Sinhalese on the island. Such arguments have drawn on the ontological potential of the cosmic order of Sinhalese Buddhism, which is fundamentally hierarchical in intent. Here I argue that the diffused nature of this cosmic order provides the ontological grounding for a decentralized state structure that can accommodate ethnic difference in a non-hierarchical relation. Thus, the legacy of Sinhalese Buddhism can be rescued from the forces of Sinhalese Buddhist nationalism.
title: Buddhism, the Asokan Persona, and the Galactic Polity: Rethinking Sri Lanka's Constitutional Present

abstract: Diasporic communities, as geographies of national cultures abroad, are central to cultural hybridity as new cultures emerge when migrants intersect with their host communities. They have also been construed by national governments as informal trajectories for continuities of economic and diplomatic relations. This study examines the cultural intersectionality of the Yoruba and Chinese diasporic communities by situating the points of convergence for normative ethics within the Yoruba – Chinese sociocultural experiences as cross-cultural templates for diasporic spaces serving to consolidate official national partnerships. The study explores case studies from performances of the Chinese Ru tradition, founded on three basic virtues of ren, yi and li, and juxtaposes them with Yoruba ethical equivalents of ṣ’ènìyàn (humaneness), òdodo (righteousness) and ìwà-ètọ́ ̣(propriety) as prerequisites for qualifying as omo ̣ lúàbí ̣ . The study contends that these ethical codes, retained in diasporic communities through family traditions, music and theatre, are viable templates for smooth Nigeria-China relations in building the proposed community of shared future within the context of the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI).
title: Yoruba-Chinese Ethical Intersectionality: Towards a Community of Shared Future in Afro-Asian Diasporic Spaces

abstract: Conversational AI agents are commonly applied within single-user, turn-taking scenarios. The interaction mechanics of these scenarios are trivial: when the user enters a message, the AI agent produces a response. However, the interaction dynamics are more complex within group settings. How should an agent behave in these settings? We report on two experiments aimed at uncovering users' experiences of an AI agent's participation within a group, in the context of group ideation (brainstorming). In the first study, participants benefited from and preferred having the AI agent in the group, but participants disliked when the agent seemed to dominate the conversation and they desired various controls over its interactive behaviors. In the second study, we created functional controls over the agent's behavior, operable by group members, to validate their utility and probe for additional requirements. Integrating our findings across both studies, we developed a taxonomy of controls for when, what, and where a conversational AI agent in a group should respond, who can control its behavior, and how those controls are specified and implemented. Our taxonomy is intended to aid AI creators to think through important considerations in the design of mixed-initiative conversational agents.
title: Controlling AI Agent Participation in Group Conversations: A Human-Centered Approach

abstract: Abstract This chapter studies Herodotus’s reception in the literary essays of Dionysius of Halicarnassus. Dionysius defends Herodotus’s narratorial behavior, including his choice of topic, his attitude toward his characters and readers, and his “ethics of representation.” The chapter demonstrates how Dionysius attributes “writerly lives” to his predecessors, in which authorship does not simply mirror one’s nature but rather depends on an active choice (prohairesis) for fair-minded representation. It suggests ways in which Dionysius’s positive acclamation of Herodotus involves his own kinetic imitation, and consequently the transportability of Herodotus’s voice into Dionysius’s literary criticism. The Herodotean ethos emerges as self-reflexive for Dionysius in his own critical role. The adoption of a Herodotean ethical persona through “submerged imitation” grounds Dionysius’s own self-portrait as a critic.
title: The Ethics of Authorship

abstract: Transparency in AI-supported decision systems is widely required but poorly defined. Existing approaches treat transparency as a property of systems or components, producing characteristic failures: assessments that do not transfer across organizational boundaries, stakeholder questions that cannot be formulated within the available frame of analysis, and component-level findings that say nothing about system-level behavior. We propose treating transparency as a relation: a system is transparent to a stakeholder to the degree that their legitimate questions are answerable from its structure. We formalize this using information flow networks, in which transparency questions are expressed in terms of network structure and answerability is the condition that the system settles them. The framework supports three dimensions of analysis: structural answerability from the network alone, compositional answerability across organizational boundaries for deployed systems, and role-dependent answerability given a stakeholder's accessible sub-network. We demonstrate the framework on a real pre-integration assessment of an AI recruitment tool in a public sector municipality. The assessment uses participatory design and interviews to model the decision system structure. We show how structural and role-dependent transparency questions can be formally stated and analyzed across the Provider and Deployer boundary where the AI system is composed together with the deployer's decision process.
title: Transparency as Answerability: Role-Dependent Information Flow Modeling

abstract: Portfolio optimization is constrained by linear assumptions and limited integration of multi-modal information. Throughout this study, BERT serves only as a text encoder producing a scalar sentiment score from headlines; it is fine-tuned offline once and then held fixed, so its parameters are neither updated nor jointly optimized with the policy, and its scores are pre-computed static inputs. We propose a cross-modal gated Actor-Critic framework (SBCA) for multi-asset portfolio optimization, addressing two gaps in deep reinforcement learning: reliance on a single affine concatenation layer for price-text fusion, and the absence of downside-risk and turnover penalties in reward designs. SBCA learns gated cross-modal interactions and embeds both penalties in its reward. On 11 years of U.S. equity data, SBCA outperforms Equal Weight, Buy & Hold, the Dow Jones index, MVO and PPO on all metrics in the 2- and 4-asset groups, and in the 6-asset group trails only Equal Weight and MVO in absolute return. Block-bootstrap tests give exploratory, uncorrected evidence for the Actor-Critic component over gated fusion in the 2-asset group, though no component-level comparison survives correction; cost sensitivity gives descriptive evidence of robustness. SBCA thus combines offline text preprocessing with a jointly trained policy for dynamic portfolio decision-making.
title: SBCA: cross-modal gated actor-critic with frozen BERT-based sentiment features for multi-asset portfolio optimization

abstract: Sycophancy, where an LLM becomes overly agreeable, deferential, or flattering toward the user, has been identified as a major failure mode. While post-training has been implicated as a cause, how it internally gives rise to sycophantic behavior remains insufficiently understood. Post-training transforms the model's output from text completion into utterances directed toward an addressee, thereby giving the output \textit{addressivity}. We hypothesize that the accompanying pressure to follow the addressee's instructions and align with their preferences links this addressivity to sycophancy. To test this, we use Sparse Autoencoders to extract addressivity directions from pre-trained and post-trained models and examine their relationship with sycophancy. Steering models with addressivity directions can amplify or suppress sycophancy, and this effect is observed only in post-trained models. Furthermore, comparing the internal mechanisms of both model types confirms that the association between addressivity and sycophancy is strengthened through post-training. Finally, through a controlled post-training experiment, we find that models are sycophantic not toward a specific addressee but toward any recognized addressee, suggesting that the presence of an addressee, rather than the addressee's identity, is what elicits sycophancy.
title: No Matter Who You Are: Addressivity and Sycophancy in Large Language Models

abstract: Personality, a fundamental aspect of human cognition, contains a range of traits that influence behaviors, thoughts, and emotions. This paper explores the capabilities of large language models (LLMs) in reconstructing these complex cognitive attributes based only on simple descriptions containing socio-demographic and personality type information. Utilizing the HEXACO personality framework, our study examines the consistency of LLMs in recovering and predicting underlying (latent) personality dimensions from simple descriptions. Our experiments reveal a significant degree of consistency in personality reconstruction, although some inconsistencies and biases, such as a tendency to default to positive traits in the absence of explicit information, are also observed. Additionally, socio-demographic factors like age and number of children were found to influence the reconstructed personality dimensions. These findings have implications for building sophisticated agent-based simulacra using LLMs and highlight the need for further research on robust personality generation in LLMs.
title: Is persona enough for personality? Using ChatGPT to reconstruct an agent's latent personality from simple descriptions

abstract: This paper examines the Italian Constitutional Court’s recent ruling on the constitutionality of Article 8 of Law no. 40/2004 concerning the legal status of children born through medically assisted procreation (MAP) carried out abroad by same-sex female couples. The Court limited its analysis strictly to the child’s status (status filiationis), excluding broader questions such as the right to parenthood for same-sex couples or the prohibition of surrogacy. Central to the judgment is the best interest of the child, which serves as the sole criterion guiding the constitutional scrutiny. By excluding other intersecting yet distinct legal claims, the Court emphasizes the need for clear, focused evaluation of the child’s fundamental rights, especially in light of their heightened vulnerability. This methodological choice does not deny the relevance of other legal interests but underscores their irrelevance within the scope of this specific case. The judgment thus reflects a deliberate constitutional strategy to safeguard the child’s legal protection in an effective and timely manner.
title: Oltre il limbo giuridico della persona minore: Nota alla sentenza n. 68 del 2025, Corte costituzionale

abstract: The present research project has as a main goal, the universal access focused on inclusive design, in conditions of safety and comfort, facilitating the mobility of the most vulnerable groups, in this case, people with disabilities, making their environment more friendly and natural as possible, ensuring the constitutional right to equality...
title: Complejo residencial para personas con discapacidad física

abstract: L’articolo esamina il problema del diritto alla salute determinato tra la selezione eugenetica e la dignità della persona. Il diritto alla salute è reclamato sia nella procreazione medicalmente assistita, sia nell’aborto, sia nell’eutanasia. In queste tre situazioni il diritto alla salute è inteso come pubblico e come individuale. In tale scenario il diritto alla salute si ritrova in mezzo tra la volontà di selezionare eugeneticamente le persone e il dovere di rispettarne la dignità. Ma cosa è il diritto alla salute? E cosa la dignità della persona? A queste domande risponde il seguente lavoro. ---------- The article examines the issue about the right to health between the eugenetic selection and human dignity. The right to health is claimed in assisted reproductive technologies, in abortion, in euthanasia. In these three situations the right to health is understood as public and as an individual. In this perspective, the right to health is to be found in the middle between the desire to select eugenically people and the duty to respect their dignity. But what is the right to health? And what dignity? These questions answer the following work.
title: Il diritto alla salute tra selezione eugenetica e dignità della persona / Right to health between eugenetic selection and dignity of person

abstract: Providing emotional support through dialogue systems is becoming increasingly important in today’s world, as it can support both mental health and social interactions in many conversation scenarios. Previous works have shown that using persona is effective for generating empathetic and supportive responses. They have often relied on pre-provided persona rather than inferring them during conversations. However, it is not always possible to obtain a user persona before the conversation begins. To address this challenge, we propose PESS (Persona Extraction through Semantic Similarity), a novel framework that can automatically infer informative and consistent persona from dialogues. We devise completeness loss and consistency loss based on semantic similarity scores. The completeness loss encourages the model to generate missing persona information, and the consistency loss guides the model to distinguish between consistent and inconsistent persona. Our experimental results demonstrate that high-quality persona information inferred by PESS is effective in generating emotionally supportive responses.
title: Persona Extraction Through Semantic Similarity for Emotional Support Conversation Generation
