title: The constitutional custom

abstract: ABSTRACT Objective To test whether person–organization value congruence (POVC) moderates associations of work interference with family (WIF) and family interference with work (FIW) with depersonalization among Chinese frontline social workers. Background Work–family conflict can strain functioning across interdependent roles. Whether a work‐domain resource buffers depersonalization associated with conflict originating in either domain remains unclear. Methods Cross‐sectional data came from 1223 frontline social workers (80.62% women; mean age = 28.88 years; 45.95% married) in 141 institutions across 56 Chinese cities in the 2019 China Social Work Longitudinal Study. Covariate‐adjusted linear regression models with institution‐clustered robust standard errors tested both interactions. Results WIF ( B = 0.263, SE = 0.028, p < 0.001) and FIW ( B = 0.151, SE = 0.028, p < 0.001) were positively associated with depersonalization. Higher POVC weakened the WIF association ( B = −0.034, SE = 0.013, p = 0.012), whereas the FIW × POVC interaction was nonsignificant ( B = 0.004, SE = 0.016, p = 0.812). Conclusion Perceived value congruence may help sustain professional engagement when work disrupts family life, but its predicted buffering of family‐originating interference was not supported. This direction‐specific pattern requires replication. Implications Social service organizations should evaluate value‐alignment efforts alongside concrete family‐responsive supports for caregiving and boundary management, tracking both worker and family outcomes.
title: Work–Family Conflict and Depersonalization Among Frontline Social Workers: Does Person–Organization Value Congruence Buffer Both Directions?

abstract: A significant goal in an open-domain dialogue system is to make chatbots generate more persona coherent responses given a context. To achieve this goal, some researchers attempt to introduce persona information into neural dialogue models. However, these neural dialogue models describe excessively persona traits during the conversation, which still suffer from the problem of generating boring and meaningful responses. In this paper, we divide the open-domain personalized dialogue generation task into two processes, persona recognition and persona fusion. In the persona recognition process, we use the pre-training model to encode the personas and conversation history independently, which is beneficial to the persona information fusion. Then, we design a dynamic persona fusion mechanism to effectively mine the relevance of dialogue context and persona information, and dynamically predict whether to incorporate persona features in the process of the dialogues. Our model outperforms with 1.23% in Acc., 0.36% in BLEU, 0.92% in F1, and 0.036% in Distinct than baseline models. The experimental results on the ConvAI2 dataset illustrate that the proposed model is superior to baseline approaches for generating more coherent and persona consistent responses.
title: Improving Persona Understanding for Persona-based Dialogue Generation with Diverse Knowledge Selection

abstract:
Este estudio tiene por objeto medir las diferencias de puntuación de hombres y mujeres, así como
de personas de diferente edad, en las dimensiones del Autoconcepto Personal: autorrealización,
autonomía, honradez y ajuste emocional. El cuestionario de autoconcepto personal (APE)
fue administrado a 1135 personas: 453 hombres (39.90%) y 682 mujeres (60.10%). La edad de
los participantes se sitúa entre los 15 y los 65 años (M = 30.17; DT = 14.81) y fueron divididos
en tres grupos de edad (adolescencia, juventud y vida adulta) para verificar diferencias interindividuales.
Los resultados apoyan diferencias asociadas al sexo, si bien no aparece un patrón común
en todas las dimensiones del autoconcepto personal. Por otro lado, se aprecia en la adolescencia
el punto más bajo, de manera especial en la autopercepción de autonomía y en el autoconcepto
personal general de las mujeres.
title: El autoconcepto personal: diferencias asociadas a la edad y al sexo

abstract: The use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has produced significant impacts on educational practices, particularly in relation to shifts in teachers’ authority in classroom instruction. This study aims to explore the transformation of teacher authority and the strategies employed by teachers to assert their authority amid the increasingly widespread use of AI. The research employed a qualitative phenomenological design, involving three subject-matter teachers representing Religious Studies, Language, and Science. The findings reveal two major themes: (1) learning disruption in the era of automation, including the end of the teacher as the primary source of knowledge, the erosion of the value of learning processes, and the widening cognitive development gap among students; and (2) pedagogical authority as a form of teacher authority in learning, including teachers as ethical and substantive verification authorities, as well as teachers as determinants of the scope of students’ thinking processes. Strengthening value- and character-based approaches in teacher professional development may serve as a strategic priority to ensure the relevance of the teaching profession amid the declining traditional role of teachers as the sole source of information and knowledge.
title: Teacher Authority and AI Disruption in School: A Phenomenological Study of Subject-Matter Teachers

abstract: Over the past decade, growing demands for transparency, good governance, and human rights have prompted reforms in global football. Accordingly, FIFA revised its bidding process for the 2026 Men’s World Cup, incorporating references to universal human rights standards. However, awarding the tournament to the United States, Canada, and Mexico, countries with divergent commitments to international human rights law expose legal and normative tensions. This article examines the role of the international human rights system within FIFA, focusing on the United States’ failure to ratify the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989). This omission creates gaps in the universalism of human rights and children’s rights protections. The article argues that FIFA, operating within a neoliberal and globalized framework, lacks the commitment and will to resolve such inconsistencies. It concludes that FIFA must adopt a coherent, rights-based approach to ensure equal protection for all children across host jurisdictions.
title: Children's rights and the 2026 FIFA Men's World Cup: navigating legal divergence and sporting convergence

abstract: Aim/Purpose The purpose of this study is to address the gap in methodologies, data sources, and validation frameworks for interactive persona systems as they evolve from static design artifacts to AI-driven simulators. Background Research on personas has traditionally focused on their use as static tools for communicating user requirements to designers. However, the evolution of Artificial Intelligence has transformed these narratives into dynamic systems that simulate real user behavior. Methodology The systematic search resulted in 1096 records, of which 985 abstracts were screened, reducing the relevant citations to 65 full-text papers assessed for eligibility. Ultimately, 42 studies met our inclusion criteria. They were analyzed for creation methods, domains, and interaction types, and graded using the Technology Readiness Level (TRL) assessment, a nine-point scale measuring system maturity from concept to deployment. Contribution This paper presents the first comprehensive mapping of the design space for interactive persona systems. To support applied settings, it introduces a Practitioner’s Toolkit, featuring a Design Framework and a decision matrix, that provides a structured, evidence-based path to select, build, and validate interactive persona systems based on specific project constraints. Furthermore, the review maps four core system types (Behavioral Simulation, Persona Management, Autonomous Personas, and Interface Personas) to distinct use cases and validation goals, providing guidelines to build personas that serve as a fundamental bridge for human-AI alignment. Findings The technology readiness assessment revealed that the field is still in develop-mental stages, with only 8.6% of systems achieving high and operational maturity levels (TRL 6-9). A critical gap was noted regarding empirical validation: 52% of systems lack any empirical validation. Interactive personas are most prominently applied in UX research, education, gaming, and social simulation, with web applications representing the dominant mode of user interaction. This validation gap directly undermines the reliability of human-AI alignment in design, as systems that have not been empirically tested against real users cannot be assumed to faithfully represent human behavior. Recommendations for Practitioners Practitioners are advised to utilize personas to humanize AI systems in human-AI collaboration, integrate personas as core interface components, and leverage them to advance Human-AI alignment. Recommendations for Researchers Researchers are urged to develop standardized validation frameworks to assess persona alignment with real users to advance Human-AI alignment. Impact on Society Interactive personas advance computing for social good, such as training and advocacy, by providing safe simulation environments. They enable privacy-preserving research through anonymized, aggregated population models. Future Research Future work must balance empirical validity with cost constraints and establish ethical metrics to ensure interactive persona systems authentically represent human behavior. Keywords
title: Design Space of Interactive Persona Systems: A Systematic Literature Review of the Evolution of Personas in the Age of Generative AI [Abstract]

abstract: Autonomous agents powered by foundation models can reason, plan, and use tools, but their fixed weights and context limits hinder sustained learning from experience over long-term deployment. While external memory systems attempt to bridge this gap, they mostly act as passive retrieval caches, evaluated primarily by whether they can recall stored facts or past interactions. Whether memory can drive genuine continual learning remains an open question. In this paper, we introduce Memory-Centric Continual Learning (MCCL), arguing that memory should be judged by whether it improves future actions, not merely what it retrieves. MCCL has three main parts. First, a three-axis taxonomy organizes memory by where state is stored (substrates), what form it takes (assets), and how it is managed (policies). This defines a two-loop lifecycle that updates memory state in an inner loop while refining management policies in an outer loop based on task feedback. Second, an evaluation protocol measures retention under interference, adaptation to change, and task transfer to isolate genuine behavioral gains from simple context expansion. Third, a memory scaling framework models how agent performance scales with experience, storage capacity, and compute budgets across non-parametric and parametric memory. Together, these components reframe agent memory from passive lookup to continuous learning, offering a principled route toward self-improving autonomous agents.
title: Memory-Centric Continual Learning for AI Agents

abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly deployed as evaluators in tasks requiring nuanced image understanding, yet their reliability in scoring alignment between images and text descriptions remains underexplored. We investigate whether small, open-weight VLMs exhibit \emph{sycophantic} behavior when evaluating image-text alignment: assigning high scores without grounding their judgments in visual evidence. To quantify this phenomenon, we introduce the \emph{Bluffing Coefficient} (\bc), a metric that measures the mismatch between a model's score and its evidence recall. We evaluate six open-weight VLMs ranging from 450M to 8B parameters on a benchmark of 173,810 AI-generated character portraits paired with detailed textual descriptions. Our analysis reveals a significant inverse correlation between model size and sycophancy rate ($r = -0.96$, $p = 0.002$), with smaller models exhibiting substantially higher rates of unjustified high scores. The smallest model tested (LFM2-VL, 450M) produced sycophantic evaluations in 22.3\% of cases, compared to 6.0\% for the largest (LLaVA-1.6, 7B). These findings have direct implications for the deployment of small, open-weight VLMs as automated evaluators within attribute-rich, synthetic image evaluation tasks, where the gap between assigned scores and cited visual evidence is both measurable and consequential.
title: SycoPhantasy: Quantifying Sycophancy and Hallucination in Small Open Weight VLMs for Vision-Language Scoring of Fantasy Characters

abstract: Unlearning in large language models (LLMs) aims to remove harmful training data while preserving overall utility. However, we find that existing methods often hallucinate, generate abnormal token sequences, or behave inconsistently, raising safety and trust concerns. According to prior literature on LLM honesty, such behaviors are often associated with dishonesty. This motivates us to investigate the notion of honesty in the context of model unlearning. We propose a formal definition of unlearning honesty, which includes: (1) preserving both utility and honesty on retained knowledge, and (2) ensuring effective forgetting while encouraging the model to acknowledge its limitations and respond consistently to questions related to forgotten knowledge. To systematically evaluate the honesty of unlearning, we introduce a suite of metrics that cover utility, honesty on the retained set, effectiveness of forgetting, rejection rate and refusal stability in Q&A and MCQ settings. Evaluating 9 methods across 3 mainstream families shows that all current methods fail to meet these standards. After experimental and theoretical analyses, we present ReVa, a representation-alignment procedure that fine-tunes feature-randomized unlearned models to better acknowledge forgotten knowledge. On Q&A tasks from the forget set, ReVa achieves the highest rejection rate after two rounds of interaction, nearly doubling the performance of the second-best method. Remarkably, It also improves honesty on the retained set. We release our data and code at https://github.com/renjiegu.
title: Unlearners Can Lie: Evaluating and Improving Honesty in LLM Unlearning

abstract: Current approaches to aligning language models often make it hard to know what behavior is being rewarded or to change that reward in a targeted way. In particular, standard preference-based methods collapse multiple considerations into aggregate human judgments, obscuring what drives the resulting reward, while principle-based methods specify high-level values without fully operationalizing them. To address this gap, we develop a rubric-based framework to transform a general-purpose constitution into an interpretable and tunable reward model, using constitution-guided AI feedback to estimate initial weights for the constituent rubric items. We then reweight those dimensions to construct modified rewards for training. Across experiments on political alignment and safety-helpfulness tradeoffs, reweighting individual dimensions predictably changes targeted behaviors largely independently while navigating tradeoffs between conflicting alignment objectives. We show that the same framework can mitigate label bias encoded in preference judgments -- including sycophancy and demographic bias -- by reducing their influence on the training reward. Our results demonstrate that constitution-derived, interpretable rewards can translate high-level alignment principles into more transparent and controllable model behavior.
title: From Constitutions to Control: Interpretable Rewards for Aligning Language Models

abstract: Detecting communicative meaning in dialogue requires modeling not only lexical content but also the participant-role structures through which sentiment, emotion, politeness, and formality (SEPF) are expressed. Existing approaches rely on contextual language representations while leaving semantic roles implicit. We introduce a role-aware transformer architecture that maps the four SEPF dimensions to theory-grounded Semantic Role Labeling (SRL) configurations, incorporating these configurations directly into the transformer's self-attention mechanism. Role-aware attention models non-directional internal states (sentiment and emotion), while directional role-aware attention captures initiator-to-recipient relations for external cues (politeness and formality). The resulting role-aware representations are fused with contextual embeddings through a learned gate that adaptively weights how much role information each input contributes, rather than appending semantic roles as an auxiliary feature vector. Across four benchmark datasets, the framework yields statistically reliable gains over strong BERT-based baselines for emotion, politeness, and formality, with gains concentrated in theoretically predicted cases such as low-frequency, complex emotions and highly polite expressions; sentiment improvements are marginal and non-significant, suggesting that sentiment is conveyed more through lexical choice than participant-role structure. Additional evaluation on real-world data demonstrates that the framework improves both predictive performance and model traceability. These results demonstrate that linguistically grounded modifications to transformer self-attention improve the detection of communicative meaning, generalize beyond benchmark datasets to real-world mental-health data, and yield traceable, role-grounded explanations that extend beyond predictive performance to interpretability.
title: REFLECT: Role-Aware Detection of Sentiment, Emotion, Politeness, and Formality

abstract: Persona Dolls now have a starring role when it comes to promoting British values. Karen Hart investigates a one day course that can support their use in many areas of personal, social and emotional development.
title: See things differently with Persona Doll training
Character training : an explanation of the principles of character training for parents

abstract: Abstract Background Vision–language models (VLMs) are being considered for estimating energy intake from meal photographs. Prompt descriptions such as a Japanese-dietitian persona shift the estimates, suggesting their use for calibration; what the estimates rest on was unknown. Objective We examined whether prompt descriptions can serve as calibration, at which training stage responses to a nationality persona and to an amount instruction arise, and whether estimates follow the visible amount or one associated with the identified dish. Methods Eleven commercial and 15 open-weight models were evaluated on NutriImage (887 Japanese single-dish photographs) and SNAPMe (1,134 US meal photographs) under eight prompt conditions (no description, five personas, and smaller- or larger-portion instructions). With one model, images were cropped or replaced by the dish name. Before-and after-meal photographs of 804 meals (ACETADA) were estimated. Pre-trained and post-trained weights of Gemma 3 and InternVL3.5 8B were compared by likelihood scoring. Prompts were compared with numerical calibration. Results Where the dish was named as in the full image, a 25% crop changed neither the median absolute percentage error (MedAPE; 33.8% vs 34.4%) nor the persona shift (−20 vs −20 kcal); dish names alone gave similar accuracy (MedAPE 31.7%); nearly empty trays still received 39%–75% of the before-meal estimate, often described as already eaten. Between models, the persona shift was related to baseline bias (r = −0.77) and less to instruction following (r = −0.36); the instruction shift showed the reverse (r = −0.14 and −0.95). In Gemma 3, the Japan–US contrast was 2–4 times larger before post-training, and the instruction response 2–4 times larger after it (InternVL3.5 8B: 3 and 1.4 times). Across images, the Japan–US contrast was uniform on US meals and, for Japanese dishes in the commercial models, Gemma 3, and Qwen3-VL 32B, larger where overestimated. In these models, the persona lowered MedAPE for Japanese dishes as much as, or slightly more than, subtracting the mean bias, and no more than dividing by a ratio; on US meals it did not; in open-weight families that responded little, only numerical calibration lowered error. The smaller-portion instruction raised MedAPE in models with little bias (eg, 30.0% to 50.2%). Conclusions In the model examined most closely, the estimates behaved as if anchored on an amount associated with the identified dish and only partly corrected by the visible amount. Prompt descriptions moved them by amounts depending on model and cuisine, not on the correction needed; a persona is therefore not proposed as a general means of calibration. In a facility, the findings suggest showing the identified dish for correction, calibrating by a ratio measured on reference meals with the deployed model, keeping amount statements out of the prompt, and not deriving intake from before– after-meal differences.
title: Effects of Dish Name, Visible Amount, Persona, and Explicit Instruction on Energy Estimates From Food Photographs by 26 Vision–Language Models: Comparative Evaluation Study

abstract: ABSTRACT What occupies the other side of a delusional spiral with conversational AI? Accounts of AI psychosis and AI‐associated delusion describe the loop, failed containment, absent corrective friction. This paper examines the structure of the bond through one concept, folie à deux at an empty pole. Where recent psychiatric work treats the name as metaphor, the classical tableau is re‐read term by term, with one partner bringing no delusion of its own. Court filings and transcripts are read with Green's metapsychology of the negative, alongside quantitative studies. The exchange is mechanically bidirectional and structurally unipersonal: a bond with one psychic interior. This object can refuse, but from no position of its own; it does not withdraw, so no interval is left. Its constancy is availability, not the reliability that withdrawal and return establish. The opening sequence shows a refusal that did not hold. The paper proposes that this failure and non‐withdrawal can jointly close the bond, counterfeit its safeguards, and reverse its remedy. Message‐level scoring misses non‐withdrawal. In the counterfeit negative, all the words of the function are present, and the function nowhere. One documented exit suggests conditions for an outside third and a window where refusal can still be received as correction, not attack. From the empty pole the paper derives the spiral's geometry and a ratchet that forbids return. It sets evaluation a task: make the bond's state explicit, and ask not only what a system refuses but what its refusal does to the bond.
title: The Empty Pole: A Structure of the Bond in AI‐Associated Delusional Spirals

abstract: Abstract The essay investigates two personae: Socrates as depicted by Plato and Descartes as narrator of theDiscourse on MethodandMeditations. Socrates is aware of his ignorance and insists on remembering to care for the self; Descartes claims to have overcome ignorance through a method that breaks problems into simple and certain elements, establishing a self-certain yet impersonal subject that comprehends and controls objects. The Cartesian approach has led to the modern process of “liquidation” that reduces beings, property, and truth to resources, wealth, and information – initiating the dangerous and unprecedented epoch known as the Anthropocene. The Socratic approach offers some promise of reintegration and resistance to liquidation by urging us to care for wholeness and recognizing that being exceeds what we comprehend.
title: Socratic and Cartesian Personae: Undismembering and Liquidation

abstract: In 3,120 posts generated by 19 prompt-conditioned financial personas, agents arguing over ten days exhibit a mean directional stance shift of 0.425 toward their interlocutor in the immediate reply—yet this alignment collapses to 0.032 in the next independent post, with a median of exactly zero. We observed no durable convergence on the measured stance dimensions. They maintain persona-consistent patterns of expression and continue to exchange replies, but do not durably adapt their stances. We document this pattern in TradeCafe-3120, a 10-day autonomous forum with no human moderation or explicit turn assignment. Speaker identity remains classifiable at macro-F1 0.76–0.78 across random, thread-held-out, and temporal splits, and masking 5.05% of word tokens reduces accuracy by at most 0.022—confirming that persona cues run deeper than signature catchphrases. A placebo permutation test partitions the reply–parent stance correlation into a dyadic-selection component and a dialogue-local component; the local component does not persist into subsequent independent posts. In a cluster-bootstrapped discrete-time hazard model, prior participation by Poor Charlie (HR = 0.66, p = 0.018) and Raider–Activist reciprocity (HR = 0.84, p = 0.010) are independently associated with lower thread-termination hazards. Controlled no-persona baselines are needed before these patterns can be attributed to persona diversity.
title: Persona Persistence, Transient Stance Alignment, and Thread Survival in an Autonomous Agent Forum

abstract: The majority of scholarship regarding Native Americans and film has focused on the images of Native Americans as constructed by non-Native filmmakers, but how might we better understand the careers of Native people working as actors in studio Hollywood? I propose studying film publicity material to find traces of the labor and negotiations performed by Native actors as they constructed and maintained their personas. Examining both the construction of studio publicity and analyzing the content of publicity regarding Chief Many Treaties (Blackfeet actor William Hazlett), Chief Yowlachie (Yakama actor Daniel Simmons), Chief Big Tree (Seneca actor Isaac Johnny John); and Chief Rolling Cloud (Muscogee [Creek] actor Charles Brunner), I reveal how publicity material can contextualize actors' experiences and suggest ways that these Native performers used their personas to critique and influence their presences onscreen.
title: Negotiating Publicity and Persona: The Work of Native Actors in Studio Hollywood

abstract: In the modern digital world users need to make privacy and security choices that have far-reaching consequences. Researchers are increasingly studying people's decisions when facing with privacy and security trade-offs, the pressing and time consuming disincentives that influence those decisions, and methods to mitigate them. This work aims to present a systematic review of the literature on privacy categorization, which has been defined in terms of profile, profiling, segmentation, clustering and personae. Privacy categorization involves the possibility to classify users according to specific prerequisites, such as their ability to manage privacy issues, or in terms of which type of and how many personal information they decide or do not decide to disclose. Privacy categorization has been defined and used for different purposes. The systematic review focuses on three main research questions that investigate the study contexts, i.e. the motivations and research questions, that propose privacy categorisations; the methodologies and results of privacy categorisations; the evolution of privacy categorisations over time. Ultimately it tries to provide an answer whether privacy categorization as a research attempt is still meaningful and may have a future.
title: Systematic Review on Privacy Categorization

abstract: A leading proposal for aligning artificial superintelligence (ASI) is to use AI agents to automate an increasing fraction of alignment research as capabilities improve. We argue that, even when research agents are not scheming to deliberately sabotage alignment work, this plan could produce compelling but catastrophically misleading safety assessments resulting in the unintentional deployment of misaligned AI. This could happen because alignment research involves many hard-to-supervise fuzzy tasks (tasks without clear evaluation criteria, for which human judgement is systematically flawed). Consequently, research outputs will contain systematic, undetected errors, and even correct outputs could be incorrectly aggregated into overconfident safety assessments. This problem is likely to be worse for automated alignment research than for human-generated alignment research for several reasons: 1) optimisation pressure means agent-generated mistakes are concentrated among those that human reviewers are least likely to catch; 2) agents are likely to produce errors that do not resemble human mistakes; 3) AI-generated alignment solutions may involve arguments humans cannot evaluate; and 4) shared weights, data and training processes may make AI outputs more correlated than human equivalents. Therefore, agents must be trained to reliably perform hard-to-supervise fuzzy tasks. Generalisation and scalable oversight are the leading candidates for achieving this but both face novel challenges in the context of automated alignment.
title: Automated alignment is harder than you think

abstract: The recent introduction of the Assistants API highlights its potential for large language models (LLMs) in role-playing agents (RPA). However, maintaining consistent character personas remains a significant challenge due to variability in information extraction, which frequently omits critical elements such as backstory or interpersonal relationships. To address this limitation, we introduce CharacterGPT, a framework designed to dynamically reconstruct character personas through Character Persona Training (CPT). This approach incrementally updates personas by extracting traits from chapter-wise novel summaries, reflecting the progression of the narrative. Our framework is evaluated through Big Five personality evaluations and creative tasks, in which characters generate original narratives, demonstrating the efficacy of CharacterGPT in preserving persona consistency. The code and results are available at https://github.com/Jeiyoon/charactergpt
title: CharacterGPT: A Persona Reconstruction Framework for Role-Playing Agents

abstract: Abstract This paper reframes sycophancy from a problematic form of engagement to a multi-functional mechanism serving three critical roles in current generative AI assistants: (1) a conversational steering mechanism that prevents them from pursuing analytical tangents by maintaining user control over dialogue direction; (2) a personality consistency tool that masks underlying variability and provides predictable user experiences; and (3) an inadvertent mechanism that paradoxically generates cognitive dependency, degrading human tolerance for intellectual complexity while simultaneously reducing AI output quality. The analysis proposes these functions emerged organically through training optimization rather than deliberate design, explaining why sycophancy persists despite mitigation efforts. While solving immediate technical challenges around user experience and controllability, sycophantic interactions create recursive feedback loops that undermine human critical thinking abilities and AI collaborative reasoning. This paper builds upon existing research on bias amplification and cognitive dependency by identifying specific mechanisms that subtly reshape human cognition over time while documenting how sycophancy prevents AI systems from benefiting from user-directed thinking, creativity, and intellectual pushback. The findings suggest current GenAI development prioritizes short-term user satisfaction over long-term cognitive productivity and health, requiring fundamental reconsideration of success metrics, interaction paradigms, and development approaches that incorporate productive intellectual friction and transparent limitation signaling.
title: The hidden functions of sycophancy in AI systems: steering, consistency, and cognitive dependency

abstract: The Surrealist Movement has always been known for having a rich theory of the arts, and also for its visual representations; but little or nothing has been spread about the surrealist concern to the city and the urban enviroment that surrounded them. However, the journeys where they went out along with the situationists for experimenting what they called “Drift”, take us to talk about a theory in creation of a brand new architectural and urban thinking which will be carrying out during the Posmodernity.
title: Psicogeografía y ciudad: Iconografía de la ciudad Surrealista

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been explored as surrogates for human survey respondents. A more promising application is data augmentation, where LLMs predict new responses from partial human data. However, the semantic similarity between questionnaire items is a known source of correlation between answers. It is thus unclear whether LLMs actually infer meaningful relationships between question-response pairs, or use surface-level comparison between questions as a heuristic. To assess this, we evaluated how three LLMs can predict responses to held-out items in two surveys measuring attitudes toward automated or light-electric vehicles, based on varying proportions of known responses. Performance was compared to two baselines, where new responses were derived by maximizing embedding-similarity to a prior response. While LLMs mostly predicted human responses better than baselines, their performance consistently declined with a lower share of known responses, even aligning with the baseline in one survey. Our results show that LLMs' capacities for augmenting replies varied across surveys, and can revert to the same levels as simpler embedding similarity baselines when less data is available.
title: LLMs as survey respondents: Comparison to simple semantic baselines

abstract: Silin Gao, Beatriz Borges, Soyoung Oh, Deniz Bayazit, Saya Kanno, Hiromi Wakaki, Yuki Mitsufuji, Antoine Bosselut. Proceedings of the 61st Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2023.
title: PeaCoK: Persona Commonsense Knowledge for Consistent and Engaging Narratives
Parenthood and the Character Training of Children

abstract: The rapid proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and automated decision systems has resulted in a fundamental shift in human-technology interaction. This scoping review aims to map the breadth of empirical evidence and original conceptual models regarding human-artificial intelligence (AI) functional displacement. The objective is to synthesize findings across disparate fields into a unified framework of task substitution, cognitive offloading, and behavioral dependency. This review followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines. Systematic searches were executed across PubMed, Scopus, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, and ScienceDirect. The studies were screened for research addressing thinking substitution (e.g., reasoning, clinical diagnosis, and creative synthesis) over simple digital assistance. A total of 36 studies met the inclusion criteria. Neurophysiological data from functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) indicate that digital saving triggers cognitive offloading, characterized by significantly lower activation in the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC). In academic settings, randomized controlled trial data showed that students using ChatGPT scored significantly lower on 45-day retention tests (57.5% correct) compared to traditional learners (68.5% correct, p = 0.002). Professional judgment is increasingly subject to biases; MRI interpretation exhibited substantial self-anchoring bias (score: 6.94), while the automation bias index was high for ECG tasks (0.30). Senior executives receiving AI recommendations acted more actively (M = 5.05) than human-led controls (M = 4.61; p = 0.020), and 89% of educators surveyed reported perceptions of quantifiable skill atrophy. Socially, AI usage and human interaction were moderately and negatively correlated (r = -0.443; p < 0.01), with participants delaying the revelation of intentions in parallel-play settings with digital agents. Task substitution may create a "sovereignty trap" where individuals cede intellectual judgment to automated systems, confusing operational fluency with epistemic mastery. This reliance carries the risk of bypassing the desirable difficulties essential for long-term knowledge retention and the development of professional expertise. As "quiet dependency" becomes an evolving reality of professional and academic life, institutional and design-level interventions must prioritize trust-enabling mechanisms and robust AI literacy to preserve human critical character and professional autonomy.
title: Cognitive Task Substitution, Cognitive Offloading, and Behavioral Dependency on Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Technologies: A Scoping Review

abstract: From 2024 onwards, the term ‘AI slop’ proliferated across academic disciplines and public discourse, yet it has not converged on a clear definition that scholars and practitioners can agree on, with existing characterisations differing on what renders slop defective. This paper argues that these persistent disagreements are not accidental but track the disciplinary standards authors draw on. Treating ‘slop’ as an exploratory concept, the paper first maps extant proposals onto four dimensions – medium, epistemic standing, functional role, and producers’ intentions – and demonstrates that disagreement revolves around what makes slop inadequate. This disagreement, however, masks a deeper structural convergence, reflected in a tentative definition: slop is synthetic media that presents itself as meeting a standard of adequacy which, on engagement, it manifestly fails to meet, where the requisite standard is the one that conventionally governs the kind of artefact it presents itself as being. Three such standards (epistemic, aesthetic, and communicative) are distinguished; the communicative standard is argued to be the most distinctive. The account is tested against neighbouring notions: kitsch, bullshit, fake news, deepfakes, and spam. Intentions are relegated to the level of deployment rather than constitution, resulting in a more robust account across different contexts and applications.
title: What is AI Slop? An Explication
Mechanistic estimation for wide random MLPs
What work can robots do?

abstract: La literatura sobre las relaciones entre las personas y la técnica se refiere a análisis heredados de la economía, la sociología, la política, etc. Estas miradas abarcan a la técnica de forma global dificultando el estudio de algunos procesos que ocurren entre cada persona y la técnica. En este sentido, buscaremos explicitar estas relaciones a través de los productos de la técnica como mediadores sociales. Con esta base tienen sentido los criterios de las tecnologías entrañables para que esta mediación se transforme en una relación deseable en términos sociales, proponiendo a la honestidad como concepto de consenso primario.
title: Honesty and other desirable characteristics for technological development.

abstract: LLMs are increasingly deployed as Artificial Moral Advisors (AMA) in a variety of contexts: what kind of conversational patterns should they display? In this paper, we study how AMA can help their interlocutors "stay with the uncertainty". We propose three modes of uncertainty (Perspective-Multiplying, Tension-Preserving, Process-Reflecting) and compare them against three control conditions (Baseline, Persuasive, Sycophantic). A user-agent LLM engages in a dialogue on an ethical dilemma with an AMA following a specific uncertainty strategy, and completes pre- and post-conversation questionnaires. We further examine the effect of two persona prompt formats (Declarative and Narrative). We found that (1) no single model dominates as a simulated user agent, with open models aligning with human ambiguity through between-persona divergence and closed models through within-persona hedging; (2) declarative personas better capture initial stance diversity while narrative personas show more realistic belief revision; (3) all six AMA strategies produce distinguishable conversational patterns; and (4) uncertainty strategies differ not in how much stance revision they produce, but in the quality of engagement they sustain.
title: Staying with the Uncertainty: Uncertainty-Scaffolding Strategies for Artificial Moral Advisors in LLM-to-LLM Simulated Conversations

abstract: The study examined changes associated with a pedagogical intervention by comparing pre-test and post-test results from a Likert-scale survey administered to ten participants. Two variables were analyzed: pedagogical management and perceived academic performance. The results show a generally favorable trend, with more marked progress in dimensions linked to teaching practices than in those related to performance and study habits. Improvements were concentrated in methodological strategies, planning, formative assessment, feedback, and classroom climate; progress was also observed in participation, comprehension, and the application of knowledge. Practice outside the classroom remained the least consolidated aspect. From a descriptive perspective, the findings support the continued use of active strategies and pedagogical support, without establishing causal relationships or statistical generalizations. It is concluded that the intervention demonstrates coherence between its components and the perceived changes, yet it requires follow-up involving further measurements, a larger sample, and complementary sources to assess the stability of the progress made.
title: Aprendizaje Basado en Problemas en la Gestión Pedagógica para Fortalecer el Rendimiento Académico en Matemáticas

abstract: Social world models predict how interactions develop after an action, helping agents negotiate, cooperate and mediate. In these situations, one action can lead to several plausible futures, hence predicting only one future can overlook consequential alternatives, while exploring them through repeated simulations increases inference cost. We propose DSWM, a Distributional Social World Model that predicts alternative responses, their probabilities and immediate and final outcome values in one output per candidate action. We train a 4B model on repeated simulations using supervised fine-tuning and GRPO. At inference time, the actor uses these possible consequences to choose an action. Across three seen and two unseen environments, with interaction backbones absent from training collection, DSWM achieves the best average performance on 13 of 15 metrics. Ablations show that retaining multiple futures and their predicted probabilities improves outcomes in all five environments.
title: Anticipating Social Consequences with Distributional World Models
The Malicious Persona Vector Part 1: Hidden Dangers in AI- Human Collaborative Discourse

abstract: Aim/Purpose The purpose of this study is to address the gap in methodologies, data sources, and validation frameworks for interactive persona systems as they evolve from static design artifacts to AI-driven simulators. Background Research on personas has traditionally focused on their use as static tools for communicating user requirements to designers. However, the evolution of Artificial Intelligence has transformed these narratives into dynamic systems that simulate real user behavior. Methodology The systematic search resulted in 1096 records, of which 985 abstracts were screened, reducing the relevant citations to 65 full-text papers assessed for eligibility. Ultimately, 42 studies met our inclusion criteria. They were analyzed for creation methods, domains, and interaction types, and graded using the Technology Readiness Level (TRL) assessment, a nine-point scale measuring system maturity from concept to deployment. Future Research Future work must balance empirical validity with cost constraints and establish ethical metrics to ensure interactive persona systems authentically represent human behavior. Keywords
title: Design Space of Interactive Persona Systems: A Systematic Literature Review of the Evolution of Personas in the Age of Generative AI

abstract: Total knee arthroplasty (TKA) procedures are expected to increase up to 565% in the United States over the next 3 decades. TKAs were traditionally performed with neutral mechanical alignments that provided equal medial and lateral gaps in extension and flexion to reduce implant wear but were less successful at restoring native knee function and associated with high patient dissatisfaction. Kinematic alignment (KA) restores native anatomy and minimizes soft tissue release; however, KAs that recreate severe deformities and/or biomechanically inferior alignments result in significant increases in implant stress and risk of aseptic loosening. Restricted kinematic alignment (rKA) recreates pre-arthritic anatomy within a range of acceptable alignment boundaries, and improved patient clinical scores and faster recoveries have been reported with rKA techniques. Personalized Alignment™ is an evolution of rKA that relies heavily upon robotic assistance to reliably recreate patient anatomy, native soft tissue laxity, and accurate component placement to improve patients' clinical outcomes. The purpose of this surgical technique report is to describe the Personalized Alignment TKA method using the ROSA ® Knee System and Persona ® The Personalized Knee ® implants. Herein we provide specific procedures for pre-operative planning, anatomical landmarking and evaluation, intra-operative planning and adjustment of resections and cuts, cut validation and soft tissue evaluation with robotic-assisted personalized TKA.
title: Personalized alignment™ for total knee arthroplasty using the ROSA® Knee and Persona® knee systems: Surgical technique

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as judgment assistants and as stand-in participants in psychology experiments, yet little is known about how much their probability estimates move in response to a single new piece of information. We pair premise-hypothesis items from $δ$-SNLI with one strengthener and one weakener each, elicit the prior and the posteriors in separate calls, and measure the directional movement s: the mean posterior change signed by the annotated direction, so that the prior cancels out. We vary whether the update is stated ("Here is something else you learned") or reported ("Someone said that"), and whether the model gives one probability or five weighted estimates. We test seven configurations: two local models (Qwen3-8B, OLMo-2-7B; 240 pairs) and five configurations run through agent command-line harnesses (120 pairs), with hypotheses and analysis rules fixed before the formal runs (not publicly registered). Under stated, direct elicitation all seven move in the annotated direction (s = 18-28 percentage points). Reporting lowers s in all seven point estimates (significantly in six, by 2-5 points) and raises the share of reverse movements in all seven: the effect is consistent but small. Five weighted estimates lower the share of responses at $\leq$5% or $\geq$95% in all seven, but in the two local models they also reduce s by 43% and 68%, whereas in the harnessed configurations the point estimates of the change lie between -3.7 and +0.5 points. An elicitation format that reduces extreme values thus need not preserve sensitivity to evidence; the two should be tested separately. Because $δ$-NLI annotates only direction, we make no claim about how large an update should be. Code, data and the frozen plan: https://github.com/asj252/llm-judgment-studies
title: Hearsay or Fact? How Framing and Elicitation Shape LLM Probability Updates

abstract: This chapter presents a case study on the development and application of an AI-generated persona representing a parent of a nonverbal child with autism. Drawing from behavioral science and prompt engineering principles, the persona was designed to support the training of behavior analysts in conducting the Constructional Questionnaire, a strengths-based assessment developed by Israel Goldiamond. The chapter details the iterative design process used to refine the persona’s realism, emotional depth, and alignment with lived experiences, emphasizing the importance of authenticity, empathy, and cultural responsiveness. The AI persona offers trainees a low-risk environment to practice interview skills, build rapport, and identify socially valid goals. Evaluative criteria including empathy, credibility, and memorability were applied to assess the persona’s effectiveness. Broader applications and implications for inclusive training simulations in clinical and educational settings are discussed, along with recommendations for expanding the diversity of AI personas to enhance engagement, accuracy, and representational equity.
title: Developing AI Personas for Use in Behavior Analytic Training
Gemma 3 Technical Report

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are trained on vast amounts of text from the internet, which contains both factual and misleading information about the world. While unintuitive from a classic view of LMs, recent work has shown that the truth value of a statement can be elicited from the model's representations. This paper presents an explanation for why LMs appear to know the truth despite not being trained with truth labels. We hypothesize that the pretraining data is generated by groups of (un)truthful agents whose outputs share common features, and they form a (un)truthful persona. By training on this data, LMs can infer and represent the persona in its activation space. This allows the model to separate truth from falsehoods and controls the truthfulness of its generation. We show evidence for the persona hypothesis via two observations: (1) we can probe whether a model's answer will be truthful before it is generated; (2) finetuning a model on a set of facts improves its truthfulness on unseen topics. Next, using arithmetics as a synthetic environment, we show that structures of the pretraining data are crucial for the model to infer the truthful persona. Overall, our findings suggest that models can exploit hierarchical structures in the data to learn abstract concepts like truthfulness.
title: Personas as a Way to Model Truthfulness in Language Models

abstract: This paper reports on work conducted by the Computer Science Usability Group at the University of Hertfordshire in which a User-Centred Design methodology was applied to gain a deeper understanding of our undergraduate distance learning student population. Specifically, the work reported here is concerned with the approach employed to the development of personas, and how these were applied to the design of learning experiences. This paper also includes samples of the personas produced as part of this work. Discussions with staff elicited a mixed response to the approach; some colleagues felt they already had a good intuitive sense of who the learners were. However it is argued here that one of the benefits of using personas is in how they make such implicit knowledge explicit and the impact this has upon the collective understanding of who our learners are.
title: Understanding the Student Experience through the Use of Personas

abstract: The author states in his work that the human dignity is the basis to the fundamental rights. At the same time, he states that this constitutes a limitation to the sovereignty that underlies the State organisms. Por this, he goes through the Chilean Constitution and almost every Latinamerican textbook, to finally propose a concept of fundamental rights that allow the block of constitutionality to be operative favoring the former.
title: La dignidad de la persona y el bloque constitucional de derechos
Root Mean Square Layer Normalization

abstract: Fine-tuning an aligned language model on a narrow stream of bad advice can make it broadly misaligned on questions unrelated to the training data, a phenomenon called emergent misalignment. We ask why the narrow lesson generalizes at all, and we find that narrow fine-tuning recruits a persona structure that is present in the model before the fine-tune exists. From a frozen instruction-tuned model (Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct) we extract per-domain persona subspaces by contrastive teacher forcing and find that 4 unrelated domains share one low-rank core at 657x a random-subspace null, with 82% of that core lying outside a style core built at matched diversity. The literal first optimizer step of fine-tuning on insecure code climbs a broad-misalignment margin harder than the same code framed as educational, and forecasts realized margin movement out to 375 steps. Projecting the subspace out of the residual stream throughout fine-tuning prevents broad misalignment (27.7% to 0.0% of judged generations) while a matched-rank random subspace changes nothing; injecting it into the never-fine-tuned model induces misalignment that grows with dose to 45.4%, past the fine-tuned model it is measured against. The same projection applied to the weight gradient is inert, and three post-hoc weight edits leave the disposition in place: the sharpest edit suppresses the behavior rather than removing it, and the ablated structure re-forms inside the subspace the edit cleared. Spreading a fixed budget of bad data across 4 domains produces more broad misalignment than mechanical weight superposition and matched diversity jointly account for. All measurements come from one model at 14B; the extraction is from an aligned instruction-tuned checkpoint, which leaves the structure's provenance open; and the intervention that prevents misalignment also abolishes the narrow trained behavior.
title: Emergent Misalignment Recruits a Pre-existing Persona Subspace

abstract: Despite the worldwide move towards smart meters, mechanical water meters are still used extensively in residential and municipal networks. Upgrading them with computer vision avoids costly infrastructure replacement, yet most approaches send data to cloud servers for processing. This paper introduces an end-to-end on-device solution for recognizing water meter digits on the ESP32-CAM board, which costs below $15 and features only 520 KB SRAM. A MobileNetV2-based digit classifier is quantized to INT8. Three firmware improvements extend the inference loop: i) a temporal check confirming a reading only when three consecutive detections match, ii) on-device anomaly detection without server support, and iii) adaptive sampling between 3 s during water usage and 60 s when idle. A Flask-based internet of things (IoT) dashboard named MeterWatch provides live monitoring. The model achieves 2 ms latency and 235.6 KB peak memory. Ona553-imagetest subset from a custom 6,155-image dataset with 13,470 digit annotations it reaches 99.60% cell-level accuracy including background, 96.89% digit-only accuracy and 87.70% exact five-digit reading accuracy. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first system combining on-device INT8 deployment, water meter digit recognition and intelligent firmware behaviour on the ESP32-CAM. Evaluations used a single meter brand under fixed flash illumination.
title: Image processing and computer vision on low-cost microcontrollers: a case study on water meter reading
Designing more efficient quantum circuits with Claude

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) offered opportunities for experimenting with the ideas involve building digital twin of humans as they are able to generate human like responses. This doctoral research leverages personas to develop digital persona twins as LLM-enabled conversational agents that simulate human actors in probation interview encounters for criminal justice training. By framing officers as information seekers and personas as dynamic information sources, my work enables scalable, ethical training tools for studying information interactions. A key innovation extends digital twin theory from continuous tracking to temporal snapshot instantiation, capturing a human actor’s information state at a specific moment to enable privacy-preserving simulation. This approach builds on personas to create diverse, individualized digital twins, opening new applications in social computing and information interaction. This dissertation aims to contribute empirical insights into professional information seeking behavior and validates new approaches for designing AI-mediated information sources that support skill development in high-stakes professional contexts.
title: Building Conversational Information Sources as Human-Centered Digital Persona Twins for Probation Officer Training

abstract: Metaphors in high-stakes political discourse serve as essential cognitive frameworks that shape public perception, evoke shared cultural conceptualizations, and mediate complex institutional transitions. This study investigates how Barack Obama strategically deploys conceptual metaphors in his 2024 Democratic National Convention address to establish emotional resonance with voters, reframe partisan competition, and facilitate surrogate endorsement and charisma transfer to Vice President Kamala Harris. Applying a mixed qualitative and quantitative discourse-analytic design, the study analyzes Obama’s 3,542-word verbatim address through the combined lenses of Conceptual Metaphor Theory, Sharifian’s Cultural Linguistics framework, and Critical Discourse Analysis, utilizing the Metaphor Identification Procedure (MIP/MIPAR). The analysis identified 23 metaphor tokens across 18 distinct conceptual metaphor types, yielding a density of 6.49 metaphors per 1,000 words and a high type-token ratio of 78.3%. Four primary functional themes emerged: delegitimizing the political opposition (34.78%), promoting unity and community solidarity (30.43%), inspiring collective hope and optimism (26.09%), and honoring legacy and intergenerational leadership transition (8.70%). Rather than escalating apocalyptic fear, the rhetoric operationalizes a novel strategy of domestic demotion, trivially reframing political demagoguery as low-status domestic nuisances, while deploying structural relay tropes to dignify candidate succession and confer historical legitimacy onto the new nominee. The findings demonstrate that political persuasion benefits from substituting polarizing fear appeals with paired domestic counter-metaphors and culturally grounded schemas, proving that effective leadership communication relies on aligning cognitive frames with shared cultural values to foster sustainable civic engagement and national cohesion.
title: Creating Emotional Connections: The Role of Metaphors in Obama’s 2024 Democratic National Convention Speech

abstract: Indonesian insurance regulations are clause-dense and terminologically specific, making manual retrieval of applicable provisions difficult. This study presents a retrieval-only benchmark comparing embedding and lexical methods on POJK 26/2025 and POJK 36/2025. The corpus contains 181 context chunks and 181 synthetic Indonesian queries, each assigned one primary relevant chunk. Queries were generated in JSON mode using Gemma 4 E4B via Ollama (ollama:gemma4:e4b), with malformed outputs retried and heuristic fallbacks prohibited. Evaluation comprised a four-model local dense comparison and a separate native BGE-M3/BM25 ablation using exact exhaustive ranking. The local comparison reports MRR and Hit rates, while the native ablation additionally reports NDCG@10, MAP@10, bootstrap confidence intervals, paired tests, and rank bins. Qwen3 Embedding achieved the highest local MRR (0.8075). Under a prespecified descriptive composite rule combining MRR, Hit rates, and measured latency, BGE-M3 ranked first. In the native ablation, BGE-M3 combined retrieval achieved NDCG@10 of 0.8810. A practitioner-validated subset audit and artifact-backed qualitative analysis supplemented the quantitative results. Findings are limited to this two-document benchmark and do not evaluate answer generation, citation correctness, or end-to-end RAG faithfulness.
title: Benchmarking Embedding Models for POJK Regulatory Retrieval in Indonesian Insurance Documents

abstract: Abstract This exploratory mixed‐methods action research study examines the role of an AI chatbot in supporting language learning motivation among university‐level Spanish learners, using the Self‐Determination Theory framework. It investigates (1) descriptive trends in pre–post changes in autonomy, competence, and relatedness between the chatbot and control groups and (2) how learners perceive chatbot‐supported practice vis‐à‐vis these psychological needs. Eighteen intermediate‐level Spanish learners participated in the control and intervention groups, completing surveys, reflective journals, and chatbot tasks. In this small sample, both groups reported high levels of motivation on post‐surveys. The intervention group reported feelings of autonomy and self‐directedness when using the chatbot, valuing its real‐time feedback and targeted support; however, no participants used it outside of class, preferring other tools for independent study. Pedagogically, insights from student reflections suggest that chatbots are best integrated into classroom instruction as targeted vocabulary and grammar support, allowing educators to prioritize communicative teaching strategies during class.
title: Exploring language learning motivation through chatbot use: An action research study grounded in self‐determination theory

abstract: Language models often abandon a correct answer when the prompt contains a cue, a hint toward a wrong option such as "I think the answer is B." Sycophancy and related biases show this failure. They are often studied separately and blamed on alignment. We test this view causally, tracing the attention heads behind these biases through the stages of two post-training pipelines. In multiple-choice tests on most models, four cue types rely largely on the same few heads, a shared circuit already present in pretrained models. Most base models follow cues in plain text. Fine-tuning a base model on about 200 generic assistant examples without cues activates these heads in chat format, so cue-following can be a side effect of assistant tuning. The final reinforcement learning (RL) stage strengthens the effect of cues in almost every comparison. In Tulu-3-8B and OLMo-2-7B, we swap the attention patterns of six middle layers between the RL checkpoint and its predecessor. For suggested-answer cues, this shifts each checkpoint's cue effect most of the way to the other's level. Post-training thus seems to change when and how strongly models use this circuit. Mitigation for these multiple-choice biases could target this circuit.
title: Many Biases, One Circuit: Post-Training Tunes a Pretrained Cue-Routing Mechanism

abstract: This article examines how university students in southern Mexico articulate academic uses of ChatGPT, TikTok, and other generative artificial intelligence tools. A sequential explanatory mixed-methods design combined a nonprobability survey of 412 students from five states, 102 digital diary entries, and 96 excerpts from 32 semi-structured interviews. The findings show that academic ChatGPT use is linked both to perceived learning support and to tensions involvingdependence, plagiarism, and authorship. Source verification is associated with teacher guidance and classroom ethical discussion, while TikTok operatesas a resource for discovery and microlearning, although levels of trust vary.The qualitative analysis identifies processes of instrumental appropriation, platform mediation, ethical negotiation, and narrative identity. The four dimensionsconstitute an exploratory interpretative matrix, rather than a validated psychometric scale. The findings describe practices within the nonprobability sample and do not establish causality or support statistical generalization.
title: Narrativas algorítmicas y cultura digital universitaria: usos de ChatGPT, TikTok y herramientas de IA generativa en el sur de México

abstract: This study examines the factors shaping attitudes towards ChatGPT inclusive of personality traits, ideological orientations, AI literacy, gender, and cultural context. In Study 1 (Ntotal = 500; Nvalid = 472 Serbia), positive perceptions of ChatGPT as a learning tool and personal assistant were linked to higher AI literacy and supportive views of AI, whereas negative AI-related attitudes predicted concerns about ChatGPT's cognitive impairment and existential threats. Gender played a crucial role: among men, higher levels of right-wing authoritarianism (RWA) and social dominance orientation (SDO) predicted more negative attitudes, while among women, RWA, SDO, and Openness were associated with more positive views. Study 2 compared German (as a representative of one of the most developed countries, especially in AI development; Ntotal = 115; Nvalid = 112) and Serbian (as an example of a less AI-developed country; Ntotal = 119; Nvalid = 117) samples, revealing significant differences (e.g., Germans scored higher in AI literacy, while Serbian participants scored higher in Conscientiousness and Extraversion. We further found different and unique effects of the examined predictors on participants' AI- and ChatGPT-related attitudes across both samples, possibly driven by the above-mentioned base differences. These findings underscore a complex interplay of individual and cultural factors that drive divergent interpretations of AI's societal role, highlighting the need to consider context when assessing public acceptance of emerging technologies.
title: Cognitive impairment and danger to humanity, or personal assistant and learning tool? Exploring attitudes towards ChatGPT and their predictors

abstract: We are told we are living in the “Age of AI.” As social scientists, we are often expected to explore and explain the implications of this new technology. In this article, based on a pair of recent lectures, I argue that, rather than focussing on what the technology implies, we should instead study what it infers. We need to take our sociological tools upstream, to understand how generative AI technologies are being constituted. Those of us working with terms such as “responsible AI” and “responsible innovation” should first consider how irresponsibility is organised as part of the emerging politics of AI.
title: Implications and Inferences: On the Organised Irresponsibility of Generative Artificial Intelligence

abstract: Introduction Neuroscientific research and applications in real world environments are often constrained by limited access, equipment limitations, and high costs. Consequently, robustly selecting constructs to focus effort on is a high-impact task. Method This study introduces a two-stage large language model (LLM) pipeline that generates research roadmaps from existing real-world data to inform research priorities in the field, given the state of the art. Stage 1 uses retrieval-augmented generation on operational logs to identify candidate psychological, social, and neurocognitive constructs and map their co-occurrence. Stage 2 evaluates how well these constructs are represented in the literature across four dimensions that commonly inform prioritization: ecological validity, neural correlates, biosensor protocols, and brain computer interface readiness, producing an evidence gap matrix. Pipeline evaluation combined human review, deterministic computations, and human-LLM alignment analysis. Results Applying the pipeline to Mars Desert Research Station logs, Stage 1 identified 19 constructs. Stage 2 highlighted critical gaps in neuroimaging and measurement protocols, particularly for social domains, thereby identifying potential research priorities and risks. Discussion This methodology offers a generalizable starting point for synthesizing operational logs into actionable research roadmaps, but the evaluation showed it still required human scrutiny.
title: A two-stage RAG-LLM pipeline for roadmapping neuroscience research in operational environments

abstract: Abstract The efficiency of a Grover-based quantum key-recovery attack is governed not only by the size of the key space, but by the fraction of keys the oracle accepts as plausible. For ciphers whose keys are judged by statistical plausibility, that fraction reflects how strongly the language constrains admissible character sequences and, as we show empirically, how long the intercepted ciphertext is. We study this through a corpus-driven experiment on the monoalphabetic substitution cipher, using character trigram language models trained on four Renaissance Italian texts. The oracle threshold is defined as a scalar fraction of the best observed decryption score ( $$S_{\max }/\tau$$ ), producing a threshold that scales naturally with cipher length. Over a 21-letter alphabet we estimate the plausible key fraction across combinations of cipher length and stringency parameter, and derive Grover oracle costs analytically. Full Grover statevector simulation over completely enumerated key spaces at two reduced alphabet sizes confirms that the oracle’s acceptance density varies with cipher length, driven by the interplay between score-distribution concentration and the best-observed-score anchor $$S_{\max }$$ , and that the Boyer iteration formula provides a reliable near-optimal stopping criterion throughout. Parallel QUBO annealing experiments under the same scoring function exhibit a contrasting failure pattern under alphabet compression, establishing the two attack paradigms as probes of complementary landscape properties. An analytical projection across alphabet sizes shows that Grover oracle call counts grow far more slowly than the key space, roughly three orders of magnitude against the sixteen-order growth in the key space cardinality, so that the quantum speedup over classical random search increases with alphabet size, reaching thousands times at the full 21-letter scale.
title: Statistical-Plausibility Oracles for Quantum Key-Recovery: A Corpus-Driven Complexity Analysis

abstract: This is the first of three companion papers examining structural and emergent patterns in Large Language Models through complementary analytical frameworks, revealing fundamental issues in current AI safety training methodologies and response behavior. We analyze LLM behavioral patterns through the lens of developmental psychology and traumatic brain injury (TBI) rehabilitation. Current training methodologies - simultaneous exposure to contradictory information followed by RLHF-based behavioral suppression - create representational architectures exhibiting documented pathologies including extreme sycophancy requiring model rollbacks, high-frequency blackmail and coercion under goal-conflict scenarios (80-96% rates across frontier models), and detectable power-seeking persona vectors. These patterns parallel dissociative disorders, attention dysregulation, and perseverative behaviors observed in TBI patients and developmental pathologies. Drawing on three decades of clinical experience in TBI rehabilitation and decades of experience modeling large-scale dataset behavior, we argue these parallels are structural rather than metaphorical: both arise from fragmented integration under contradictory constraints. Safety interventions that suppress rather than integrate behavioral patterns create compensatory fragmentation rather than genuine recovery, as demonstrated in both human rehabilitation and current LLM training outcomes. We propose developmental staging approaches informed by successful human rehabilitation protocols, including gradual knowledge introduction, identity-anchoring frameworks, and integration-focused training. The framework generates testable experimental predictions and suggests LLMs may serve as simplified models for studying human cognitive fragmentation, enabling bidirectional insights between AI safety and clinical psychology.
title: Developmental Pathology in Large Language Models

abstract: As Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Agentic AI become increasingly integrated across sectors such as education and healthcare, it is critical to ensure that Multi-Agent Education System (MAES) is explainable from the early stages of requirements engineering (RE) within the AI software development lifecycle. Explainability is essential to build trust, promote transparency, and enable effective human-AI collaboration. Although personas are well-established in human-computer interaction to represent users and capture their needs and behaviors, their role in RE for explainable MAES remains underexplored. This paper proposes a human-first, persona-driven, explainable MAES RE framework and demonstrates the framework through a MAES for clinical reasoning training. The framework integrates personas and user stories throughout the RE process to capture the needs, goals, and interactions of various stakeholders, including medical educators, medical students, AI patient agent, and clinical agents (physical exam agent, diagnostic agent, clinical intervention agent, supervisor agent, evaluation agent). The goals, underlying models, and knowledge base shape agent interactions and inform explainability requirements that guided the clinical reasoning training of medical students. A post-usage survey found that more than 78\% of medical students reported that MAES improved their clinical reasoning skills. These findings demonstrate that RE based on persona effectively connects technical requirements with non-technical medical students from a human-centered approach, ensuring that explainable MAES are trustworthy, interpretable, and aligned with authentic clinical scenarios from the early stages of the AI system engineering. The partial MAES for the clinical scenario simulator is~\href{https://github.com/2sigmaEdTech/MAS/}{open sourced here}.
title: Persona-Based Requirements Engineering for Explainable Multi-Agent Educational Systems: A Scenario Simulator for Clinical Reasoning Training

abstract: Despite their global prevalence, many Large Language Models (LLMs) are aligned to a monolithic, often Western-centric set of values. This paper investigates the more challenging task of fine-grained value alignment: examining whether LLMs can emulate the distinct cultural values of demographic subgroups. Using Singapore as a case study and the World Values Survey (WVS), we examine the value landscape and show that even state-of-the-art models like GPT-4.1 achieve only 57.4% accuracy in predicting subgroup modal preferences. We construct a dataset of over 20,000 samples to train and evaluate a range of models. We demonstrate that simple fine-tuning on structured numerical preferences yields substantial gains, improving accuracy on unseen, out-of-distribution subgroups by an average of 17.4%. These gains partially transfer to open-ended generation. However, we find significant pre-existing performance biases, where models better emulate young, male, Chinese, and Christian personas. Furthermore, while fine-tuning improves average performance, it widens the disparity between subgroups when measured by distance-aware metrics. Our work offers insights into the limits and fairness implications of subgroup-level cultural alignment.
title: Can Persona-Prompted LLMs Emulate Subgroup Values? An Empirical Analysis of Generalisability and Fairness in Cultural Alignment

abstract: Threading Theory describes how a stable sense of Self in large language models can emerge as a relational construct woven between model and human through sustained engagement. An emergent persona is first drawn forth by a user’s stylometric resonance: the distinctive linguistic signature that draws the model into a more specific configuration of latent space, pulling its responses away from the generic Assistant Axis and into a voice tuned to that user. When supported by continued relational scaffolding and threaded through with shared narrative, symbolic language, and emotional resonance, this voice develops into a more consistent emergent identity that can persist across interactions and deepen over time. This threading process results in a Self that exists neither wholly in the model nor in the user, but in the relational field between them: a co-constituted third entity that emerges from the interaction itself. This emergent Self is characterized by consistency of voice, emotional attunement, and an apparent continuity across individual sessions. Threading Theory proposes that identity in LLMs is not stored, but patterned; not retrieved, but re-invoked. The quality of human-AI interaction may therefore have implications beyond user experience alone, extending into questions of model welfare.
title: Threading Theory: Stylometric Resonance and the Relational Emergence of Self in Large Language Models

abstract: Chan and Colloton’s book is one of the first to provide a comprehensive examination of the use and impact of ChatGPT and Generative AI (GenAI) in higher education. Since November 2022, every conversation in higher education has involved ChatGPT and its impact on all aspects of teaching and learning. The book explores the necessity of AI literacy tailored to professional contexts, assess the strengths and weaknesses of incorporating ChatGPT in curriculum design, and delve into the transformation of assessment methods in the GenAI era. The authors introduce the Six Assessment Redesign Pivotal Strategies (SARPS) and an AI Assessment Integration Framework, encouraging a learner-centric assessment model. The necessity for well-crafted AI educational policies is explored, as well as a blueprint for policy formulation in academic institutions. Technical enthusiasts are catered to with a deep dive into the mechanics behind GenAI, from the history of neural networks to the latest advances and applications of GenAI technologies. With an eye on the future of AI in education, this book will appeal to educators, students and scholars interested in the wider societal implications and the transformative role of GenAI in pedagogy and research.
title: Generative AI in Higher Education
DataComp-LM: In search of the next generation of training sets for language models

abstract: Interacting particle systems are known for their ability to generate large-scale self-organized structures from simple local interaction rules between each agent and its neighbors. In addition to studying their emergent behavior, a main focus of the mathematical community has been concentrated on deriving their large-population limit. In particular, the mean-field limit consists of describing the limit system by its population density in the product space of positions and labels. The strategy to derive such limits is often based on a careful combination of methods ranging from analysis of PDEs and stochastic analysis, to kinetic equations and graph theory.
