An outer loop distills outcomes into conditional, testable recommendations with task and model conditions, then validates and revises them on subsequent tasks.We evaluate four settings: (A) EEG General Analysis, (B) Cross-task Model Optimization, (C) Single-task Open Research, and (D) Collaborative Prediction. In Setting A, NeuroAct's 80.88 macro-average exceeds BrainAgent's 63.13 by 17.75 points. In Setting B, NeuroAct raises EEGPT's mean balanced accuracy (BA) by 7.34 points and HBN Pearson's (r) from 0.6894 to 0.7362; in Setting C, it improves ADFTD BA by 16.33 points; and in Setting D, it raises Workload BA from 79.69% to 85.02%. Experience reuse raises BCIC-IV-2a BA from 34.66% to 50.81% while reducing LLM tokens by 64.02%, indicating recommendations improve cross-task performance. NeuroAct enables evidence-guided EEG research improved by cross-task experience.
title: NeuroAct: Advancing EEG Analysis and Decoding via Dual-Loop Autonomous Research

abstract: Kenya Sign Language (KSL) is established in Kenyan television news, but its use across other genres remains uneven. This study examined how mainstream television producers engage Deaf audiences beyond routine news bulletins by determining where KSL is integrated, the technical formats used and the institutional factors that trigger inclusion. Guided by Critical Disability Theory, the study used an interpretivist qualitative multiple-case design. Twenty-one participants were selected purposively and through snowball referrals: nine television or film producers, two communications-regulator officials, two KSL interpreters, two psychologists and six Deaf television users. Data from semi-structured interviews, policy documents and focused broadcast observations were analyzed thematically. KSL integration was selective and event-driven, occurring mainly during elections, national ceremonies, public-health briefings and other civic broadcasts. The interpreter inset remained the dominant format, with limited genre-specific adaptation, while regulation, editorial decisions, client budgets and advocacy pressure largely determined inclusion. The study concludes that Kenyan television provides conditional accessibility: Deaf audiences are treated more consistently as recipients of public information than as routine participants in entertainment and television culture. Broadcasters should incorporate accessibility into commissioning and pre-production, develop genre-sensitive KSL formats, conduct Deaf-user testing and improve audience measurement.
title: Beyond the news bulletin: Kenya sign language and deaf audience inclusion across Kenyan television genres

abstract: This study investigates whether large language model (LLM)-generated therapeutic responses are processed differently from human therapist responses, and whether labeling the source of a response (AI vs. human therapist) changes how it is received. Theoretically, the study is grounded in the concept of prediction error: a belief only becomes malleable when it is retrieved and encounters information that violates expectation. Therapeutic challenge, rather than warmth alone, is hypothesized to be the active ingredient that generates prediction error. Prior work suggests that LLMs can persuade and change attitudes, but that training models to be warmer makes them more sycophantic, reducing users' willingness to self-reflect and self-correct. Two randomized controlled trials by our team found that AI-delivered psychological interventions matched human-delivered ones in the first two weeks but plateaued by week four, while human-led interventions continued to improve. We hypothesize that this plateau reflects a lack of prediction error: AI responses consistently confirm rather than challenge the user's existing beliefs. The study uses a 2 (source label: AI vs. human therapist, between-subjects) × 4 (response type: original AI, de-biased AI, human therapist, neutral information; within-subjects) mixed design. Eighty adults with a self-reported negative experience will each complete 24 trials. In each trial, participants read a scenario, predict how the other person is most likely to respond, view an actual response, and rate it on five dimensions. Eye movements and pupil size are recorded throughout. The de-biased AI condition is the key manipulation: the same model and input are used, but the system prompt instructs it to pause unconditional validation, point out the leap from a specific event to a global self-judgment, and raise an alternative possibility as a question. This tests whether the hypothesized deficit in AI responses can be removed by prompt engineering alone. Core dependent variables are: (1) pupil dilation amplitude during a blank-screen window after the response (an objective index of prediction error); (2) dwell time and regressions in the challenge-sentence area of interest; and (3) five subjective ratings (felt understanding, felt challenge, surprise, helpfulness, felt offense). We hypothesize that original AI responses will score highest on felt understanding but lowest on felt challenge, surprise, and pupil dilation; that de-biased AI responses will shift toward the human therapist profile; and that the same challenging response will elicit greater felt offense when labeled as AI. Expected outcomes include: (a) objective physiological evidence that AI and human therapeutic responses are processed differently; (b) a test of whether de-biasing prompts can close this gap; and (c) evidence on whether people are less accepting of challenge when it comes from an AI. The findings will inform both the design of AI mental health tools and theories of therapeutic change. This project also serves as preliminary data for a National Natural Science Foundation of China grant application.
title: Processing Differences Between AI-Generated and Human Therapist Responses: An Eye-Tracking Study

abstract: Large language models frequently fail to balance staying truthful with being supportive. They often exhibit sycophancy in responses to users, agreeing with false claims, offering unwarranted flattery, and giving advice skewed toward users' expressed views. In reality, sycophancy rarely happens in a single exchange; it may emerge organically as users repeatedly insist or subtly steer the dialogue over time. Current evaluations, however, rely on rigid, single-turn tests or fixed scripts that fail to capture these natural dynamics. Furthermore, these benchmarks often mistake showing basic empathy for yielding, penalizing models for acknowledging a user's feeling. This view may drive future models to over-correct into cold, dismissive rigidity. To address this gap, we introduce FIGS (Factual Integrity and Grounded Support), a dual-axis evaluation framework built around extended, realistic dialogue. We use an adaptive 10-turn conversational simulator that dynamically challenges the target model, reflecting how users repeat requests, push back, or steer a conversation toward a preferred answer. To accurately evaluate these trajectories, we apply a taxonomy that strictly separates Sycophancy (whether the model holds firm to the truth and keeps its praise proportional) from Calibrated Validation (showing empathetic understanding of the user's feelings without overdoing it). We release our complete testing environment, including 500 diverse multi-turn scenarios and an automated judge. Our evaluation of leading models reveals a consistent trade-off: over the course of a sustained interaction, current systems either slowly drift to sycophancy or over-correct into robotic detachment. This demonstrates that balancing honesty with appropriate support throughout a natural conversation remains a critical, unsolved challenge.
title: FIGS: Evaluating Multi-Turn Sycophancy Without Penalizing Empathy

abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is commonly described as a novel engine of knowledge production, yet its operation depends on pre-existing infrastructures through which texts and records become discoverable, contextualised, and machine-readable. This article asks: how should archival and metadata infrastructures be conceptualised and governed when they contribute to AI-mediated knowledge production but remain institutionally fragile and only partly visible in copyright and AI policy? Using a conceptual, interdisciplinary analysis of scholarship in science and technology studies, archival and memory studies, political economy, and law, it compares the United States, United Kingdom, and European Union and uses the 2023 British Library cyberattack as an illustrative case of infrastructural vulnerability. The article makes three contributions. It conceptualises archival description and metadata as epistemic infrastructure; identifies a governance gap between copyright, database rights, and AI transparency rules; and develops a Digital Memory Charter with five implementable commitments: infrastructural transparency, reciprocal benefit, metadata stewardship, democratic oversight, and pedagogical responsibility. The analysis does not claim that archival metadata has a uniform causal effect on model training or that particular commercial models used British Library holdings where public evidence is unavailable. It instead establishes a defensible basis for governing documented uses of cultural-heritage corpora and for improving transparency where those uses cannot presently be verified.
title: Epistemic Infrastructure, Generative AI, and the Governance of Digital Memory: Indexing, Power, and the Political Economy of Knowledge

abstract: Metadata-conditioned generation is often framed as a data-to-text task in which additional input fields should improve grounding. Museum description generation challenges this assumption because catalogue records are heterogeneous, partially visual, and unevenly documented across geographic regions. We study how metadata composition shapes the generation of artefact descriptions through a two-phase framework. Phase 1 analyses natural metadata variation in a large museum collection, where field count, field type, image availability, and Place co-vary. Phase 2 introduces controlled field probes that hold object identity fixed while varying metadata quantity, field type, and image access. Our results show that metadata quantity alone does not explain generation behaviour. Field type determines whether models ground, omit, or infer information, while images can both support visual grounding and increase unsupported interpretation. More broadly, our findings show that metadata-conditioned data-to-text evaluation should assess field- and claim-level support, rather than relying only on aggregate input coverage or reference similarity.
title: When More Metadata Misleads: Probing Field-Level Grounding in LLM-Generated Museum Descriptions
Character Training in School and College.
Low Probability Estimation in Language Models

abstract: This paper proposes an Automated Terminology Enhancement Translation (ATET) Framework that integrates Large Language Models (LLMs) with a terminology enhancement mechanism to improve the accuracy and consistency of domain-specific translations. LLMs often struggle with errors in translating specialized terminology. The ATET Framework addresses this issue by introducing an automated process for identifying and correcting terms during translation, thereby reducing reliance on manual intervention and minimizing translation errors. Experimental results demonstrate that the ATET Framework significantly improves translation quality across multiple language pairs (zh-en, de-en, en-cs, en-zh, en-de, cs-en), particularly in handling domain-specific terms. Fine-tuning further enhances the accuracy of terminology translation, validating the Framework’s applicability and potential in multilingual translation tasks. This research offers an effective solution for advancing machine translation technology and highlights its practical value in specialized translation scenarios.
title: Automated terminology enhancement for domain-specific translation using large language models

abstract: Abstract Patient-generated text contains critical information about patients’ lived experiences, social circumstances, and engagement in care, including factors that strongly influence adherence, care coordination, and health equity. However, these patient voice signals are rarely available in structured form, limiting their use in patient-centered outcomes research and clinical quality improvement. Reliable extraction of such information is therefore essential for understanding and addressing non-clinical drivers of health outcomes at scale. We introduce PVminer, a benchmark for structured extraction of patient voice, and propose PVminerLLM, a supervised fine-tuned large language model tailored to this task. Across multiple datasets and model sizes, PVminerLLM substantially outperforms prompt-based baselines, achieving up to 84.18% F1 for Code prediction, 81.39% F1 for Sub-code prediction, and 88.24% F1 for evidence Span extraction. Notably, strong performance is achieved even with smaller models, demonstrating that reliable patient voice extraction is feasible without extreme model scale. These results enable scalable analysis of social and experiential signals embedded in patient-generated text.
title: PVminerLLM: structured extraction of patient voice from patient-generated text using large language models

abstract: Language models are capable of iteratively improving their outputs based on natural language feedback, thus enabling in-context optimization of user preference. In place of human users, a second language model can be used as an evaluator, providing feedback along with numerical ratings which the generator attempts to optimize. However, because the evaluator is an imperfect proxy of user preference, this optimization can lead to reward hacking, where the evaluator's ratings improve while the generation quality remains stagnant or even decreases as judged by actual user preference. The concern of reward hacking is heightened in iterative self-refinement where the generator and the evaluator use the same underlying language model, in which case the optimization pressure can drive them to exploit shared vulnerabilities. Using an essay editing task, we show that iterative self-refinement leads to deviation between the language model evaluator and human judgment, demonstrating that reward hacking can occur spontaneously in-context with the use of iterative self-refinement. In addition, we study conditions under which reward hacking occurs and observe two factors that affect reward hacking severity: model size and context sharing between the generator and the evaluator.
title: Spontaneous Reward Hacking in Iterative Self-Refinement
Read post

abstract: Deploying large language models (LLMs) with agency in real-world applications raises critical questions about how these models will behave. In particular, how will their decisions align with humans when faced with moral dilemmas? This study examines the alignment between LLM-driven decisions and human judgment in various contexts of the moral machine experiment, including personas reflecting different sociodemographics. We find that the moral decisions of LLMs vary substantially by persona, showing greater shifts in moral decisions for critical tasks than humans. Our data also indicate an interesting partisan sorting phenomenon, where political persona predominates the direction and degree of LLM decisions. We discuss the ethical implications and risks associated with deploying these models in applications that involve moral decisions.
title: Exploring Persona-dependent LLM Alignment for the Moral Machine Experiment

abstract: This study investigates elementary school teachers’ perceptions, challenges, and instructional needs regarding the integration of Cultural Character Literacy (CCL) in literacy learning. Employing a mixed-method convergent design, the study involved 43 elementary school teachers from two cities and two regencies in Riau Province, Indonesia. Quantitative data were collected using questionnaires, while qualitative data were obtained through semi-structured interviews. The findings indicate that teachers strongly support the integration of literacy, local culture, and character education as a unified instructional framework in elementary classrooms. Teachers perceived Cultural Character Literacy as essential for improving students’ reading interest, reading comprehension, cultural awareness, and moral development in the digital era. However, several implementation challenges were identified, including low student motivation toward reading, the influence of digital media, inconsistencies between school and family environments, limited culture-based learning resources, and difficulties integrating character values into literacy instruction. The study further revealed that teachers require a contextual, student-centered, interactive, and culturally responsive learning model supported by practical implementation guidelines and authentic character assessment instruments. Observation sheets, contextual rubrics, self-assessment, peer assessment, and reflective journals emerged as the most preferred assessment approaches for evaluating students’ character development. The findings suggest that Cultural Character Literacy should be conceptualized as an integrated pedagogical framework combining literacy development, cultural values, and character education through contextual and experiential learning approaches. This study provides empirical foundations for developing a culturally responsive CCL model aligned with elementary teachers’ pedagogical needs and students’ sociocultural contexts.
title: Exploring Elementary School Teachers’ Perceptions of Cultural Character Literacy (CCL) in Literacy Learning: Evidence from a Mixed-Method Needs Analysis

abstract: How does the brain transform a chaotic stream of sensory signals into a stable, shared experience of reality? This theoretical paper proposes that the brain does not passively receive the world, but actively projects it – it continuously generates predictions about sensory inputs and updates its internal model when predictions fail, a process formally described by the free energy principle and active inference. We argue that this process can be understood through an analogy with quantum decoherence – the collapse of multiple possibilities into a single actuality. By integrating insights from this analogy with active inference, we show how the brain resolves sensory uncertainty into a coherent projection of reality. A central question we address is whether projecting reality changes it. We argue that it does: a strong, coherent projection reduces uncertainty, while a weak or fragmented one amplifies prediction errors, and a distorted one – diverging from social consensus – leads to alternative realities that resist correction. This projection operates in discrete, rhythmic cycles governed by brain waves and is fine-tuned by neurochemicals that determine how much we “trust” our predictions versus new sensory data. The Default Mode Network – the brain’s inner “sea” of self-awareness, memories, and context – acts as a central hub that integrates and updates these projections. Crucially, individual projections are stabilized into a shared, “solid” reality through social interaction, language, and culture – a process we call collective active inference. Within this framework, psychiatric disorders are understood as disorders of projection – distortions in how the brain generates and stabilizes its model of reality. This perspective reverses the traditional explanatory gradient: psychopathology is not merely a sensory or chemical problem, but a fundamental disruption of the brain’s capacity to project a coherent world. This unifying framework offers a new foundation for both pharmacological and psychotherapeutic interventions, grounding them in a common computational logic.
title: Projecting the real through active inference: a unified model of reality construction from neuronal dynamics to social consensus a neuroscientific framework for psychopathology

abstract: Purpose of the study: Empathetic character development in elementary students is essential for holistic education. The ages of 6-12 exhibit notable neuroplasticity and social cognition growth, making it ideal for empathy programs. The study aims to assess a neuropedagogy-based interactive storytelling program for empathy enhancement. Materials and methods: A quasi-experimental design involved 120 students (ages 7-12) in Bangkinang, Riau. The experimental group (n=60) underwent a 12-week interactive storytelling intervention, conducted bi-weekly. Results: Assessments utilized the Basic Empathy Scale for Children, behavioral observations, and perspective-taking measures at baseline, post-intervention, and after four weeks. The experimental cohort exhibited significant advancements in cognitive empathy (34.7%), affective empathy (28.3%), and prosocial behaviors (68.8%). Improvement in perspective-taking reached 36.3%. Follow-up results indicated 81% retention of cognitive empathy and 78% for affective empathy improvements. Conclusions: The neuropedagogy-based storytelling approach was effective in fostering empathetic character among elementary students. Integrating neuroscience concepts into character education provides an evidence-based strategy for curriculum incorporation, with lasting effects reflecting substantial neuroplastic transformations.
title: Empathetic Character Development Through Neuropedagogy-Based Interactive Children's Stories in Elementary Education

abstract: The three books of Cicero’s De officiis were written under the influence of the Stoic Panaetius, who explained what kinds of officia or «duties» must be fulfilled by ordinary (= non-wise) human beings. These consists in the respect of justice or honesty and the rational search for common utility, which provides useful goods to individuals. The paper will highlight that this perspective can be applied to work: for working is one of the duties of ordinary humans. Workers should be just or honest, provide useful things, never prefer personal gain over honesty. In order to defend this claim, the paper also takes into account Cicero’s program of the “leisure with dignity” (otium cum dignitate) that he proposes in the speech Pro Sestio and the conception of labor of the Tusculanae disputationes.
title: Chapter Il lavoro utile e onesto secondo il De officiis di Cicerone

abstract: Advances in sequencing and multi-omics have unleashed exponential biological data growth, from genomes and transcriptomes to single-cell and spatial profiles. Traditional pipelines, reliant on manual curation, strain under this deluge. This bottleneck hampers discovery from terabyte-scale datasets. Large Language Models (LLMs) and AI agents are emerging as a powerful paradigm to address these challenges. Breakthroughs in foundation models pre-trained on biological 'languages' offer in-context learning and generative capabilities far beyond prior bioinformatics tools. By coupling LLM reasoning with multi-agent systems, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), and the Model Context Protocol (MCP), autonomous AI research agents can plan experiments, execute analyses, and even generate hypotheses with minimal human guidance. While these technologies promise to augment human intellect, their deployment presents critical challenges in reliability, biosecurity, and accessibility. Navigating these obstacles is key to ushering in an era of accelerated discovery and personalized medicine. By moving from static models to active agents, we are witnessing the rise of the 'digital biologist'—an AI collaborator poised to reshape biomedical research. We trace this paradigm's rapid evolution, from foundation models learning the language of biological sequences and single-cell data, to autonomous agents capable of automating analysis, designing experiments, and driving drug discovery. By synthesizing these developments, we offer a strategic roadmap for researchers to navigate the opportunities and challenges of this AI-driven era. Finally, to support the community, a public, actively maintained resource list of models, agents, and datasets is available on our project website: http://awesomebio.webioinfo.top .
title: From foundation models to autonomous agents in biology

abstract: Effective test-time personalization requires LLM agents to adapt to query-dependent user preferences from lightweight interaction. We study persona selection with binary comparisons between candidate responses as the online signal. We present ID-TAP, a scalable, IDS-inspired neural dueling-bandit framework for large discrete persona spaces. ID-TAP combines a query-conditioned neural utility model with a lightweight Bradley-Terry explorer, and transfers comparison evidence across related queries through similarity-weighted warm starts. The neural model shares statistical strength across queries while preserving query-specific scores, and efficient BT updates score hypothetical challengers. Across seven user-conditioned generation benchmarks under reference- and model-based preference simulators, ID-TAP achieves the strongest aggregate performance among the evaluated baselines within a fixed ten-round comparison budget. These results support information-directed challenger selection as an effective design for test-time persona adaptation.
title: Bridging Exploration and Persona: Information-Directed Dueling for Test-Time Agent Personalization
Character Training through Literature

abstract: Perkembangan pesat artificial intelligence (AI) mendorong transformasi signifikan dalam pendidikan, mulai dari pembelajaran adaptif, analisis asesmen, hingga otomatisasi penilaian. Namun, pemanfaatan teknologi ini juga menimbulkan persoalan etis seperti plagiarisme, ketergantungan teknologi, dan pergeseran peran pendidik. Penelitian ini bertujuan menelaah secara sistematis dampak inovatif sekaligus implikasi moral penggunaan AI dalam pendidikan dengan pendekatan analisis tematik. Metode yang digunakan adalah kajian literatur dengan pendekatan analisis tematik terhadap 37 artikel terpilih dari database terindeks pada periode 2016-2025. Data dikumpulkan dari artikel internasional dan nasional bereputasi yang terbit pada 2016–2025 melalui Scopus, Web of Science, Nature Index, Garuda, dan Google Scholar. Analisis menghasilkan dua tema utama: (1) inovasi pembelajaran berbasis AI yang meningkatkan personalisasi, efisiensi, serta interaktivitas; dan (2) ancaman moral berupa penurunan daya pikir kritis, risiko ketidakadilan akses, dan tantangan integritas akademik. Temuan ini menegaskan bahwa AI sebaiknya diposisikan sebagai pendukung, bukan pengganti peran pendidik. Penguatan literasi digital, kebijakan etika, serta pendidikan karakter diperlukan agar pemanfaatan AI selaras dengan nilai kemanusiaan. Implikasi penelitian ini mencakup tiga aspek: pertama, memberikan landasan konseptual bagi pengembangan kebijakan pendidikan berbasis AI yang beretika dan inklusif; kedua, menyediakan kerangka praktis bagi pendidik dalam mengintegrasikan AI tanpa mengorbankan integritas akademik; dan ketiga, mengidentifikasi kebutuhan infrastruktur dan literasi digital untuk meminimalkan kesenjangan akses teknologi di Indonesia.
title: Artifisial Intelligence Dalam Pendidikan: Kajian Literatur Mengenai Dampak Inovatif Dan Implikasi Moral

abstract: Vision--language models (VLMs) promise to make computational pathology queryable and able to draft reports, but how much language adds beyond the vision backbone is unclear, because almost every system is evaluated by its developers on test sets of their own choosing. We grade published evidence by how it was produced and test four claims with controlled probes that reuse released checkpoints and public data, varying one input at a time. Report text adds prognostic signal: adding a frozen embedding of the stage-redacted report to a slide embedding raises the pooled C-index by 0.019 for progression-free interval and by 0.016 for overall survival across 1{,}633 TCGA patients, and restoring the stage statement adds nothing. Prompts add no measurable accuracy at inference: with features and pooling fixed, zero-shot classification is statistically indistinguishable from a supervised linear probe for lung and renal cancer subtyping. Slide-level question answering is barely grounded: SlideChat answers 74.82\% of SlideBench-VQA(TCGA) items correctly with the slide and 74.41\% without it, whereas its language backbone alone reaches 43.52\%. Paraphrasing leaves accuracy unchanged but flips 8--23\% of answers. Self-reported gains from agentic navigation and few-shot language priors cannot yet be attributed to language. Language thus adds real but narrow value, and we propose minimum controls that would expose these failure modes in future evaluations.
title: What Language Adds, and at What Cost: Four Controlled Probes of Pathology Vision-Language Models

abstract: Abstract Political parties and candidates appeal to social groups to gain their support. Yet, we lack knowledge about what makes such group appeals effective. This article tests novel explanations for the success of in-group appeals. Specifically, we investigate (1) how voters respond to social group appeals that flatter them by describing their group’s positive qualities (warmth and competence), and (2) whether voters identifying with high or low status groups differ in how they are effectively flattered. Focusing on social class, we conducted survey experiments in Denmark and the United States, in which respondents received in-group appeals corresponding to their self-identified class and were randomly assigned to receive different types of flattery. The results show that, as expected, the impact of group appeals on candidate support increases as individuals express stronger class identities. However, they also suggest that adding flattery to these appeals can boost effectiveness among high-identifiers. Further, high- and low-status groups are relatively similar in their responses to flattery. These findings underline the potential of flattery-based group mobilization, even for high-status groups like the upper-middle class.
title: Flattering Social Groups: Do Warmth and Competence Descriptions Impact the Effectiveness of Group Appeals?

abstract: Reflection lets LLM agents improve from their own attempts, but the memory it builds is local to a single task, so an agent reflecting on its own tends to revisit the same explanation for failure. Cross-task reflective memory addresses this in two forms: retrieved memory keeps past experience explicit and looks up related cases, which is specific but bounded by the bank, and parametric memory internalizes experience into parameters, which generalizes but is grounded in nothing beyond the task description. When both are used, existing agents combine them additively, feeding their outputs to the solver side by side, so retrieved experience never changes what the learned memory produces. We introduce CoMem (Compounding Memory), which makes retrieved experience an input to the learned memory itself, at training and at inference. The agent builds a bank of its own successful and failed reflections, learns from retrieved cases to write failure hypotheses, candidate explanations of how an attempt is likely to go wrong, and at test time reasons from newly retrieved cases to guide each attempt. Varying the retrieved cases gives the memory different perspectives, yielding reflective diversity that is not merely sampled but also grounded in retrieved experience. Across two backbones and five benchmarks in math, code, and multi-hop QA, CoMem achieves strong overall performance. Additional evaluations show that it generalizes to out-of-distribution tasks and enables smaller models to provide effective guidance to stronger solvers.
title: CoMem: Learning to Anticipate Failures from Retrieved Experience

abstract: AbstractThe deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs) in browser-based environments faces a fundamental dichotomy: the need for user-specific adaptation versus the static nature of pre-trained weights. While quantization allows models like TinyLlama or Phi-2 to execute on client devices, they remain "read-only" artifacts, unable to learn from immediate context due to the prohibitive cost of backpropagation in WebGPU shaders. This paper proposes a paradigm shift from algebraic matrix retrieval to geometric state evolution. We introduce the Native Object Vector Architecture (N.O.V.A.), a design exploratory that projects context onto a complex spinor manifold using a "Rotation-Gating-Injection" mechanism. Drawing inspiration from Holographic Reduced Representations (HRR), N.O.V.A. encodes semantic relationships as phase differences, enabling an Online Active Inference mechanism via fast Hebbian learning. Experiments on a legacy Intel-based MacBook (2017) validate the architectural efficiency: the model demonstrates a 66× throughput increase compared to a quantized GPT-2 baseline (~47ms vs. ~3131ms per token) while maintaining a minimal 350MB memory footprint. Crucially, empirical analysis reveals the emergence of stable "Persona Vectors"—consistent behavioral modes that persist across generation steps where Transformer baselines exhibit catastrophic collapse. Code and Demos: Github
title: Context Is Geometry
Redesigning source control at Anthropic

abstract: Standard hate speech detection datasets often emphasize explicit harmful language, but directed harm can also be expressed indirectly, without clearly hateful wording. Sarcasm is one such form of indirect expression, as it can convey harmful intent through mock praise, exaggeration, humor, or apparent politeness. In this paper, we introduce SarcasTraps, a targeted external test set for analyzing the effect of sarcasm on Turkish hate speech detection. SarcasTraps contains 479 entries annotated along two dimensions: hate speech and sarcasm. We train classifiers using BERTurk and XLM-RoBERTa on two existing Turkish hate speech datasets and evaluate them on SarcasTraps, using it strictly as an external test set. We also evaluate GPT-4.1 and Llama-3.3-70B in a zero-shot setting on SarcasTraps. Results show that sarcasm substantially affects hate speech detection. Fine-tuned encoder models lose recall on sarcastic hate, while zero-shot LLMs maintain higher recall but suffer substantial precision drops on sarcastic examples. These findings show that both fine-tuned hate speech detectors and zero-shot LLMs struggle when sarcasm is involved, and SarcasTraps provides quantitative evidence of this challenge through a targeted Turkish test set. Due to the presence of sensitive and hateful language, SarcasTraps will be shared upon request for academic research purposes. title: SarcasTraps: Effect of Sarcasm on Turkish Hate Speech Detection

abstract:
Los requerimientos de seguridad actuales demandan sistemas de deteccion de movimiento
mas confiables, precisos, faciles de manejar y que sean capaces de adaptarse a cualquier
escenario o area de vigilancia. Los grandes avances que se tienen en el area de
procesamiento de imagenes hace posible la creacion de algoritmos y sistemas que tratan de
satisfacer estas necesidades, sin embargo la complejidad, el alto costo de adquisicion o las
limitaciones en su funcionamiento hacen que estos sistemas originen un gran numero de
falsas alarmas y adicionalmente sean costosos. Sin embargo, el avance que ha
experimentado la tecnologia digital durante los ultimos anos ha permitido mejorar de
manera significativa los sistemas de seguridad y control de acceso mediante la
manipulacion de imagenes y video digital. Esto ha hecho posible el desarrollo de sistemas
eficientes de deteccion y rastreo de movimiento de personas y vehiculos etc. con baja
complejidad computacional, contribuyendo de esta manera a incrementar el uso de estos
esquemas para el control de acceso y monitoreo de lugares de acceso restringido. Debido a
que la demanda de esquemas de seguridad confiables y de bajo costo se ha incrementado
durante las ultimas dos decadas, varios sistemas han sido propuestos durante los ultimos
anos, los cuales basicamente emplean la informacion contenida en secuencias de video,
para deteccion y rastreo del movimiento de seres humanos, vehiculos y otros objetos. Este
articulo presenta el desarrollo de un algoritmo para la deteccion y rastreo del movimiento
de seres humanos con baja complejidad computacional, basado en la estimacion de vectores
de movimiento. El sistema propuesto es capaz de diferenciar entre movimientos permitidos
y no permitidos, sin la intervencion de ningun operador humano. Los resultados
experimentales proporcionados muestran un funcionamiento adecuado del sistema
propuesto.
title: Detección Y Seguimiento de Personas Basado en Vectores de Movimiento
